# CAMPANELLA’S
## OF THE ORDER OF PREACHERS <note>The Dominican Order, known for its intellectual tradition.</note>
## Six Books on Astrology

->IN WHICH<-
->Astrology, with all the superstition of the Arabs and Jews <note>Campanella refers here to medieval judicial astrology, which he sought to purge of "pagan" elements to make it acceptable to the Catholic Church.</note> removed, is treated physiologically <note><term>physiologically</term>: In the 17th century, this meant treating a subject according to the laws of nature and physics, rather than the modern biological definition.</note>,<-
->According to the Holy Scriptures, and the doctrine of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, and Albert <note>Albert the Great</note>, and the greatest theologians;<-
->So that they may be read with great benefit within the Church of God, without any evil suspicion.<-

<summary>The title page for Tommaso Campanella's "Six Books on Astrology," positioning the work as a scientifically grounded and religiously orthodox study of the stars. It claims to align astrological practice with the teachings of Church Fathers and the Bible, distancing it from older "superstitious" traditions.</summary>

**I**N THE PREFACE <note>original: "PRÆFATIONE"</note> it is taught that physical astrology <note>The study of how celestial bodies physically influence the Earth (such as weather, tides, and biology), which Campanella distinguishes from "judicial astrology" that often overstepped into predicting human choice.</note> must be separated from superstitious astrology: and that through the former, neither divine providence nor the power of God is overturned, nor the freedom of human choice. It is explained that it is partly a science, partly conjecture, and partly suspicion, much like medicine; and how one must proceed in it; and that the stars act in a fourfold manner upon lower things <note>The "lower" or "sublunary" world—our Earthly realm beneath the heavens.</note>; and which authors should be utilized in this study.

# SIX BOOKS
## OF ASTROLOGY.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut headpiece featuring a central grotesque mask with elaborate scrolling acanthus leaves. On the left and right sides, nude mythical figures are depicted grappling with beasts among the foliage.</image-desc>

---

*PHYSICAL ASTROLOGY* <note>original: "Astrologiam Physicam." In the Renaissance, "physical" astrology referred to the study of the stars' natural influence on the Earth and the body, as opposed to "judicial" astrology, which was often criticized for claiming to predict certain fate or human choices.</note> *is to be separated from the superstitious kind; through it, neither the providence and power of God nor the freedom of human choice is overturned. It is explained how it is partly science, partly conjecture, and partly suspicion—just like medicine—and how one must proceed within it. It also addresses how the stars act upon lower things in a fourfold manner, and which authors, or rather observers, should be utilized in its study.*

### PREFACE.

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'T' set within a square frame, featuring two figures (cherubs or putti) amidst vines and foliage.</image-desc>

THEN man most desirously perceives himself to be a participant in divinity above all things, when he is either joined to God and the heavenly beings—from which he obtains the most wonderful affections and intuitions of things above the world—or when he acquires, by whatever means, a knowledge of the future, which belongs to God alone. For this reason, all the divining sciences, however trifling <note>original: "nugaces," meaning frivolous or worthless</note>, are sought after excessively. Indeed, man embraces false praises of himself with a ready mind, and kisses the images and shadows of his beloved. This affection, if not regulated by higher reason, drags us into various and dreadful errors: so that men even treat the signs of things as if they were causes, and things more base than themselves as if they were better <note>The author is warning that people often mistake the stars (the signs) for the actual causes of events, or value material celestial bodies more than the human soul.</note>, men

<summary>This preface introduces a defense of astrology as a natural science (physical astrology), arguing that it does not conflict with religious faith or free will. The author compares the predictive nature of astrology to the practice of medicine, noting both rely on observation and conjecture.</summary>
<keywords>physical astrology, divine providence, free will, divination, natural science, philosophy of astrology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the preface. The previous page ended mid-sentence discussing why humans seek knowledge of the future. The catchword "venerentur" (they might worship) at the beginning of this page completes the thought that humans often turn to the natural world to find the divine.</meta>

->## PREFACE.<-

...they might worship. This is evident in the teachings of the **Pagans** <note>original: "Gentilium," referring to non-Christian or polytheistic cultures of antiquity</note>, who adore birds as if they were gods, as well as rivers, snakes, stones, and trees, wherever they perceive some spark of divinity. Furthermore, they even worship the passions themselves: for the Romans worshipped **paleness** and **trembling** in temples as if they were gods. It is no wonder, then, if the stars—which are the manifest causes of all changes in the lower world—are worshipped with such great honor among these nations. For through the stars, it is granted to us to know and foresee many of the effects of things.

But while it is clear that the stars do not have a "mind" or intention to cause what happens—just as fire (which is of a celestial nature) and earth do not strive to do anything other than be fire and earth—it is also true that while they struggle by a certain fate (that is, by a coincidence of causes and necessity), they harmoniously produce animals, plants, stones, liquids, and all other things that complete the universe and sustain each other through various mutual uses. From this, it becomes clear that there are more noble causes in the world which use the stars and elements for the production and transformation of things. 

Just as a blacksmith uses fire, a hammer, an anvil, a file, and other tools to create a well-crafted sword that is useful for its purpose, we find the "First Cause" in <term>Metaphysics</term> <note>the branch of philosophy concerned with the first principles of things, such as being and cause</note>, which we call God. We recognize the "secondary intelligences" <note>original: "intelligentias," referring to celestial beings or angels believed to direct the movement of the heavenly spheres</note> as the executors of His providence within the elements. To say that the physical stars are the primary causes of things is the same as if someone claimed the fire and the hammer were the cause of a sword or a hoe, rather than the mind of the smith and the skill of the craftsman. We know these same truths from the sacred oracles, and we have been taught by the First Cause in His own school how we ought to proceed in divinations. This is so that we do not err or slip gradually into **idolatry**, as the **Chaldeans**, **Egyptians**, and **Greeks** once did.

Furthermore, I saw others wrongly rejecting this science as deceptive and unworthy of the name "science"—even claiming it is subject to demons. However, it is manifest that demons cannot change the order of the universe, nor can they give the stars a different position or different powers. By that same logic, medicine would have to be rejected far sooner, for it is well known that demons can truly interfere in medicine and cause dreadful things. 

It is also evident that the four seasons of the year are created for us by the **Sun**, and within those seasons, the certain production of fruitful things occurs. Likewise, the **Moon** causes monthly and daily changes as it aligns with the Sun and the **Planets**, so much so that it compels doctors, sailors, and farmers to take account of it. (In the same way, the other planets must be thought to have their own "planetary years" and months.) Moreover, we see the forms of the constellations expressed even in small stones—such as the **Pleiades** <note>a prominent star cluster</note> mirrored in number and arrangement within the <term>sunstone</term> <note>original: "sandastro," a sparkling gemstone described by ancient naturalists as containing golden "drops" resembling stars</note>—and we see a natural sympathy in herbs...

The author uses the analogy of a blacksmith's tools to explain that while stars influence the physical world, they are secondary causes directed by a higher divine intelligence.</summary>

->## PREFACE.<-

...with the Sun and Moon, with which they turn, and with other planets: (whereby the **heliotrope** <note>a plant named for its habit of turning toward the sun</note> and the **lupine** indicate the movement of the Sun’s longitude and the hours; while the elm, willow, linden, poplar, and olive trees show the movement of latitude between the tropics by their own turning, occurring in harmony with the solar movement). There are also animals in India that change their colors according to the variations of the Moon; just as in Ireland, straps made from the skin of the **hairy seal** <note>original: "porcelli marini," literally "sea-piglet," a common term used for seals</note> raise and lower their fur according to the ebb and flow of the sea, which follows the logic of the Sun. Even the ants and bees follow a certain rhythm of the stars and the Moon, even if only through their natural impulses. The seas, meanwhile, have a daily tide from the Sun and a monthly tide from the Moon; and many springs derive certain properties from the stars. Human illnesses are likewise subject to the stars, and all changes provoke the stars as "changing causes," though these causes are hidden to us in other things, they are most well-known in the great lights of the sky. 

On the other hand, I see others so devoted to **astrology** that they subject all things, human and divine, to the stars—no differently than the **Machiavellists** <note>followers of Niccolò Machiavelli; here, the author uses the term to describe those who prioritize cold, calculated "political reason" over spiritual truth</note> do with political reason. This is what the Arabs and the ancient Pagans once did, against whom **St. Ambrose** and **St. Augustine** justly lash out in their writings. (For who would subject the craftsman to his own tools? Or a free man to a slave?) For bodies only act when moved and agitated by more noble, elective causes. I see that man is so free that he cannot be conquered by any tortures or deaths if he is unwilling. How much less, then, can he be conquered by the stars, which do not press upon him so cruelly? Furthermore, if they burn the body, they do not touch the **will**, since it is the offspring of the "primality" <note>a philosophical term referring to the fundamental, first principles of the soul</note>, as we have demonstrated in our *Metaphysics*. Therefore, it is foolish to bind either God or human freedom to fate, or to judge all things as certainties. **Solomon** says: that all science comes from the First Wisdom, and politics, physics, and logic are its handmaidens. He adds this concerning Astrology: 

*It knows things past, and conjectures the things to come; it knows the signs and wonders before they happen, and the events of times and ages.* <note>A reference to the Book of Wisdom 8:8, attributed to Solomon</note> 

(And this is true, as we shall say: partly through demonstration and partly—just like Medicine—through estimation, as they are.) For this reason, I have decided to write on **Astrology** according to the rules of physics, which can be read within the Church of God without suspicion.

For although **St. Augustine** (who, it seems, was unskilled in mathematics—for he even denies that the **Antipodes** <note>the idea that people could live on the opposite side of the globe</note> exist and errs regarding the placement of things) says that Astrology was granted more to the ancients until they recognized Christ prefigured in the stars as **Balaam** had prophesied; but after His coming, since we have been taught by the Prophets, it is not permitted to us in the same way.

...we do not for that reason immediately abandon our purpose. For that holy man <note>St. Augustine, referencing his *Confessions*</note>, although he confirms celestial influences in his book *The Confessions*, feared for the frailty of men (whence also certain Churches forbid these things as evil, and others as dangerous, as witnessed by **Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan, a 15th-century Dominican theologian</note> and **St. Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>). He believed that demons could involve themselves in this art whenever suspicion or frivolity is present, as St. Thomas declares in his book *On Lots*: namely, when we proceed in science neither from causes, nor from effects, nor from certain signs according to the Author of nature (whereby we deserve to be mocked by the demon). Or, perhaps, if someone should think the stars are Gods, as St. Ambrose warns, or that our liberty is directly subject to them; or because Augustine thought that a holy Christian man should consult God rather than the stars.

Yet, since **St. Jerome** in his prologue to the Bible enumerates **astrology** <note>In this period, "astrology" and "astronomy" were often used interchangeably to mean the study of the heavens</note> as much as **astronomy** among the useful sciences—which Solomon also does—its utility in physical matters has not ceased after the coming of Christ. For the farmer, the sailor, and the physician do not make use of oracles and miracles, but rather of physical skill. Moreover, Christ himself—not to mention **Balaam** <note>a biblical figure who prophesied the "Star of Jacob"</note>—commanded us again to observe the stars, so that we might know His future judgments. For He said: *“There will be signs in the sun, and the moon, and the stars, and the powers of the heavens shall be moved, and the stars shall fall from heaven.”* <note>original: "Nam erunt, ait, signa in sole..." citing Luke 21:25 and Matthew 24:29</note> 

Furthermore, the Apostle Paul commands us to be vigilant regarding the judgments of God and the signs given, lest the Day of the Lord catch us like a thief sleeping in the night. These signs cannot be known without a knowledge of the changes that occur in the heavens, such as the **apogees** <note>the points in an orbit farthest from the Earth</note>, the **obliquity** <note>the tilt of the Earth's axis relative to its orbit</note>, **eccentricities** <note>the degree to which an orbit deviates from a perfect circle</note>, **equinoxes**, and the like. From these, innumerable effects and continuous, extraordinary changes follow. These things are not known except to those who are watchful; therefore, I do not believe the study of astrology should be neglected. 

For from the ordinary physical movements of the heavens, we detect what is extraordinary and investigate the signs given by God; for they were not given except that we might watch. This work began wonderfully in this century with **Copernicus**, was followed better by **Tycho** <note>Tycho Brahe, the Danish astronomer known for his accurate celestial observations</note>, and pursued more deeply indeed by **Galileo**. Yet all these men, being attached to physical truths, have hardly philosophized concerning the future judgments of God through these symptoms—which is what we do in our prophetic writings. Indeed, human science without divine science is incomplete, as St. Ambrose witnesses. It does not assign causes for the sake of the primary causes, but seeks and invents principles such as man imagines—possible things, and often impossible ones.

We therefore, supported by the doctrine of St. Thomas, **Albert the Great**, and the most subtle Theologians, say that man's **free will** <term>arbitrium: the capacity for human choice and agency</term> is not directly subject to the stars, but only accidentally, insofar as the body...

<sig>A 3</sig>

...[the body] is affected by the heavens and the stars; likewise the **animal spirit** <note>In early modern medicine, "animal spirits" were believed to be subtle, thin vapors that acted as the medium between the soul and the body</note>, which is thin and bodily, and the humors themselves. Passion <note>In this context, "passion" refers to the state of being acted upon by an external force</note>, however, overflows into the soul—which is infused by God but not "confused" <note>original: *confusam*; meaning mixed or blended into the physical matter</note> with it, as **St. Ambrose** learnedly says—and the soul has the power to either pursue or reject that passion. And since man for the most part follows his sensual passions more than his free rational will, for that reason the astrologer often divines even in arbitrary actions and outcomes, as **St. Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century theologian</note> says in his *Against the Gentiles* <note>original: *Contra Gentes*</note>. There, he also believes that something is imprinted by the heavens whereby men become effective in their crafts: the physician in healing, the farmer in planting, and the soldier in conquering.

And there he even canonizes that saying of **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure to whom many ancient texts on astrology and magic were attributed</note>, which he thinks belongs to **Ptolemy**: *Mercury in the house of Saturn, being well-placed, gives an understanding of things to their very marrow.* This, he explains, happens **dispositively** <note>meaning the stars set a physical tendency or "disposition" in the body, but do not force the mind to act</note>. For the heavens act upon the soul dispositive-ly and indirectly, by affecting the humors and spirits just as they do the water and the air; an angel or a demon acts through persuasion; but God alone acts through **motion**—that is, by changing a thing physically. And in the book *On the Government of Princes* <note>original: *De regimine principum*</note>, he attributes the customs of nations to the planets in this way, and makes the **Jews** "Saturnine" <note>influenced by the cold, slow, and melancholic planet Saturn</note> along with **Macrobius** <note>a 5th-century Roman writer</note>, as **Haly** <note>Haly Abenragel, a famous 11th-century Arab astrologer</note> also teaches. Such are the words of that holy man. 

Truly, in his book *On Fate* and in his short work *On Astrological Judgments*, he resolves the argument of **St. Augustine** concerning **Jacob** and **Esau**, who were born under the same constellation yet were so different. He says that the heart—the principle of life—for Esau was in a different position relative to the horizon and the stars than was the heart of Jacob; and so, there was a better disposition in the one than in the other. But we shall note many twins of the same fate further below. Nevertheless, a man is able to follow the disposition of the law of God rather than that of the elements. For we see that, for the sake of God, those prone to lust do not indulge in it; it is not that they are not affected, but rather that they are not conquered. But if someone is so conquered that he becomes delirious, he is free from blame, because then the soul is unable to use its own duty and instruments.

Concerning divine things, we say that this science does not proceed except from a sign given by God, the author of nature, as **St. Leo** <note>Pope Leo the Great</note> says. In the elements themselves, he says, we receive the signification of the divine will as if in public pages. Therefore, when the **Magi** <note>the "Wise Men" from the Biblical Nativity story</note> saw the star of Christ, **St. Augustine** says: the Magian was struck with wonder, the Astrologer looked on; they thought it was fate, but it was a sign. 

Yet nothing prevents there being contributing causes. For example, when God wishes to make a most excellent Religious man, He can use the stars and the elements to properly temper the body for the reception of the soul, and thereby create animal spirits that are thin and pure. From this temperament and organization of the body, we reason about morals through a **physiognomic** <term>physiognomy: the practice of judging a person's character or fate from their physical features</term> syllogism. Yet this is not true in all cases, as **Cardano** <note>Girolamo Cardano, a controversial 16th-century polymath who famously cast a horoscope for Jesus Christ</note> does, who [concerning] the man Christ...

...[dispositio]nis of God <note>The text begins mid-word: "dispositionis," referring to the divine arrangement or temperament</note> is not at all subject to the heavens, since it is established that the harmony of the heavens was not then so great as to construct such a body as was fitting for the God-man <note>Christ</note>, but that it was fashioned by the Holy Spirit far better than by the stars; and the effects of the stars in Christ were modified, not only by a fated concurrence of superior and inferior causes, but also immediately by the most universal first cause <note>God</note>. Moreover, in the sect of Muhammad, **Haly** <note>Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer</note> philosophizes well concerning the character of **Muhammad** <note>original: *Macometus*</note> and his sect based on the great constellation in Scorpio, though not entirely: for we know there is no malice in the stars; yet there is a manner of receiving in the elements which can be depraved, but a manner of using in the soul infused by God which can become good from depraved. Indeed, we see that the same storm sent from heaven provokes some sailors to prayers and others to blasphemies, according to how each was previously disposed. A constellation always effects something, but according to the nature of the one receiving and using it.

There are also some who are well-born and some who are ill-born from the heavens themselves, as **St. Thomas** very acutely notes in the *third book of Against the Gentiles*; these people, by their own temperament and the new influences of the heavens, are instigated in their senses to desire and pursue what is harmful to them. And the mind is then simultaneously incited to choosing evil or good—something which I myself have experienced a thousand times. And **Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan, a prominent 16th-century theologian</note>, in his commentary on the *Secunda Secundae* <note>the second part of the second part of Aquinas's *Summa Theologiae*</note> in the treatise on religion and superstition, considers this wonderfully; he thinks that for this reason astrologers are able to judge and foreknow matters of free choice <note>original: *arbitrariis*</note>, although not entirely infallibly. For just as the heavens act upon water and air, so they act upon the humors and upon the **animal spirit** <note>the subtle fluid then believed to transmit sensory information to the mind</note>, to which the mind is united.

Therefore, the whole of **Astrology** either proceeds from causes that are always necessary—such as the fact that when the Sun enters **Aries**, spring begins, even if it is mistaken by some degrees or moments of time regarding the exact point of entry, and even if an unforeseen variety very often occurs through anomalies (but the same happens in other sciences); or it proceeds from causes that are contingent for the most part, such as that in spring all trees bloom and it grows warm; or from causes that are sometimes contingent, such as that in this year the air grows cold in spring because **Saturn** is found in the first degree of **Aries** (for this rarely occurring event can be prevented in its effect); similarly, that this herb produces more flowers then because it is "Saturnine" <note>governed by or associated with the planet Saturn</note>; or it proceeds from causes by accident and indirectly, such as that a man whose **Moon** is in the fourth Oriental house <note>a specific placement in an astrological birth chart</note> should take a wife in his youth (for taking a wife is an act of free choice, nor is it subject to the Moon in such a position, except accidentally and by way of disposition, as **St. Thomas** said). Sometimes the astrologer...

->## PREFACE. 7<-

[The astrologer] proceeds from effects, just as one investigates the ruling power of a star from the color of a comet. Similarly, he reasons about the powers of the planets from the rainbow and other atmospheric impressions. Or, he proceeds from a sign, either one given by God—as in the star of **Balaam** <note>A reference to the prophecy in Numbers 24:17: "A star shall come out of Jacob"</note> and in the signs given to us in the Sun, Moon, and stars concerning the second coming of **Christ**—or one given by nature, such as when we consider the nature of stars from their color. Or, he reasons from one effect which the stars produce in trees to the knowledge of another to be manifested in our own bodies, proceeding by way of a similarity. For this is what it means to proceed by way of a sign, as we have stated in the *Topics* <note>original: *topicis*; a reference to Aristotle's work on logic and dialectical reasoning</note>. Indeed, the astrologer most often divines in this way. For if an eclipse happens at the **zenith** <term>zenith: the highest point in the sky directly above an observer</term>, he considers it to have significance over kings and illustrious matters; if at the rising, over new things, children, and sprouts; if in the western angle, over the elderly and ancient things. All the signs of the heavens seem to behave in this way. For if a constellation occurs in the "watery" signs <note>Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces</note>, it indicates influence over waters and things living in water. It is clear, however, that the heaven is not water, nor is that shape in the sky actually water, but it is so called from its effect, with which it has a symbolic link—not the thing itself, as it seemed to **Plotinus** <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher who argued that stars are signs, not causes</note>, but the power proceeding from it, modified in such a way as it reaches us that it accords with the nature of water.

Furthermore, those men who handed down to us such sympathies, antipathies, and the names of the stars in relation to lower things must have been divine, or taught by God, as **Plato** advises; and **Philo** and **Josephus** <note>Philo of Alexandria and Flavius Josephus, Jewish historians who sought to link Greek wisdom to biblical patriarchs</note> relate that such a wonderful **Astrology** was brought by **Abraham** into Egypt. It is consistent to believe that Abraham learned it from **Noah**, Noah from the fathers all the way back to **Adam**, and Adam from God. The Greeks—most foolish and always children <note>A common Renaissance trope, originally from Plato's *Timaeus*, suggesting Greek culture was young and derivative compared to the Ancient Near East</note>—adapted the images of the heavens to their own most recent heroes, even though it is established from the monuments of the **Chaldeans** that the Ship <note>The constellation Argo Navis</note> was marked in the heavens countless years before the **Argonauts**. Likewise, **Arcturus**, **Orion**, and the **Pleiades**, and other images were mentioned by **Moses** in the history of **Job**, who preceded the Greeks by a long time. A sign, therefore, is a teaching cause, not a physical cause, as has been said elsewhere.

This science proceeds sometimes *demonstratively*, such as the fact that when the **Dog Star** <term>Canicula: the star Sirius, associated with the "dog days" of summer</term> is rising, if **Mars** stands witness, there will be a dire heat. For it demonstrates this rightly from causes, though usually common ones. Sometimes it proceeds *probably*, such as the prediction that a birth will be twins if it occurs while the sign of **Gemini** is at the **horoscope** <term>horoscope: here referring to the Ascendant, or the sign rising on the eastern horizon</term> along with two planets; for it is possible that this might not happen. Sometimes it proceeds *conjecturally*, such as the prediction that **Peter** will be enriched when the **Part of Fortune** <term>Part of Fortune: a specific mathematical point in a birth chart used to predict prosperity</term> arrives by direction at the body of **Jupiter**; for this is neither necessary, nor perhaps even probable. To enrich...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on why astrology is not a simple deterministic science, explaining that human life is influenced by many factors beyond just the stars. It addresses the theological tensions between scripture and celestial study.</meta>

->### PREFACE. 8<-

...for in the case of a human being, it is not only a heavenly cause that converges, but also human freedom, one's homeland, the law, customs, business dealings, the death of ancestors, the piety of benefactors, the ministry of Angels, and many other causes of fate. For this reason, a true science cannot be formed from a single cause known to the astrologer. However, when an effect is singular—such as rain—and it has only one or two natural causes, we then reason with probability if we consider both. This is why in Lombardy <note>A region in Northern Italy</note> the same constellation produces terrible hailstorms in the summer, which in Calabria <note>A region in Southern Italy</note> would produce heat, or barely a tempering of the warmth; for in the former, the earth is soft and marshy, while in the latter, it is dry and arid. Therefore, it is necessary for the astrologer to know both the active and passive causes beforehand, as well as what effects they usually produce. Thus, a constellation operates differently in one family than in another, let alone in a different region. Who does not know that Jupiter, when rising, produces the whitest children in Germany, but in Ethiopia, black ones? Likewise, does it not affect the family of the **Fabii** <note>A prominent patrician family of ancient Rome</note> differently than the **Lentuli** <note>Another famous Roman family branch</note>? He who does not proceed from causes, effects, or natural signs treats astrology superstitiously, and sometimes a demon mingles with his fantasies, just as happens to a superstitious doctor according to **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, who often critiqued the vanity of the arts while acknowledging natural order</note>.

Note here what I had omitted: that Saint **Isaiah** insults the Chaldean Astrologers because they presumed to divine the future from the computation of the stars; and **Jeremiah** says, "Do not fear the signs of the heavens" <note>original: "A signis cœli nolite metuere"; Jeremiah 10:2</note>. For this reason, **Pico** <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, famous for his "Disputations against Divinatory Astrology"</note> and others condemn Astrology, though not quite correctly. Is not human prudence also condemned by **Job**? And in the Prophets, does God not reprove "the wisdom of the wise"? Yet, prudence is not therefore vain; rather, it is a divine and most useful thing. Therefore, it should be understood that the Prophets condemn an Astrology that is opposed to Theology and which is proud over the Prophets, but not an "ordered" astrology such as ours. In the same way, God condemns the "prudence of the flesh" and **Machiavellian** <term>Machiavellian: referring to political strategies that prioritize power and survival over divine law or morality</term> prudence, which sets itself above the law of God, but He does not condemn human prudence that is subject to the divine. Anyone who reads Isaiah well will find this to be the case. Furthermore, Jeremiah rightly teaches that good men should not fear the heavens, for they cling to God, the author of the heavens. One who is a friend of the King does not fear the King's servants.

Moreover, not only do the Prophets teach—against the Astrologers—that God can change the courses and powers of the stars (as seen in the history of **Hezekiah** <note>In 2 Kings 20, the shadow on the sundial moved backward as a sign</note> and **Joshua** <note>In Joshua 10, the sun stood still</note>), but so too do the present symptoms of the sky. We see this in the obliquity, eccentricity, and the irregular anticipation of the **cardinal points** <term>cardinal points: here referring to the equinoxes and solstices</term> which move at God's nod, as we have proven in our prophetic writings, where it is said: "the powers of the heavens shall be moved." We discuss these matters elsewhere. You will see the arguments of Pico resolved here and there throughout this work.

<meta>This page continues the technical and philosophical defense of astrology, moving from the general complexity of human fate to the specific physical mechanisms—heat, light, motion, and aspect—through which celestial bodies influence the terrestrial world.</meta>

-># PREFACE. 9<-

### The fourfold way celestial bodies act upon
### lower things.

The stars act upon lower things through **heat**, **light**, **motion**, and **aspect** <note>The angular relationship between planets as seen from Earth</note>. St. Augustine adds "inspiration" <note>original: afflatum; referring to a celestial breath or subtle influence</note>, while St. Thomas Aquinas adds "the efficacy of aptitude" <note>referring to the inherent readiness or suitability of a material to be influenced</note>. They act through **heat** as the primary cause; through **light** as the outward "face" of that same cause, providing the occasion for many effects by manifesting objects to the senses; through **motion** as the delivery mechanism of that cause to affect things; and through **aspect** in a modifying way.

For in different positions, the stars act differently upon the same thing; just as the **Sun** provides more heat at the **zenith** <note>the highest point in the sky directly overhead</note>, less in the morning, and a moderate amount in the evening. At every single point, the action, the reception of that action, and the resulting impression already placed within the object vary. The same applies to stars configured in relation to one another.

It has been proven in physics that heat is the active cause of secondary beings. It was likewise shown in that same field that no cold comes from the stars; rather, a lesser degree of heat is regarded as cold. This is not the case when it is added to something even cooler (for then it increases the heat), but when it is added to matter in which there is already greater heat. For example, lukewarm water poured into boiling water reduces the intensity of the heat by spreading that heat over a greater amount of matter. Alternatively, a gentle softening agent provides an outlet for a powerful hardening force that has trapped itself. This is evident in inflammations cured by lukewarm water rather than cold water, which actually increases the inflammation through **antiperistasis** <note>A term in natural philosophy referring to the intensification of a quality when surrounded by its opposite, such as heat concentrating when surrounded by cold</note>.

In this way, the stars cause cooling, or perhaps by opening the pores so that external cold may enter. **Light**, however, is the "face" of heat, and the stars also act upon our vision through their heat mixed with other qualities, and likewise through their light. There is a light in the air at night that is unknown to us, but not to hares. Therefore, some people incorrectly argue that the **Medicean** <note>The four largest moons of Jupiter, discovered by Galileo</note> and **Saturnian** planets <note>Likely referring to the rings or newly discovered moons of Saturn</note> do not act upon other things simply because they do not affect our eyes.

**Motion**, however, does not create heat, as **Aristotle** foolishly believes, since motion is rather an effect of heat. Neither do the approach and retreat of the stars, insofar as they are motions, cause generation and decay; rather, they do so because they carry the **Luminaries** <note>The Sun and the Moon</note>, the true causes, to different positions of changeable matter. Insofar as the motion of a star pushes the air, that force hardly reaches us; it is the heat that moves into the lower realms.

Finally, **aspect** varies and modifies the powers of heat, making them either beneficial or harmful to the things the stars loom over—though differently for different things. From this position arises such a great association that a **magnet** always turns toward the pole of the earth, the **heliotrope** <note>A plant that turns toward the sun, such as a sunflower or turnsole</note> toward the Sun, and a corpse floats with its face turned toward heaven, just as it was positioned in the womb. Likewise, little iron rods floating on cork turn themselves toward that position which by craft...

<meta>This page continues the physical and philosophical justification for astrology. -># PREFACE. 10<-

...[the blow] they received from the striking blacksmith. For if artificial objects maintain their specific **position** and are, in a sense, sustained by it, this is even more true for natural things. Therefore, observing positions is not a superstition, as many think, but a rational teaching. 

Thus, **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose "Tetrabiblos" was the standard textbook for astrology</note> learnedly observes the **aspects** <note>The angular relationships between planets</note> of the stars, the relationship of various regions to those stars, and the original configurations of particular things that mirror the heavens. For example, he shows how an **eclipse** <note>original: eclipsis</note> indicates different outcomes when it occurs in the eastern **angle** <note>the Ascendant or eastern horizon of a chart</note> compared to when it occurs in the western angle. We shall, therefore, construct our reasonings from these principles. 

And since within heat and light—modified in this way—there exist the power, the sense, and the "love" <note>an interpretive term for the attraction or affinity between celestial and terrestrial qualities</note> to be modified, it follows that beyond the manifest physical forces, there must also be the **metaphysical** forces already mentioned within things affected by the heavens. This allows different things to be affected in different ways, and to possess different wisdoms and powers. These aspects are modified by the necessity and harmony of **fate**. This is the **hidden influence** <note>original: influxus latens</note> from the heavens, which consists of more than just heat and light, as discussed in the *Metaphysics* <note>Referring to the author's other philosophical writings</note>.

We follow **Ptolemy**, who compiled all the decrees of the **Chaldeans**, **Egyptians**, **Indians**, **Greeks**, and **Latins** produced through the observations of so many centuries. This system of thought proceeds from what has been observed. I would be a fool if I wished to speak of new things while omitting the old, especially since I have examined **birth charts** <note>original: geneses; the configuration of the stars at the moment of birth</note> for barely ten years. Therefore, we shall add to his words our own reasons, strength, corrections, and whatever is missing for the perfection of this science. As for the rest, we shall present what has been correctly stated as it stands, usurping no one else's glory. For all the astrologers of all times, from the beginning of the world until our own day, are not sufficient to complete the whole of Astrology correctly. Thus, we add a portion to this collective labor that is neither light nor small.

## BOOK ONE.

->*That the causes and beginnings of the changes in lower things*<-
->*must be derived from the variety of the planets,*<-
->*the fixed stars, and the lower things themselves.*<-

### CHAPTER I.

1 Unless the active or passive causes were varied, the effects and transformations would not vary, but would always remain the same.
2 If the causes were to vary in a circular motion, the effects would also vary in a circular motion.
3 Things that endure for a long time are produced by causes—or by a conjunction of causes—that are great and rare. Things that last for a short time arise from causes that are variable, or from a swift and frequent conjunction.
4 The stars are the causes of variety in lower things <note>the terrestrial world</note>, either because they themselves move, or the earth moves, or both <note>This reflects the author’s awareness of both the traditional Ptolemaic geocentric model and the emerging Pythagorean/Copernican heliocentric model</note>.
5 Variations in the heavens arise from motion and **station** <term>station: the point where a planet appears to stop in the sky before changing direction</term>; likewise from the longitude of motion and its latitude, and from elevation, depression, velocity, and slowness. Whichever star possesses more of these **passions** <note>original: passionum; here meaning physical properties, states, or ways of being affected</note> affects lower things more powerfully or more variably.
6 Those stars which persevere in the same position and motion for the longest time are called **fixed**, and they are thought—at least for the sake of teaching—to be in the same region. They are considered immovable by the **Pythagoreans** <note>who believed the Earth's rotation caused the appearance of the stars' movement</note> and moved by the **Ptolemaic** followers. Those which continually change their position and motion are called **wandering stars**, or **planets**, which to us through

4 The Sun is like a Leader, King, and Father. The Moon is like a Queen, Mother, and Nurse. Jupiter is like a Governor <note>original: "Gubernator"; implies a pilot or steersman of a ship</note>. ### *Concerning the Nature of the Planets Individually.*

### ARTICLE II.

1 The Sun is clearly very hot and very moist, because it is very thin and melts and thins all things. Indeed, fluidity and thinness are forms of moisture. However, it is considered moderately hot and moderately dry by Astrologers; for they do not judge things as they are in their own essence, but as they affect the lower things of Earth. The heat and moisture of the Sun relate universally to all lower things, but they are modified by the other planets, and it is this modification that the astrologer considers. And because heat is increased by Mars, Mars is thought to be hotter than the Sun, because it heats with an extraordinary heat alongside the Sun. The Sun's ordinary heat, however, appears gentle—that is, suited to the ordinary temperament of things. Similarly, the Sun accidentally dries out moist parts by raising them <note>through evaporation</note>, and it is considered moderately dry even more so than Mars; for the Sun only dries things moderately once they are formed, whereas with Mars, it dries immoderately. Therefore, the Sun is ordinarily considered hot and dry.

2 The Moon is moist and cold to Astrologers because it possesses a gentle heat and light, which draws out thick vapors and thins the waters and makes them swell <note>a reference to the tides and the "swelling" of moisture in plants and animals</note>, but does not refine them. To us, however, it seems that moisture is the proper quality of water and thick vapors. Where there is thinness and water vapor, external cold is easily introduced; therefore the Moon also appears cold. But yet, in its first quarter it is considered cold and moist, in the second hot and dry, in the third hot and moist, and in the fourth cold and dry, just like the four quarters of the year and the day. But we shall speak differently on this below.

3 Saturn is called cold and dry because it is most distant from us; its gentle heat, when mixed with the heat of the Sun, creates a sensation of cold, and a certain hardness and rawness in the earth and in the things to which it is applied. The <note>original: "Ptolemaici"</note> Ptolemaics—followers of the ancient astronomer Ptolemy—are not correct in claiming Saturn is cold simply because it is far from the Sun. After all, the <term>Canicula</term> <note>the Dog Star, Sirius</note> is even further away, yet it is hot. Rather, Saturn must be called cold for the reasons stated above. Nor does its meager heat compress vapors, as some claim, but it fails to raise them. I also believe that a certain disposition—which exists in the senses, in power, and in love (the elements that constitute heat)—descends from Saturn in such a way that its things are slow, sluggish, and hard, just as its motions are characterized by a lack of vigor. I believe such a modification of the Sun's influence is what we call "Saturnine."

4 Jupiter is called moderately hot and moist: because it raises vapors along with the Sun and moistens them, and when its rays are mixed with the Sun, it produces things that are succulent and beautiful in a climate suitable for us. For while Jupiter is harmful to snakes, it is beneficial to us, just as Saturn is beneficial to them <note>The author refers to the ancient idea that creatures of a "cold" nature like serpents thrive under cold planets like Saturn, while human life thrives under the "temperate" Jupiter</note>.

5 Mars is called hot and dry, not because it is closest to the Sun—as Ptolemy thinks, since Venus is actually closer—but because it is of a dense, red mass, and in its mixture with the Sun, it overheats excessively and dries up vapors as it raises them. The Sun does all these things on its own, but it acts one way with Mars and another way with Saturn.

6 Venus is hot, but more moist; not because it is near the Earth or the Sun, but because its physical mass is such that, when imbued with light in its particular position relative to them, it produces such effects.

7 Mercury is considered <term>anceps</term> <note>original: "anceps" meaning "two-headed" or "ambiguous"; in astrology, it means a planet that takes on the nature of whatever it is associated with</note>: for it takes on the qualities of the stars with which it is joined by body or by ray. When closer to the Sun as a morning star, it dries and heats; conversely, when closer to the Moon at its <term>perigee</term> <note>the point in an orbit where a planet is closest to the Earth</note>, it takes on those lunar qualities.

1 All planets are "happy" or fortunate within themselves, but some favor us while others harm us—just as a gentle fire is useful, but a great fire is destructive.

Conversely, they are "Misfortunes" to serpents, to things hostile to us, and to barbaric nations that have abandoned humanity. ...harmful in its temperament. Similarly, it is harmful to the animals that serve us, and to our crops and wealth; for external goods are adapted to internal ones. Mars is called the <term>lesser misfortune</term> <note>original: "infortuna minor"; in astrology, a planet that causes trouble or disruption, though less severely than Saturn</note>, because its heat and dryness harm us and our affairs due to its hostile imbalance, and consequently affect our external well-being.

3 The Sun is considered to have a dual nature: since it is a universal cause, its power helps or hinders depending on how it is modified by specific planets. In a good position, it performs acts of magnificent generosity. It appears cold when with Saturn for the reasons already mentioned, and hot when with Mars, even though the Sun itself provides all things to all beings.

4 The Moon also appears <term>malefic</term> <note>harmful or ill-intentioned</note> when joined with other malefic planets, yet it is always moist and gently warm. For this reason, it is worse when paired with Saturn than with Mars.

5 Mercury is of a versatile nature; it increases the powers and decrees of others. It is good when with the good, and wicked when with the bad; this depends especially on how it is positioned in relation to the Sun.

## *On the Daytime and Nighttime Nature of the Planets.*

### ARTICLE IV.

1 Saturn and Jupiter are called <term>diurnal</term> <note>from the Latin "diurnus," meaning belonging to the day</note>, because they harmonize with the Sun. Saturn's malice is moderated by the light of day, while Jupiter's benevolence is cheered by it. Therefore, Saturn is worse at night than during the day. By its own nature, then, it is nocturnal, but for our purposes, it is diurnal.

2 Venus and Mars imitate the condition of the nocturnal <term>Luminary</term> <note>The Moon, the primary light of the night</note>. Venus is nocturnal because she abounds in moisture and is like a "lesser Moon"—for just as the Moon waxes and wanes, so does Venus, as is clearly seen through the <term>telescope</term> <note>original: "Telescopium"; this reference indicates the text was written after the early 17th-century invention of the telescope and the discovery of the phases of Venus</note>. Mars is nocturnal so that its heat and malice may be tempered by the night. Therefore, Mars is diurnal in itself, but nocturnal for us.

3 Mercury is dual: for in its morning rising, until it reaches its <term>upper apsis</term> <note>the highest point in its orbit</note>, it is diurnal; in its evening rising until its <term>perigee</term> <note>the point where it is closest to the Earth</note>, it is nocturnal.

And although Venus is hotter than Saturn, she is nevertheless not masculine, because she does not perfect the good she begins, just as Saturn perfects the evil he starts.

Planets also become masculine when they are morning stars, in the East, or in the <term>angles</term> <note>the most powerful points of an astrological chart: the Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli</note>; just as they become feminine when they are evening stars, in the West, or <term>falling</term> <note>original: "cadentes," referring to houses of the zodiac that are considered weaker</note>. This is because they are granted weaker powers over their effects, so that we may rightly equate masculinity with efficacy.

### *On the Friendship and Enmity of the Planets.*
## ARTICLE VI.

1 There are perfect friendships between all those who agree in qualities, such as Venus and Jupiter. 2. Those who agree in fortune and misfortune. 3. Those who agree in their timing. 4. Those who agree in gender. Conversely, those who disagree in the aforementioned things are enemies. Mercury, however, adapts himself to everyone.

2 By reason of their <term>houses</term> <note>the zodiac signs where a planet is said to "rule" or feel most at home</note>, some are more or less hostile. For Mercury is an enemy to Jupiter, Saturn to the <term>Luminaries</term> <note>the Sun and the Moon</note>, and Mars to Venus, as we shall see below. And the aspect of enemies is called the <term>opening of the gates</term> <note>original: "apertio portarum"; a significant alignment that triggers major physical or meteorological events</note> for great effects, as will be shown.

---

Planets are therefore said to "ascend" once they have passed the perigee until they reach the apogee through half a circle, which is 180 degrees; conversely, they "descend" from the apogee to the perigee.

2 The better Astrologers believe that the planets are purer, more fortunate, and better when in apogee, because they are closer to the most noble starry heaven; but in perigee they are stronger, because being nearer they act more upon us. Yet, they are considered less fortunate there, because they are more "impure." Indeed, I think this happens because they stir up more vapors, and their strong and powerful action disrupts the <term>temperament</term> <note>the healthy balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities</note>. Nevertheless, nothing prevents them from being even more fortunate when another cause or contributing cause preserves our temperament.

3 The Moon, however, does not have its <term>apogee</term> and <term>perigee</term> <note>the furthest and closest points to Earth in an orbit</note> in fixed parts of the sky. Instead, it is always found in apogee during its <term>conjunction</term> <note>new moon</note> and its <term>opposition</term> <note>full moon</note> with the Sun. Yet in its <term>quadratures</term> <note>the quarter moons, when the Moon is 90 degrees from the Sun</note>, it is in perigee, because it is raised up directly by the light of the Sun, as we have taught elsewhere. Nor is it at its worst when in perigee; rather, it is better and purer, and indeed more robust, even if it is less bright. However, it can be equally bright in the perigee of its <term>epicycle</term> <note>a smaller circle that a planet follows, while that circle itself moves along a larger one</note>, as we shall discuss. The reason is that the Moon has a shared nature with the Earth, of which it seems to be a handmaid; perhaps this is because the Moon itself receives reflected light back from the Earth, as *Galileo* observes <note>Referring to Galileo Galilei's observation of "earthshine" or the "ashen light," where the dark part of the moon is faintly lit by sunlight reflecting off the Earth</note>.

4 The other reason is that the planets have a different elevation and depression relative to the Sun, which the followers of Ptolemy describe as occurring in an <term>epicycle</term>, just as they called the previous type the <term>eccentric</term> <note>an orbital path where the Earth is not exactly at the center</note>; they speak *theoretically, not in reality* <note>original: "doctrinaliter non realiter"</note>. For when the <term>superior planets</term> <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> are joined to the Sun, they are elevated to their highest point from us, because the Sun is the center of their love, saturating them with more abundant light; at that time, they are said to be in the apogee of the epicycle. However, when they are in opposition to the Sun, they are lowered and move at their swiftest, so much so that they seem to surpass the fixed stars in their forward progress. Ptolemy calls this *retrogradation* <note>the appearance of a planet moving backward in the sky</note>, but we call it *velocity*, because they are describing a narrower circle which is more easily traversed.

5 But Venus and Mercury ascend to the <term>apsis</term> <note>the highest or lowest point of an orbit</note> of the epicycle when they appear as morning stars, and in truth they orbit above the Sun. When they begin to lag behind the Sun, they descend from the great circumference of their circle to the lower apsis beneath the Sun. For they are neither strictly above the Sun, as *Timaeus* and *Aristotle* thought, nor strictly below, as *Ptolemy* believed: rather, they circle around the Sun. However, because of their narrow orbit, they do not move away from it, but seem to walk with it and surround it.

6 Since the Moon's epicycle is unstable, it is discerned from tables and <term>ephemerides</term> <note>daily charts of planetary positions</note>. Always remember, however, that epicycles and eccentrics are *theoretical* constructs, not *real* physical things. The planets move by their own power, and by the light of the Sun and their affinity for higher things, these phenomena occur as we have said elsewhere.

7 They are called *Direct* when they move in the sequence of the zodiac signs but slower than the fixed stars. They are *Retrograde* when they move against the sequence of signs and faster than the fixed stars, because they are closer to the Earth and traverse a smaller circle. They are *Stationary* when they move at the same speed as the fixed stars; this happens to them before and after retrogradation, when they are in the middle lengths of their epicycle. They are called *slow* when their motion is less than their average, and *fast* when it is greater. Now, we say this regarding their motion following the sequence of the signs, because astrologers [say] this is the

### CHAPTER IV. ARTICLE I.

1 After having spoken of the nature of the Planets regarding us, and of the conditions arising from their accidental motion, the order of our work requires that we discuss the parts of the sky in which the <term>decrees</term> <note>astrological influences or fates</note> are carried out by the Planets and the fixed stars, leading to the change of things within our system.

2 It must be presupposed from Astronomy that the whole heaven is divided in the middle by a very large circle which we call the <term>equinoctial</term> <note>original: "æquinoctialem"; the celestial equator</note>. From this, two circles called <term>tropics</term> are distant to the South and North, so named because the Planets, according to our senses, run out as far as those circles and no further, but return, always describing new <term>parallels</term> <note>latitudinal paths</note> by moving obliquely. At this time, these circles are distant from the equator by almost 23 degrees and 28 minutes, and they are always incessantly narrowing <note>The author is noting the gradual decrease in the "obliquity of the ecliptic," a phenomenon where the tilt of the Earth's axis (and thus the sun's path) appears to change slightly over centuries</note>, because the Sun does not travel as far from the equinoctial every year, but returns before it completes its full excursion. However, the motion of the Sun...

The oblique path among these spheres forms the circle we call the **Zodiac**, whose poles are marked as being as many degrees distant from the poles of the world as the tropics are from the equator. The circles in which the poles of the Zodiac are located are called one the **Arctic** and the other the **Antarctic**; similarly, the poles of the equator are called the **Arctic**, which is known to us, and the **Antarctic**, which is hidden. It is clear, therefore, that these circles are required by nature itself and by the motion of the **Planets** <term>Planeta</term>.

3 Every circle is divided, for the purpose of teaching—and perhaps in reality—into 360 degrees, because they imitate the cycles of the **Sun**, which makes the same number of rotations. In its falling behind the fixed stars, the Sun appears to shift obliquely by one degree in each rotation. And although there are nearly 365 rotations, nevertheless, so that a system of teaching can be established and the number can be easily divided and taught, it seemed best to the mathematicians <note>original: "Arithmeticis"; literally "Arithmeticians," but here referring to those who calculate celestial movements</note> to divide circles into 360 parts, which we call **degrees**. Furthermore, every degree is divided into 60 **first minutes** or <term>scrupula</term> <note>scruples; a traditional term for small divisions of time or space</note>, every minute into 60 **seconds**, every second into 60 **thirds**, and so on for the rest until you reach a measure as small as a **grain of barley** <note>original: "grani hordeacei"; a metaphor for the smallest tangible unit of measurement</note>, which is very well known to us. But for one who does not wish to fail in their learning, this division proceeds into infinity.

4 In its motion of longitude from east to west, the Sun creates a **day** composed of darkness and light in 24 hours; in its latitudinal motion, which covers the whole Zodiac, it creates a **year**.

5 Because the **Moon** is joined to the Sun twelve times while the Sun completes its annual circle, they have divided the Zodiac into **twelve signs**. They have marked these with the names of animals and of lower things with which they share a symbolic nature <note>original: "symbolum"; a correspondence or shared physical quality between the stars and earthly objects</note>, so that we might know which things any Planet favors or harms in which part of the Zodiac, as nature dictates this rather than mere theory. Moreover, each individual Sign is divided into 30 **degrees**, because the Moon completes its course in the Zodiac and is joined to the Sun again in 30 days. And although some hours may be lacking, teaching dictates that there be 30 parts, just as was said regarding the motion of the Sun. From twelve times 30, the result is 360.

6 They have divided the whole heaven into 48 **images** <note>original: "imagines"; the constellations</note>, so that the number, order, and powers of the stars can be noted. Twelve of these fall within the Zodiac, the width of which is 12 degrees. The names and symbols of the aforementioned images are shown in the following table.

| ♉ Taurus (The Bull) | ♌ Leo (The Lion) | ♏ Scorpio (The Scorpion) | ♒ Aquarius (The Water-Bearer) |

namely: the **Little Bear** <note>Ursa Minor</note>, the **Dragon** <note>Draco</note>, the **Herdsman** <note>Bootes</note>, the **Great Bear** <note>Ursa Major</note>, **Cepheus**, the **Gnosian Crown** <note>original: "Corona Gnosia"; now commonly known as Corona Borealis or the Northern Crown</note>, **Hercules**, the **Lyre** <note>Lyra</note>, the **Swan** <note>Cygnus</note>, **Cassiopeia**, **Perseus**, the **Charioteer** <note>Auriga</note>, the **Serpent-Bearer** <note>Serpentarius, also known as Ophiuchus</note>, the **Eagle** <note>Aquila</note>, the **Serpent** <note>Serpens</note>, the **Arrow** <note>original: "Telum"; commonly Sagitta</note>, the **Dolphin** <note>Delphinus</note>, **Pegasus**, the **Little Horse** <note>original: "Equisectio"; literally "the section of a horse," known as Equuleus</note>, **Andromeda**, and the **Triangle** <note>Triangulum</note>. In the southern region, fifteen are placed, because the astronomers of our part of the world were not able to see that part of the sky until now, following the voyages of the **Portuguese** to the **Indies**. These are **Orion**, **Procyon**, **Sirius**, the **Hare** <note>Lepus</note>, the **Ship** <note>original: "Navis"; the great constellation Argo Navis, now divided into smaller parts</note>, the **Water Snake** <note>Hydra</note>, the **Raven** <note>Corvus</note>, the **Centaur** <note>Centaurus</note>, the **Wild Beast** <note>original: "Fera"; modern Lupus</note>, the **Censer** <note>original: "Thuribulum"; modern Ara</note>, the **Southern Fish** <note>Piscis Meridionalis</note>, the **Whale** <note>Cetus</note>, the **River** <note>Eridanus</note>, and the **Southern Crown** <note>Corona Australis</note>; to which I add the **Cross-Bearer** <note>original: "Cruciferum"; the Southern Cross</note> at the antarctic pole, predicted in some manner—I know not how—by the poet **Dante**, and now seen and so named by our people, because the stars of this image are arranged in the shape of a **Cross**. Others can also be designated if someone knows how to note the properties of the stars from their color, magnitude, and experience, as the ancients did.

8 All the aforementioned stars are noted by the places in which they exist; either by **longitude**, as in the order of the Zodiac from east to west; or by **latitude**, as in the departure outside the **ecliptic line** which intersects the Zodiac in longitude; or by **declination**, which is the distance from the **equinoctial** <note>the celestial equator</note>. It is necessary for the **Astrologer** to know these things beforehand from **Astronomy**.

9 You shall seek the powers of the images and the number of stars from Astronomy, where it is also necessary to learn the symbols and myths by which we philosophize about these images. For they were marked in this way either so that they might be held in memory, or so that we might recognize the qualities poured out into lower effects through their imagination. Hence **Plotinus** and **Ptolemy**—receiving traditions from the **Egyptians** and **Chaldeans**, who could not have investigated such images and properties without **God** as their guide—teach that the **Ship** signifies the seas and marine matters, the **Censer** signifies sacred things, the **Serpent** signifies harmful beasts, and so on for the rest; whatever the **Greeks** may babble, usurping the glory of others, as we proved by the testimony of **Job**.

...however, they do not wander more than 4 degrees beyond the tropics of the **Zodiac** <note>The "tropics" here refer to the northern and southern limits of the zodiacal belt</note>, and within that space, they undergo their influences and pour out their effects into the lower realms: especially the **Sun**, whom the others emulate: so that just as he cuts the path of the world, so they cut and traverse the path of the **Sun**. Therefore, it is necessary to speak clearly about the signs of the **Zodiac**, all the more so because we note and know the powers of the fixed stars outside the **Zodiac**, and their configurations, from this reference point.

2 The constellations <note>original: "imagines"</note> of the **Zodiac** are in the starry heaven above **Saturn**, and they begin from **Aries** and end in **Pisces**. The year also used to begin for the **Chaldeans** <note>Ancient Babylonian astronomers</note> from the first star of **Aries**, and it established four quarters there, and in **Cancer**, **Libra**, and **Capricorn**. But indeed, from the time of **Hipparchus** <note>A Greek astronomer (c. 190–120 BCE) who discovered the precession of the equinoxes</note> until our own time, the **Sun** has descended incessantly toward the earth—as the decrease in eccentricity shows—and it has continually traveled shorter circles, and does not wander as far toward the tropics as before; but always a little less. From this it happens that it intersects the equator even earlier than it did formerly. Therefore, the equinox has begun to occur not in the first degree of **Aries**, as it once did, but in **Pisces**, so much so that it is now celebrated in the 2nd degree of **Pisces**. Astronomers, however, following the ancient teaching, begin the year from the vernal equinox <note>the spring equinox</note>, as in the time of **Moses** and **Abraham**, and they simultaneously call the first point of the equinox "the first of **Aries**." Yet this point is now far away from the actual first degree of the constellation **Aries** by nearly 28 degrees. They call this new point the "non-starry" **Aries**, and that old one the "starry" **Aries** <note>This explains the difference between the "Sign" of Aries used in horoscopes and the actual "Constellation" of Aries in the sky</note>. We, therefore, when taking judgment from the constellations, will follow the starry images; but in judging the seasons of the year, we will not follow the starry ones, but rather the course of the **Sun** and its entry into the cardinal points <note>the equinoxes and solstices</note>, which by its presence and absence, its approach and departure, creates the changes and powers of the seasons.

Also from its approach and departure, two intermediate seasons are made, namely spring and autumn in our climate. But indeed in the subpolar regions the same is...

2 For those living between the tropics and the poles of the **Zodiac**, the **Zodiac** is cut into four quarters, so that each has three signs. 3 But for those who live beyond the equator toward the **Antarctic** pole, these quarters behave differently—I mean in those places at the same distance from the equator as we are. This is because these signs are defined by the **Sun**, not by the shapes of the constellations. For it is true that in ♎ <note>Libra</note> the **Sun** is "exalted" for them, and just as ♈ <note>Aries</note> "strikes" the earth <note>The name Aries (the Ram) was traditionally associated with the Sun "butting" away the winter cold</note>, so they till the earth; and the **Sun** there, like ♉ <note>Taurus, the Bull</note>, seeks with the "horn" of its rays, and in ♐ <note>Sagittarius</note> its power is doubled, just as it is for us in the sign of ♊ <note>Gemini, the Twins</note>. Moreover, when the **Sun** is in ♑ <note>Capricorn</note>, it is closest to them and produces heat, just as it does for us in ♋ <note>Cancer</note>. When it is in ♒ <note>Aquarius</note>, it is the same for them as ♌ <note>Leo</note> is for us; hence it does not seem right to place **Aquarius** <note>The Water-Bearer</note> there, since it does not give waters to them at that time, but to us. Therefore, all the figures must be exchanged in the <term>non-stellar space</term> <note>The "Tropical Zodiac," which is based on the seasons rather than the actual positions of the stars in the sky</note> insofar as they are established by the **Sun**. As for the order of the actual stars, I would say otherwise. I would not even suggest this, were it not permitted to give the figures new names, as reason demands. The ancient Astrologers, therefore, seem to have considered only our climates. But since the **Spaniards** have established colonies beyond the **Tropic of Capricorn** <note>Referring to the Spanish colonization of the Americas in the Southern Hemisphere</note>, they certainly have need of a new **Astrology**.

### *Concerning another division of the Zodiac.*

## ARTICLE V.

1 In our climates, the signs of the Zodiac are divided again into moveable, fixed, and common. Four signs are called **moveable** <note>Today more commonly called Cardinal signs</note>; these are the first cardinal signs in which the four seasons of the year begin: namely ♈ <note>Aries</note>, ♋ <note>Cancer</note>, ♎ <note>Libra</note>, and ♑ <note>Capricorn</note>. For in ♈ <note>Aries</note> and ♎ <note>Libra</note> the <term>equinox</term> <note>The time when day and night are of equal length</note> occurs everywhere; in ♋ <note>Cancer</note> and ♑ <note>Capricorn</note> the **Sun** retreats from its journey beyond the equator <note>The solstices, where the sun appears to "stand still" before changing direction</note>. They are called moveable because the year then changes its "age" <note>original: "aetatem," referring to the transition from one season to the next</note>.

2 **Fixed** signs are those in which the seasons of the year are fixed, confirmed, and persist: as in ♉ <note>Taurus</note> spring and its mildness [are fixed], in ♌ <note>Leo</note> summer and its heat, in ♏ <note>Scorpio</note> autumn and its dryness, in ♒ <note>Aquarius</note> winter and its moisture or cold.

3 **Common** signs <note>Today usually called Mutable signs</note> are those which come between the former and the latter, where the **Sun**, being present, shows the constitution of both seasons. As in ♊ <note>Gemini</note> both spring and summer seem to be present, and from here is the transition from the former into the latter. In ♍ <note>Virgo</note> there is summer and autumn, for the heat grows lukewarm; in ♐ <note>Sagittarius</note> is the constitution of autumn and winter, and immediately the change into the latter; in ♓ <note>Pisces</note> is the nature of winter and spring. For this reason, they are also called "double" by astrologers and are represented by a double image, as you see in Higidium <note>original: "Higidium," likely referring to Hyginus, a 1st-century author of a famous treatise on the stars</note>.

4 In the subpolar and equinoctial regions, you will call the middle signs (or parts of signs, as far as possible) the common beginnings of the quarters; the moveable ones follow; and the fixed ones... this is clear to those who consider it.

## *The third division of the signs of the Zodiac.*

### ARTICLE VI.

<margin>1</margin>There are other signs called northern, six in number, which look from the equator toward the north pole, namely: ♈ <note>Aries</note> ♉ <note>Taurus</note> ♊ <note>Gemini</note> ♋ <note>Cancer</note> ♌ <note>Leo</note> ♍ <note>Virgo</note>. Others are southern, which look beyond toward the south pole, namely: ♎ <note>Libra</note> ♏ <note>Scorpio</note> ♐ <note>Sagittarius</note> ♑ <note>Capricorn</note> ♒ <note>Aquarius</note> ♓ <note>Pisces</note>. These divisions hold true for every region of the world.

## *The fourth division.*

### ARTICLE VII.

<margin>1</margin>Some signs are straight <note>original: *recta*</note>, and others are crooked <note>original: *tortuosa*</note>. They are called "straight" because, in an <term>oblique sphere</term> <note>The view of the sky from any latitude other than the poles or the equator, where the celestial paths appear tilted</note>, they take up more time while rising, as they ascend along with more parts of the equator; for this reason, they are also called signs of "long ascensions." These are ♋ <note>Cancer</note> ♌ <note>Leo</note> ♍ <note>Virgo</note> ♎ <note>Libra</note> ♏ <note>Scorpio</note> ♐ <note>Sagittarius</note>. The crooked signs, however, are those that do not rise as straight, and thus are raised above the horizon in a shorter time, because more of the equator is raised than the ecliptic <note>The ecliptic is the Sun's apparent path; near the equinoxes, it crosses the equator at a sharp angle, causing signs to rise more quickly or slowly</note>; these are the signs of "short ascensions," which follow: ♑ <note>Capricorn</note> ♒ <note>Aquarius</note> ♓ <note>Pisces</note> ♈ <note>Aries</note> ♉ <note>Taurus</note> ♊ <note>Gemini</note>. Furthermore, those that rise straight descend crookedly, and they exchange their speeds of descent; the opposite is true for those that rise crookedly.

## *On the Antiscia.*

### ARTICLE VIII.

Signs that rise directly are said to "gaze upon" those that rise crookedly, and are called <term>antiscia</term> <note>From the Greek for "opposite shadows"; these are pairs of points in the Zodiac that have the same distance from the solstice points, resulting in equal day lengths</note> to them, and vice versa. This is because the Sun in these signs makes the days equal to days and nights to nights. Therefore, only those that maintain this equality are called antiscia, and we have provided a table of them here.

### On the commanding and the obedient signs, the fifth division.

#### ARTICLE IX.

Whatever signs and degrees are equally distant from the <term>equinoctial points</term> <note>The points where the sun crosses the celestial equator, marking the start of Spring and Autumn</note> are called "secondary antiscia." And because the northern signs are closer to us, and planets within them are more effective toward us, they are for that reason called "commanding signs." The southern signs, however, are called "obedient" for the opposite reasons. Therefore, every sign equally distant from the equinox, if it is northern, commands its equidistant southern sign—for example, Aries commands Pisces.

Note also that some command in a "hateful" manner, where they look upon each other hostiley, such as ♌ <note>Leo</note> and ♏ <note>Scorpio</note>, or Taurus and Aquarius; others are not hateful, as is evident. Note that in the southern regions <note>The Southern Hemisphere</note>, the southern signs command and the northern signs obey for the opposite reasons.

### On connected and unconnected signs, the sixth division.

#### ARTICLE X.

Finally, those signs are called "connected" <note>original: *coniuncta*</note> which regard each other by antiscium, or by equal distance, or by a <term>sextile</term> <note>60 degrees</note>, <term>trine</term> <note>120 degrees</note>, or <term>square</term> <note>90 degrees</note> radiation. Those that do not relate in any of these ways are called "unconnected."

2 A second rule: every <term>cardinal sign</term> <note>original: *signum mobile*, literally "movable sign," which marks the beginning of a season</note> is unconnected to its neighbor and the sign following its opposite; for example, Aries is unconnected to Taurus and Scorpio. Every <term>mutable sign</term> <note>original: *signum commune*, signs that bridge two seasons</note> is unconnected to the sign preceding it and the one following its opposite; for example, Gemini is unconnected to Taurus and Scorpio. Every <term>fixed sign</term> <note>signs that occur in the middle of a season</note> is unconnected to both the sign preceding it and the one following it, as well as their opposites; for example, Taurus is unconnected to Aries and Gemini, and likewise to Libra and Sagittarius. This holds true provided that the <term>semi-sextile aspect</term> <note>An aspect of 30 degrees, which some traditional astrologers considered too weak to count as a "connection"</note> is not considered valid; you shall say the same for the rest. We call a sign "opposite" when it is distant from another by the diameter; that is, the middle of the circle, which is 180 degrees.

### *The seventh division of the signs of the Zodiac, by sex.*

## ARTICLE XI.

Some signs are masculine and likewise <term>diurnal</term> <note>active during the day</note>; others are feminine and likewise <term>nocturnal</term> <note>active during the night</note>. If you begin from ♈ <note>Aries</note> and continue to the end, a masculine sign always precedes and a feminine sign always follows.

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| Diurnal | ♈ ♊ ♌ ♎ ♐ ♒ | are masculine. |
| Nocturnal | ♉ ♋ ♍ ♏ ♑ ♓ | are feminine. |

Astrologers do not assign a single reason for this. However, I think this division arises from the fact that the Sun, acting strongly in ♈ <note>Aries</note>, imitates the male; but in ♉ <note>Taurus</note>, performing nothing new but simply confirming the season, it imitates the female. In ♊ <note>Gemini</note>, by provoking change once again, it becomes masculine, while in ♋ <note>Cancer</note>, by not varying, it becomes feminine, and so on for the others. From this, the Platonic Metaphysicians attribute this to the union and succession of the sexes, following <note>the Neoplatonist philosopher</note> Plotinus.
