...they change it continuously as they pass through now the southern signs, now the northern; and likewise as they increase or decrease their **latitude** <term>The distance of a celestial body north or south of the ecliptic</term> from the Sun’s path. The ancient mathematicians believed the **fixed stars** <note>Stars that appear to stay in the same position relative to one another, unlike the "wandering" planets</note> maintained the same perennial declination. However, it has now been revealed that the Sun precedes the equinoxes—either because the fixed stars are moved backward by a very slow motion, as the **Ptolemaics** <note>Followers of Ptolemy, who believed the Earth was the center of the universe</note> prefer; or because the equator is on the Earth and is inclined toward the Zodiac, as it seems to the **Copernicans** <note>Followers of Copernicus, who argued for a Sun-centered system</note>; or because the Sun, having become closer to the Earth, describes narrower circles and therefore precedes the intersection of the equator, just as the Moon does the Zodiac with its shifting nodes, as we have written elsewhere. For this reason, it is necessary that the declination of the fixed stars varies gradually. This variation causes grand and slow effects and the **mutations of the ages** <note>Major historical or climatic shifts believed to be driven by astronomical cycles</note>; for the entry of great stars from one sign into another transfers the rule of the regions over which they preside, as we shall see below. Wherefore even the astrologer must be very well-acquainted with these matters from astronomy—regarding motions and anomalies—of which we will speak at another time.

2 **Latitude** is the name given to the distance from the **ecliptic** <term>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky</term>, which is the Sun’s path. One kind is southern, another northern; and it varies among the fixed stars just as and by as much as the **obliquity** <term>The tilt of the Earth's axis, or the angle between the equator and the ecliptic</term> of the Zodiac varies. We have always contended this to be the case against the Copernicans, until **Tycho** <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), a Danish astronomer famous for his precise observations</note> and the **Landgrave** <note>William IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel, an early adopter of precise astronomical instruments</note> proved it to be so through the most manifest observations. Since, therefore, the obliquity has varied by nearly 24 minutes, and the fixed stars in different parts of the Zodiac suffer that variation differently, it is necessary for the astrologer to know this, so that he is not ignorant of how to adapt his judgments to them.

3 In the **wandering stars** <note>The planets</note>, latitude is certain; for just as the Sun’s path intersects the equator, so the paths of the wandering stars intersect the path of the Sun. The points of intersection are called **nodes**; the one that carries the planet toward the South is called the **descending node** <note>original: *nodus devehens*</note> and the **Dragon’s Tail**; the one carrying it toward the North is the **ascending node** <note>original: *nodus evehens*</note> and the **Dragon’s Head**.

4 The nodes of all planets move in the **preceding signs** <note>In retrograde motion, or contrary to the order of the Zodiac signs</note>, just as the nodes of the Zodiac do in the equator. Most manifest, however, are the lunar nodes, which cover three minutes a day in forward motion and are noted in the **ephemerides** <term>Astronomical tables predicting the positions of celestial bodies</term>. Knowledge of the others is not as exact because they are very slow, so much so that they appeared stationary to the ancients. Copernicus, however, discovered they were mobile, as are the **apsides** <term>The points in an orbit where a planet is nearest or farthest from the body it orbits</term>. The change of these indeed has significance in great affairs, as we shall teach below. The North Node is symbolized thus: ☊; the South Node thus: ☋.

5 It is necessary, therefore, to note how great is the latitude of each planet...

6 When the planets are in northern latitude, they are more effective for us <note>The author likely refers to observers in the Northern Hemisphere</note>: but for those who live beyond the equator, it is the opposite.

7 The **North Node** <term>Caput Draconis, or the Dragon's Head; the point where a planet crosses the ecliptic moving north</term> is considered to be of the nature of Jupiter: and with good planets it is good, because it increases their strength; and with evil planets it is evil, for the same reason. Therefore, they do not rightly categorize it as being of the nature of Jupiter; rather, they should have ascribed to it only an "augmenting" power. Nor is the **South Node** <term>Cauda Draconis, or the Dragon's Tail; the point where a planet crosses the ecliptic moving south</term> rightly placed under the nature of Saturn, since it diminishes the decrees of both the malefic <note>Harmful planets, traditionally Saturn and Mars</note> and the benefic <note>Helpful planets, traditionally Jupiter and Venus</note> planets with which it is associated. Therefore, it only has the power of diminishing in our regions. But in the southern regions, the opposite occurs: the South Node increases, and the North Node diminishes, because the planets pass into their own or foreign places. Moreover, the position of the Moon strongly affects lower things <note>Earthly matters and the physical world</note>: for this reason, its nodes have apparent powers in connection with the other planets.

BOOK ONE.

## *Concerning the variable position of the stars resulting from the variable change of the sky, from which figures are erected.*

### CHAPTER VI. ARTICLE I.

**1** The variable daily rotation divides the sky for us—no differently than the immutable annual rotation does—into two parts, four quarters, and 12 **houses** <term>The twelve divisions of an astrological chart representing different areas of life</term> corresponding to the division into northern and southern signs. Likewise, it is divided into the four quarters of the year and into the 12 signs. For the meridian circle, like the equator, cuts the sky into an ascending and a descending portion. Furthermore, the meridian is distributed by the horizon so that four quarters are formed, just as the equator is by the **Zodiac** <term>The belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs, through which the sun and planets move</term>. Again, every quarter is divided into three dwellings <note>original: *domicilia* — a synonym for houses</note> by the circles of position, as is evident in the erection of a celestial figure <note>original: *figurae coelestis erectione* — the process of casting an astrological chart or horoscope</note>; just as every quarter of the year is divided into 3 signs and 90 degrees.

**2** The first quarter begins from the eastern angle of the horizon up to the **zenith** <term>The point in the sky directly above an observer</term>, or midheaven. It is called oriental, masculine, hot and moist, and sanguineous <note>original: *sanguinea* — referring to the "sanguine" temperament, associated with blood, spring, and a cheerful disposition</note>, corresponding to the first age of life. From here, the East Winds <note>original: *Subsolani*</note> blow. Nevertheless, it is considered by **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the influential Greco-Roman astronomer whose works formed the basis of medieval astrology</note> to be hot and dry, because the Sun then dissolves the thick night vapors and dries the air for us—although that thinness of air is actually a form of moisture. Indeed, after the sun has ascended 45 degrees, it seems to dissolve them; but in the beginning, it rather stirs up the thick humors. This quarter contains the tenth, eleventh, and twelfth houses. For the first house is positioned below the horizon, and by counting against the order of the signs, the "heart of heaven" <note>original: *cor coeli* — the Midheaven or Medium Coeli, the highest point in the chart</note> becomes the tenth.

**3** The second quarter contains the ninth, eighth, and seventh houses up to the western boundary <note>original: *finitorem* — the horizon</note>. It is hot and dry from the heat of the Sun and the South winds; it is choleric <note>associated with yellow bile, summer, and a fiery temperament</note>, meridian, and feminine. But it is strange how it could be feminine and yet hot and dry. Perhaps it is because as the Sun tends toward our sunset, it does not complete what it then begins, as it does in the eastern quarter when it rises.

**4** The third [quarter] is from the western angle to the subterranean meridian <note>The *Imum Coeli* or bottom of the sky, the point directly opposite the Midheaven</note>, embracing the sixth, fifth, and fourth houses. It is called occidental, masculine, melancholic <note>associated with black bile, autumn, and a somber temperament</note>, cold, and dry by the Arabs. However, Ptolemy says it is rather moist, because the West winds <note>original: *favonii*</note> from that direction are soft and wet, and the moisture consumed during the day begins to be replenished.

**7** Of these houses, four are **angular** <term>The houses located at the four cardinal points of the chart: 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th</term>: specifically the first, fourth, seventh, and tenth, where the powers of the stars are most potent. Others are **succedent** <term>Literally "following" the angles; houses 2, 5, 8, and 11</term>, because they follow the positions of the four aforementioned angles in the layout of the world; in these, the powers are moderate. Others are called **cadent** <term>Literally "falling away" from the angles; houses 3, 6, 9, and 12</term>, because they fall far from the angles and are sluggish and cast down. However, those houses that are configured <note>original: *configurantur* — forming a geometric relationship or aspect</note> to the **horoscope** <term>Specifically the 1st house or Rising Sign, the most important point in a chart</term> are better, even compared to those succedent houses that are not so configured, such as the third and ninth. This is even more true for those above the earth, such as the ninth; and because it follows the **Midheaven** <note>original: *cæli culmen* — the "summit of the sky" or 10th house</note>, it is far better than the eighth. Among the succedent houses, the eleventh is the best, then the second, then the fifth. Among the angles, the **Midheaven** <note>original: *M. C.* — Medium Coeli</note> is the most important, then the horoscope, then the seventh, and finally the fourth.

## *On the Dignities of the Planets.*

### CHAPTER VII. ARTICLE I.

<margin>1</margin>
The Planets have in the **Zodiac**, besides the accidental conditions already mentioned, other powers that are inherent to them: for in various places different planets prevail in different ways, as experience and reason testify. Their powers are seen to be seven, namely: **House**, where they are as if in their own home; **Trine** <term>Also known as Triplicity; a group of three signs belonging to the same element, such as Fire or Water</term>, where they are as if among family members; **Exaltation**, where they are as if in a kingdom; **Term** <term>Specific degrees within an astrological sign where a planet holds particular influence</term>, where they are as if on their own small estate; **Chariot** <note>original: *Carpentum* — a rare term for a planetary dignity, suggesting a planet is "riding" in its own strength or "throne"</note>, where they are as if in a display of their own virtue; **Face** <note>original: *Persona* — likely referring to the Decans or "Faces," which are ten-degree subdivisions of a sign</note>, where they are as if in the king’s sight; and **Joy**, where they are as if at their own festival.

## *On the Houses of the Planets.*

### ARTICLE II.

<margin>1</margin>
Not only does experience testify that the **Sun** attains the strongest powers toward us when in **Leo**, and is in it as if in its own home; but reason itself dictates the same, so that wherever a planet has the most power, there it should have its own dwelling. So also **Habakkuk** <note>A reference to the biblical book of Habakkuk 3:11: "The sun and moon stood still in their habitation."</note> says: *The Sun and Moon stood in their habitation.* Therefore, just as we assign to the Sun the sign of **Leo**—a masculine and fiery sign, because it shows its strength therein—so we assign to the **Moon** **Cancer**, a feminine sign, because it is closest to us <note>The Moon was considered the closest celestial body to Earth in the geocentric model</note>, where the Moon strongly shows its powers to us. For this reason, the entire half of the heavens from **Leo** ♌ to **Capricorn** ♑ is seen to belong to the Sun; while for the Moon, it is the half from **Cancer** ♋ to **Aquarius** ♒.

<margin>2</margin>
**Mercury** has the two houses closest to these: since it departs least of all from the Sun, no more than 27 degrees, and such a domicile is suitable for it, as it holds a permanent position near the **Luminaries** <term>A traditional term for the Sun and the Moon, the two brightest objects in the sky</term>. Indeed, the magnet and iron and many other things manifest the powers of position. Therefore, its signs are **Gemini**  Gemini and **Virgo** Virgo, which are "double" <note>original: *duplicia* — referring to "double-bodied" or mutable signs, which represent transitions between seasons</note> according to the duality of Mercury.

**Venus** is then allotted the next ones: since she herself is [of the] Light...

# Concerning the houses of the Planets for those living in the subpolar, equinoctial, and opposite regions who are equidistant from the equator.

## ARTICLE III.

For those who dwell beyond the equator looking toward the South Pole, at an equal distance from the equator as we are, the houses of the Planets are arranged in a contrary position. For because the Moon is closest to them in **Cancer** (♋), and acts powerfully upon the lower bodies there <note>The "lower bodies" refers to the earthly realm and physical matter influenced by celestial forces</note>, the house of **Cancer** belongs to the Moon. But the house of the Sun is **Aquarius** (♒): for although the Sun is closer in **Capricorn** (♑), its force is nevertheless strengthened in **Aquarius** because of the impression already made upon the subject <note>The author argues that the Sun's heat and influence linger and peak after it passes its closest point, much like how the hottest part of the day is after noon</note>. The Moon does not do this, because it is swift, whereas the Sun lingers in one sign for 30 days.

Therefore, since **Saturn** has less power there in **Capricorn** and **Aquarius**—because those houses are strengthened by the Luminaries <note>original: "Luminaribus"—referring to the Sun and Moon</note> toward their own lower regions, but not toward ours—for that reason, **Cancer** and **Leo** are the houses of Saturn for the Southern peoples. Consequently, the houses of **Mercury** will be **Sagittarius** and **Pisces**; the houses of **Venus**, **Scorpio** and **Aries**; the houses of **Mars**, **Libra** and **Taurus**; and the houses of **Jupiter**, **Virgo** and **Gemini**. This follows the exact same reasons as given above, but in reverse.

From this it is clear that the Planets do not have a symbolic connection with specific signs of the heavens, but rather with stars that match them in color and operation—and perhaps even with their figures. However, this alone does not create a "domicile" <term>A sign of the Zodiac where a planet is said to have its strongest influence and "home"</term>. For in **Gemini** there are many stars of a Martian nature, and very few in **Aries** at this time; nevertheless, **Gemini** is not a sign of **Mars** (♂), but of **Mercury** (☿). 

Therefore, since the Sun (where it hangs most powerfully) and the Moon (where it is closest) produce great effects suitable for the Luminaries, the houses of the Luminaries are located wherever such proximity and strength exists toward the regions below them. And since where they are a little distant, they produce effects suitable to **Mercury** by acting with weaker forces, those signs at such a distance are given to **Mercury**. Mercury is said to "rejoice" in them with respect to subjects in that location, because it can display its powers there once the Luminaries have influenced the lower regions with a heat like that of Mercury. But where they are further distant, they produce effects suitable to the heat of **Venus**. Therefore, **Venus** has power there and is allotted a house, though in respect to the lower bodies, not itself. And so it goes for the others, until you come to the greatest...

<meta>catchword: distance</meta>

Therefore, **Saturn** is said to inhabit the signs most distant from each region for these stated reasons.

2. For subpolar peoples, the houses are numbered in the same way: for in the Arctic, **Cancer** (♋) and **Leo** (♌) belong to the Luminaries, while **Capricorn** (♑) and **Aquarius** (♒) belong to **Saturn**. For those in the Antarctic, however, it is the opposite. The remaining signs, therefore, are arranged as they are in the first cases.

3. But for those living under the equator, **Aries** (♈) and **Libra** (♎) are the houses of the **Sun**, since there the Sun is most powerful to them; nor will it be more powerful in **Scorpio** (♏) and **Taurus** (♉) than in **Aries** and **Libra**. Just as for us it is more powerful in **Leo** (♌) than in **Cancer** (♋), because it increases its action in **Pisces** (♓) and **Virgo** (♍) just as it does in **Taurus** and **Scorpio**. However, it is not the same in **Gemini** (♊) as it is in **Leo** toward us; for while it is approaching in the former, in the latter it doubles the strength of its already neighboring power. Under the equator, however, its approach and withdrawal are equal in both position and strength.

4. Therefore, **Cancer** (♋) and **Capricorn** (♑) will be given to **Saturn** under the equator, since in those signs he has the least strength toward those people. The **Moon**, however, will possess the same houses as the **Sun**, since she is most imminent there—unless you wish to assign **Taurus** (♉) and **Scorpio** (♏) to the **Sun**, or half of these; and to the **Moon**, the "hinges" <note>The "hinges" (cardines) refer to the primary angles or pivotal points of the zodiac, which represent the peak of a planet's power</note> of **Aries** (♈) and **Libra** (♎). The Ethiopians and the people of Taprobana <note>Taprobana: the ancient name for the island of Sri Lanka</note>, and the Spaniards who possess colonies under the equator, can learn this better through experience; in the meantime, we reason through it in this manner.

5. We shall give the more temperate parts of the signs to **Jupiter** and **Venus**; the more burning parts to **Mars**; and those closer to the Luminaries to **Mercury**. For it is impossible to distribute entire signs to them in such a location. It is necessary to multiply the houses in front and behind, or on both sides, according to the stated reasoning: and to assign to the Luminaries not one, but two houses; and similarly to the others according to their distance from those two opposites as they approach the extreme Saturnian signs. ## Concerning the Exaltations of the Planets.

### ARTICLE IV.

<image-desc>A circular diagram representing the zodiac. The outer ring is divided into segments labeled with the degrees 10, 20, and 30. The second dignity is called **Exaltation**. <note>In astrology, a "dignity" is a condition that increases a planet's power. Exaltation is considered the second strongest placement after its "House."</note> For it has been found that in certain signs planets are so affected that they exert their powers potently upon lower things. <note>The "lower things" refers to the Earth and its inhabitants.</note> I have long doubted whether the dignity of exaltation took its origin from the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in a planet's orbit where it is furthest from the Earth; the author is testing if "exalted" (high) meant physically highest in the sky.</note>. For where a planet is physically elevated, it is there said to be "exalted." But astrologers maintain that we should think here not of the planet's physical height, but of the "height" of its action. For the locations of the apogees are far distant from the locations of the exaltations.

But since apogees move forward over long periods of time, perhaps this dignity began to be spoken of in relation to the apogees; once those points moved, the earlier terminology remained with the astrologers. Just as we now place **Aries** (♈︎) in the sign of Aries even though it is no longer where the stars of that constellation are. <note>original: "non stellatum." The author is referring to "precession," where the calendar signs of the zodiac have shifted away from the actual constellations of the same name.</note> Soon I found this same opinion in **Pliny**. <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman author of Natural History.</note> But since the ancients (according to **Ptolemy**) had no doubt about the stability of the apogees, and the exaltations differ greatly from them, I am not led by any historical observations to believe the astrologers' theory on this point. For even if the Sun's apogee could have moved from **Aries** (♈︎) into **Cancer** (♋︎)—which has not been observed—nonetheless **Mars** (♂) could not have reached **Cancer** from **Capricorn** (♑︎) at the same time: as the measure of its motion in **Copernicus** <note>Nicolaus Copernicus, the astronomer who proved the Earth moves around the Sun.</note> and others proves. However it may be, we must cling to tradition, which experience supports rather than refutes.

**1**   Therefore, the **Sun** is said to be exalted in **Aries** (♈︎): because there it first exerts its greater powers after the winter cold.

**2**   The **Moon** in **Taurus** (♉︎): because after its first conjunction <note>original: "copulam." This refers to the New Moon, when the Sun and Moon meet in the sky.</note> with the Sun exalted in **Aries**, the **Moon** then first shows itself to us there.

## On the Terms of the Planets.

### A R T I C L E VI.

1 The final and least significant dignity <term>Dignity; the degree of influence or "power" a planet has based on its specific position in the zodiac.</term> is the **Term** <note>original: "Terminus"; these are unequal subdivisions of each zodiac sign, where specific planets exert a secondary influence.</note>. It is found that each planet possesses some power within every sign, but specifically within certain degrees. But truly, unless this matter were revealed by God himself, I would hardly believe that enough experiments could have been performed on every single degree for a certain science to emerge from it. I would rather think that astrologers, moved by some logic of the natural succession of things, assigned the terms in such a way that the rulers of the signs hold the first parts, others the following parts, and the **malefics** <note>original: "malefici"; the "unfavorable" planets, traditionally Saturn and Mars.</note> hold the final parts, as is evident. For this reason, there is much controversy regarding the terms; some follow the **Chaldeans**, others the **Egyptians**, and others follow **Ptolemy** and the "half-torn book" <note>Ptolemy famously claimed in his *Tetrabiblos* that he discovered an ancient, damaged manuscript that contained the "true" Egyptian system of terms.</note> that was found, following him in the assignment of these terms. I have decided to provide a small table here, and leave the final judgment to those who wish to test it for themselves. For I profess that I have no absolute certainty regarding these matters, except for what logic suggests: that in all terms, one may experience both good and bad outcomes.

## Of Chariots.

### ARTICLE VII.

1 A planet is said to be in its **Chariot** <note>original: *Carpentum*</note>, its seat, or its throne, when it is in a sign <note>original: *obliquo signo*</note> where it possesses several dignities—such as Venus (♀) in Pisces (♓), where she holds both her <term>exaltation</term> <note>the sign where a planet's influence is most elevated</note> and her <term>triplicity</term> <note>a group of three signs belonging to the same element</note>. In such cases, the planet's power is multiplied.

---

## Of the Face.

### ARTICLE VIII.

1 A planet is said to be in its **Face** <note>original: *Persona*</note> when it is positioned in relation to one of the two <term>Luminaries</term> <note>The Sun or the Moon</note> in the same way that its own home sign relates to the home sign of that Luminary. This is provided that the planet is occidental (setting after) the Sun and oriental (rising before) the Moon. It should look toward the Moon against the order of the zodiac signs, but toward the Sun according to that order. Thus, Saturn (♄) is in its Face when it is five signs distant from the Luminaries in this manner; Jupiter (♃) is four signs away, Mars (♂) three, Venus (♀) two, and Mercury (☿) one.

2 This dignity is based on natural placement. For just as a magnet is naturally drawn to its original position, things spontaneously return to their source; therefore, planets "rejoice" in such a position. This dignity is called **Almugea** by the Arabs.

---

## Of Joy.

### ARTICLE IX.

1 A planet is considered to be in its **Joy** <note>original: *Gaudio*</note> when it is found within the dignities of its "friends"—for example, when nocturnal planets are in nocturnal signs, diurnal (daytime) planets are in diurnal signs, and masculine planets are in masculine signs—such as Jupiter (♃) being in a sign ruled by Venus (♀).

---

## *Of the afflictions of the planets, as they are compared to the Sun.*

### CHAPTER VIII. ARTICLE I.

1 Planets are said to be **in the heart of the Sun** <note>original: *in corde Solis*, often called Cazimi, meaning the planet is in nearly exact conjunction with the Sun</note>, **combust** <note>weakened by being too close to the Sun's heat</note>, and **under the rays**; they are also described as morning or evening stars relative to the Sun, and as having their light increased or diminished.

<summary>This page defines specific planetary dignities—Chariots, Almugea (Face), and Joy—which describe how a planet's power increases based on its position and its relationship to the Sun and Moon. It also introduces the "afflictions" planets suffer when positioned too close to the Sun's light.</summary>

<keywords>Chariot, Carpentum, Almugea, Face, Joy, Gaudio, Dignities, Combust, Heart of the Sun, Cazimi, Astrology, Planets</keywords>

<header>OF ASTROLOGICAL MATTERS</header>

2 A planet is said to be **in the heart of the Sun** <note>original: *in corde Solis*; also known as Cazimi</note> when it is joined to the Sun centrally in both longitude and latitude, or within a space equal to the sum of their semi-diameters. For example, the Sun's diameter is 30 minutes according to Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the famous Danish astronomer whose precise observations revolutionized the field</note> at its furthest point from Earth; that of Venus (♀) is 3 ½ minutes. Therefore, when the distance of their conjunction is approximately 16 minutes and 38 seconds, Venus (♀) is said to be "in the heart of the Sun." At this time, the planet is thought to be at its most powerful, as the two bodies act together as a single agent of great efficacy.

3 A planet is considered **Combust** <note>literally "burnt up" by the Sun's heat and light</note> when it is distant from the Sun by less than half of its own "orb of light." For Venus (♀), the orb of light is 8 degrees. Therefore, it is combust when it is at a distance of three, or slightly less than four degrees.

4 A planet is said to be **under the rays** when it is distant from the Sun by more than half its orb, but still within the space created by the combined orbs of both bodies. For instance, since the Sun (☉) has an orb of 17 degrees and Venus (♀) has 8, Venus is said to be "under the rays" from the 5th degree up to nearly the 20th. Others say this state lasts as long as the planet remains invisible. You should consult Astronomy to determine when a planet can be seen. In this state, the planet is less weak; it is at its weakest when it is combust. However, Mercury (☿) is not so severely harmed by combustion because it is combust so frequently.

5 Planets are called **Oriental** <note>rising in the east</note> from the Sun when they appear above the horizon in the morning before the Sun. This happens for Saturn (♄), Mars (♂), and Jupiter (♃) from their conjunction with the Sun (☉) until their opposition. Conversely, they are **Occidental** <note>setting in the west</note> from the Sun when they appear on the horizon after the Sun sets—that is, from their opposition to their conjunction.

6 Planets are said to be in the "upper apse" during conjunction and are fastest in the later signs. In opposition, however, they are in the "lower apse" and are slowest in the later signs, but fastest in the earlier signs due to the shortness of the circle. Because of this, they are called **Retrograde** <note>appearing to move backward in the zodiac</note> due to their failing motion. From this, they have four states. The first is from the morning rising until the morning "station" (the first point where it seems to stop); in this state, they are **moist**. The second is from the first station until they rise at night, occidental to the Sun (☉); these are **hot**. The third is from the nightly rising to the second station, during which they **dry out**. The fourth is from the second station until the morning rising; in this state, they are **cold**, as some teach. Indeed, it is evident that retrograde planets are closer to the Earth and possess more heating power.

7 Mercury (☿) and Venus (♀) are oriental or occidental depending on whether they precede or follow the Sun. And because they circle the Sun, they have a morning rising after their regression, when they appear before the Sun; and a morning setting <note>original: *occasum matutinum*</note> when they are hidden by the rising Sun...

# BOOK ONE

<note>This text continues a sentence describing planets</note> ...ascending to the **apogee** <note>original: *absidem*; the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth</note>: evening rising occurs when they appear at night above the western horizon after the Sun has set. Evening setting occurs when they hasten toward the **perigee** <note>original: *perigæum*; the point in an orbit closest to the Earth</note> in their second station, following the Sun because of the shortness of their circular path, by which they are **heliacally** <note>original: *heliacè*; hidden by the Sun's light</note> obscured. However, they undergo **cosmic** <note>original: *cosmicum*; rising or setting at the same time as the Sun</note> rising and setting together with the Sun. Therefore, they are considered oriental and occidental from one conjunction to the next.

8  The **Moon** is oriental from its opposition <note>the Full Moon</note> to its conjunction <note>the New Moon</note>, because it appears in the morning before the Sun. It is occidental from conjunction to opposition, because it appears in the evening after the Sun. It possesses four "affections" <note>dispositions or qualities</note> in its four quarters: for from the conjunction to the first quarter it is more **moist** than hot; in the second quarter up to the opposition it is more **hot** than dry; in the third from the opposition to the following quarter it is more **dry** than cold; then, until the conjunction, it is rather **cold** than dry. In this way, it reflects the times of the day and the seasons of the year. However, by reason of the **Zodiac**, the first and third quarters are considered "oriental" in astrological judgments; the remaining quarters are "occidental" in the Moon by itself, not in relation to the Sun.

9  **Planets** are increased in light when they move away from the Sun, or the Sun from them, for in this state their light is less hidden. Conversely, they are diminished in light when they approach the Sun, or the Sun approaches them, as is clearly shown in the study of **Astronomy**.

10  The **fixed stars** also have rising and setting relative to the Sun and to the world. Indeed, a "true mundane morning rising" occurs when a star rises exactly as the Sun is rising. A "heliacal morning rising"—that is, in relation to the Sun—is when it rises shortly before the Sun, because the Sun recedes from the stars toward the east through its slower motion <note>original: *motum subdeficientiæ*; the Sun's apparent motion against the stars</note>. A "true mundane morning setting" occurs when the star happens to go below the horizon while the Sun is rising above the eastern angle. A "heliacal morning setting," however, is when the star is rendered invisible to us by the Sun’s rays as the Sun rises. A "true cosmic evening rising" is when the star rises above the horizon while the Sun sinks below the horizon at the diametrically opposite point. A "heliacal evening rising" is when a star which had been hidden within the solar rays first begins to appear outside those rays as the Sun sets. A "true evening setting" is when the star sets below the horizon at the same time as the Sun. A "heliacal evening setting" occurs when a star, which was visible after sunset, begins to be hidden under the rays because of the Sun's approach to it.

11  However, the rising and setting of the fixed stars in relation to the planets is the same as with the Sun, in cases where the fixed stars occupy the same part of the Zodiac as the planets.

...where outside, it is also recognized by the oblique ascensions <note>the time it takes for a star to rise in a specific latitude</note> of the region for the planets and fixed stars themselves when they agree, just as culmination in the **Midheaven** <note>original: *M. C.* or *Medium Coeli*; the highest point of the sky above the southern horizon</note> is known from right ascensions.

12 Fixed stars are related to the Sun and the planets in several ways. First, when they rise or set, or reach the **Midheaven**, or reach the **bottom of the sky** <note>original: *imant cœlum* or *Imum Coeli*; the point directly opposite the Midheaven</note> together with them. Second, when they are in such a position shortly before or shortly after them. Third, when at the rising of the Sun or a planet, a fixed star is found in the west, or in the Midheaven, or in the bottom of the sky: the power of being **oriental** <note>rising in the east before the Sun</note> and being in a major **angle** <note>the four cardinal points of a chart: East, West, Zenith, and Nadir</note> is considered more significant.

13 The astrologer especially considers **vertical** and **horizontal** stars. A **vertical star** is one that passes over the **zenith** <note>original: *verticem*; the point directly overhead</note> of the region every day; it is recognized by the fact that the star's declination from the equator and the elevation of the pole <note>the observer's local latitude</note> are equal. A **horizontal star** is one that grazes the horizon; it is recognized if its declination is equal to the **complement of the pole** <note>90 degrees minus the local latitude</note> of the region. However, if the declination is greater than the complement, it always remains hidden below the horizon for us if the latitude is southern; if the latitude is northern, it is always visible (circumpolar), such as the **Great Bear** <note>the constellation Ursa Major</note>. The reverse is true for those who live in the South. The complement of the region is that which is lacking from the elevation of the pole to reach 90 degrees, which is a **quadrant of the sky** <note>a quarter of the 360-degree circle</note>.

# *On the Relationship of the Planets among Themselves in Power Arising from Position.*

## CHAPTER IX. ARTICLE I.

One planet is said to be **elevated** over another in eleven ways. First, when one is closer to its **apogee** <note>original: *auge*; the highest or farthest point in an orbit</note>, whether of its **eccentric** <note>a circular path whose center is not the Earth</note> or its **epicycle** <note>a small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger one</note>. Second, when it is in northern **latitude** <note>distance north of the ecliptic line</note> or in northern signs, and the other is in southern ones, in our northern climates; but beyond the equator, you would say the reverse. Third, when one is ascending and the other descending from the North or the apogee. Fourth, when one is in a **commanding** sign and the other in an **obeying** sign <note>Ancient Greek astrology divided the zodiac into 'commanding' northern signs and 'obeying' southern signs</note>. Fifth, the one that is more **oriental** from the Sun. <note>Note: The original text omits the number '5' but lists this condition here.</note> Sixth, the one that is closer to the Midheaven. Seventh, the one in a better **angle** <note>referring to the most powerful houses in a chart: 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th</note>. Eighth, a planet moving **direct** <note>forward through the zodiac</note> over one that is **retrograde** <note>appearing to move backward</note>. Ninth, the one that is further outside the Sun's **rays** <note>not 'combust' or blinded by the Sun's light</note>. Tenth, where near a **conjunction** <note>when two planets meet at the same degree</note>, one is **heavier** <note>original: *ponderosior*; referring to the slower-moving outer planets like Saturn</note> or more occidental. Eleventh, the one that is in more **dignities** <note>essential strengths like being in its own sign or exaltation</note> or surrounded by the light of friends <note>supported by favorable aspects from other planets</note>.

# On the Configuration and Aspect of Planets Among Themselves and with Fixed Stars.

## CHAPTER X. ARTICLE I.

1 The greatest part of **astrology** <note>original: *Astrologiæ*; at this time, the term often encompassed both astronomy and what we now call astrology</note> consists in the consideration of **configuration** and **aspect** <note>the angular relationships between celestial bodies</note>: for from the meetings and aspects of the stars, not only are heat and light increased, diminished, and modified—from which a certain change in earthly things is discerned—but even the shape, position, temperament, and the relationship of parts to themselves and to other parts of the world take their rule. This is not unlike how the position of iron, the strike of the blacksmith’s hammer upon the iron, and its orientation toward parts of the world produce a specific shape in the iron and instill a power and "love" for certain positions, which **William Gilbert** showed in his writings on magnetic philosophy through most reliable experiments. <note>original: *Gilbertus de Magnetica philosophia*; referring to William Gilbert’s 1600 work *De Magnete*, which was a foundational text in the study of magnetism</note> Trees also, and bodies crafted with skill, spread certain parts toward certain positions. Even a corpse floats in the sea according to the position it held in the womb. And a small iron rod floating on cork adapts itself to its original position. Moreover, the exterior shape is formed by the interior **temperament** <note>the balance of qualities like hot, cold, moist, and dry</note> so conceived that it is shaped in such a way. For this reason, **St. Thomas** <note>original: *D. Thomas*; Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century theologian</note> attributes the order of both physical and man-made things to the heavens. Therefore, the contemplation of aspects is of great importance in astrology.

2 The first configuration of the stars is their **conjunction** <note>when two celestial bodies appear in the same place in the sky</note>: which is observed in many ways. For they may be centered in the same longitude and latitude of the heaven; and this is of the most perfect strength—good if between friendly stars, and bad if between enemies, according to their own nature; but according to us, it is good when the power of a "malefic" <note>a planet traditionally thought to have a harsh influence, like Saturn or Mars</note> is tempered by a "benefic" <note>a planet thought to have a helpful influence, like Jupiter or Venus</note>. The second is a conjunction according to longitude in the **Zodiac** <note>the belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs</note>, but not according to latitude. The third is when they hold each other within the **orb** of their own light. <note>the surrounding area where a planet's influence is felt before the exact meeting</note> The fourth is when they are in the same sign. The fifth is when they are in the same house, or circle of position. Furthermore, there are conjunctions of two, three, four, and sometimes all the planets, about which **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary source of Hermetic and astrological wisdom</note> wrote. A conjunction is symbolized thus: ☌.

3 Beyond conjunction, the planets in the heavens have manifold, indeed innumerable, aspects toward us. However, those considered effective by **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology</note> and the ancient mathematicians are four: namely, the **opposition**, whose character is ☍; the **square**, which is □; the **trine**, which is marked thus △; and the **sextile**, which is ⚹.

<meta>catchword: chest.</meta>

4 They say these are effective for this reason: because when multiplied by themselves, they produce other major **aspects** <note>the angular relationships between planets</note> and finally complete the circle. For the **Sextile** <note>original: *Sextilis*; a 60-degree angle</note> contains 60 parts or degrees of the circle; it is the sixth part of a circle, which is made up of 360 degrees. Six times sixty makes 360. Similarly, the **Square** <note>original: *quadratus*; a 90-degree angle</note> contains 90 parts, which when multiplied by four makes 360. The **Trine** <note>original: *Trigonus*; a 120-degree angle</note> contains 120 parts, which when multiplied by three makes 360. The **Opposition** <note>original: *Oppositio*; a 180-degree angle</note> contains half the circle, that is 180 degrees, which when doubled makes 360. Furthermore, if you add a sextile to a sextile, it makes a trine; if you add another ✳ <note>sextile symbol</note>, it makes an ☍ <note>opposition symbol</note>. Likewise, on the other side of the circle, a square added to a square makes an opposition, and aspects always result from them. Similarly, a trine added to a trine makes 240 degrees, from which it is a trine aspect to 360.

But the ancient mathematicians also recognized the **octagon** <note>original: *octagonum*; a 45-degree angle, now commonly called a semi-square</note> aspect. For when the Moon departs from the Sun after a **conjunction** <note>original: ☌; when two bodies are at the same degree</note>, it appears at the 45th degree and gives a sign regarding the changes flowing from that lunar cycle—which **Ptolemy**, **Pliny**, **Aratus**, and others have confirmed through experience.

5 However, it does not seem that this aspect should be numbered among the others, because when multiplied it does not produce the other aspects, as they say. But in the circles of position, the shapes of **comets** are considered by **Haly** <note>likely referring to Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer</note> using this aspect, as well as in medical matters. For that reason, I judge that even if it is not of great efficacy, it is nonetheless not entirely ineffective, especially in the configurations of the Moon.

6 A twelfth aspect is considered by the moderns (whose booklet, long-awaited, has not yet reached me), which contains 30 degrees. It is thought to be effective, as a **semi-sextile** <note>original: *semisextilis*</note>, and of the lowest degree of "friendship." If this is so, there will be no signs in the **Zodiac** <note>the belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs</note> that do not "look upon" one another, except those opposite to the ones that see each other by this twelfth aspect. Indeed, in **peracute** <note>very sharp or sudden</note> diseases, where **critical days** <note>specific days during an illness when a change for better or worse is expected, traditionally linked to the Moon's movement</note> are contained within a shorter space of time, and in chronic ones, I find this aspect to be effective, just as I find the octagon in others. In fact, the fourth day is the indicator of the seventh, on which the Moon’s square to its starting position (where the disease began) occurs. But it would not indicate this unless its part were powerful, just as the sextile is to the trine. Therefore, because in very sharp cases we count by three-day intervals—in which there is a change of only one sign—just as in others we count by four-day intervals—in which there is a change of one and a half signs—it is clear that both are effective, especially in fast-moving matters and those of easy susceptibility. Hence, in changes of the air and waters, neither influence should be despised.

### BOOK ONE.

**aspect**. <note>The text continues the word "aspect" from the previous page.</note> Furthermore, a change of half a sign—that is, the twenty-fourth part of a circle—seems to produce a powerful aspect in acute cases. This is proven by the Ocean in Britain, which rises and falls according to the days of the Moon, and by the Indian bird <note>possibly a parrot or a mythical bird described in natural histories</note> that changes its colors along with the lunar cycle. Truly, change in the heavens is continuous; therefore, it is also continuous in lower things. However, in some things it is felt more strongly, such as the six-hour tide in the sea, or the hourly turning of the **heliotrope** <note>original: *heliotropio*; a plant like the sunflower that follows the sun</note>. For this reason, aspects are countless, though very few are known to us. The **duodenary** <note>original: *duodenus*; the 30-degree or semi-sextile aspect</note> aspect produces all other aspects when it is multiplied; therefore, it ought to be seen as effective.

7 But indeed, it must be noted that the efficacy of an aspect depends either on numbers—as the **Pythagoreans** <note>followers of Pythagoras who believed the universe was built on numerical ratios</note> say—and thus those who examine their powers will know how to philosophize about aspects. (I, however, confess that the powers of number become known to us through the things being numbered. Therefore, in as many ways as an aspect is effective, so many numbers of intercepted degrees are to be honored in this doctrine. It is, however, impossible to recognize them all; therefore, let those mentioned above suffice.) 

Or, in truth, the efficacy depends on the nature of the signs, as most **mathematicians** <note>original: *Mathematicorum*; in this era, the term specifically referred to astronomers and astrologers</note> say. In that case, every change to an opposite sign produces an aspect. And since a preceding sign is always contrary to the following one in gender and condition, the **semisextile** <note>a 30-degree angle</note> aspect will be a certain minor enmity. But the third sign <note>at 60 degrees</note> agrees with the first; therefore, it produces evidence of minor friendship. The fourth sign <note>at 90 degrees</note>, finally, is contrary; therefore, it produces an aspect of a second, greater enmity. For this reason, the Moon in the fourth sign indicates either the victory of the disease or of nature, for whom the sign that is an "enemy" to the beginning of the disease is beneficial. 

In the fifth sign <note>at 120 degrees</note>, friendship is increased because of the powers of the **trine** <note>original: *trigoni*</note> and the agreement of the signs; it is called the aspect of greatest friendship. Finally, the sixth sign <note>at 150 degrees</note> ought to make a hostile aspect. It is not, however, considered by astrologers because it does not produce other aspects; but this reasoning is not sufficiently physical. I would rather say there is a radiation to the sixth sign. But since it is contrary, and its contrariety is completed in the seventh sign—where the end of the diameter and the greatest and most adverse distance is celebrated—for that reason, the aspect of the sixth is kept silent, or it is ineffective. 

It is proven that this contrariety of signs is the cause of aspects, just as familiarity is; for a very good **crisis** <note>original: *crisis*; the decisive turning point of a disease</note> often occurs on the sixth day in illnesses, namely when the Moon, increased in motion, reaches the fourth sign before the seventh day. We shall treat this matter in our medical writings.

The **duodenary** <note>30-degree</note> aspect is thus described as <image-desc>glyph resembling a capital Q, used here to represent the duodenary or semisextile aspect</image-desc>, and the **octagonal** <note>45-degree</note> aspect as <image-desc>glyph resembling a circumflex or caret symbol (^), used to represent the octogonal or semi-square aspect</image-desc>.

# CONCERNING ASTROLOGY

->*The Scheme of Aspects follows.*<-

<image-desc>A circular astrological diagram entitled "Schema aspectuum" showing the relationships between zodiac signs and the major aspects. The outer ring contains the twelve zodiac symbols (Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, Pisces). Within the circle, geometric lines illustrate aspects: a horizontal line with small circles at the center and ends represents opposition; triangles represent trines (trigonus); squares represent squares (quadratus); and hexagons represent sextiles (sextilis). Symbols for these aspects (sextile *, square □, trine △) are annotated near the corresponding geometric intersections.</image-desc>

8 These aspects, when considered within the **Zodiac**, behave as follows. However, because the **crooked signs** <note>original: *signa tortuosa*; also known as signs of short ascension, which appear to rise more quickly and at a steeper angle over the horizon</note> ascend rapidly—and more of them pass than degrees of the equator—it happens that what is a **square** <note>90-degree</note> aspect in the Zodiac may actually be a **sextile** <note>60-degree</note> on the equator. Conversely, a **trine** <note>120-degree aspect</note> of **long ascensions** <note>signs that take longer to rise, like Leo or Virgo</note> in **straight signs** <note>original: *signis rectis*; signs that rise more vertically</note> becomes a square, which is considered a hostile aspect. Truly, in the part of the heaven where these signs ascend, they behave in this way—though not at the **Midheaven** <note>original: *M. C.* or *Medium Coeli*; the highest point of the sky</note> or the **Bottom of the Heaven** <note>original: *I. C.* or *Imum Coeli*; the lowest point</note>. On the other hand, in the western part where they descend, the signs of short ascension become signs of long descension; therefore, the opposite occurs: a square there may change into a trine, and a sextile into a square.

9 Aspects are distinguished into **dexter** <note>right-handed</note> and **sinister** <note>left-handed</note>. A **dexter** aspect occurs against the natural order of the signs; a **sinister** aspect follows the order, moving from one star or degree to another star or degree.

10 There is, furthermore, the **partile** <note>exact to the degree</note> and **platick** <note>within a wider range or 'orb' of influence</note> aspect. A partile aspect occurs when exactly as many degrees are placed between the planets as the aspect requires, such as 90 degrees for a **square** <note>original: *□*</note>. This aspect is sometimes calculated according to both **longitude** <note>position along the ecliptic</note> and **latitude** <note>distance north or south of the ecliptic</note>. In a **conjunction**, both are required to be the same. In an **opposition**, however, the longitude must be the same, but not the latitude; for if one planet is in the south, the other must be in the north to be truly opposite. In **trines** <note>original: *△*</note>, a contrary latitude is required, but it must be unequal—specifically, half the measure of the star's latitude. In a **sextile** <note>original: * * *</note>, the latitude should be the same but unequal, namely half the star's latitude. In **squares**, no specific latitude is observed, as they always fall exactly <note>original: *partiliter*</note> upon the **ecliptic** <note>the sun's apparent path</note>. Regarding where the aspects of **fixed stars** situated outside the Zodiac fall upon the ecliptic, see the table of **Thomas Fincke** <note>original: *Finchi*; a Danish mathematician and astronomer, 1561–1656, known for his work on spherical trigonometry</note>.

11 A **platick** configuration is one where the planets are joined not by their physical bodies, but by their light...

### Concerning Platic Aspects, and their Properties.

### ARTICLE II.

1 A **platic aspect** <note>original: *aspectus platicus*; from the Greek "platys" meaning "wide." This refers to an aspect that is "wide" or approximate rather than "partile" or exact to the degree.</note> is divided into **application** and **separation** <note>original: *defluxum*; literally a "flowing away."</note>. **Application** is the approach of a fast planet toward a slow one, either by body <note>a physical conjunction</note> or by ray <note>a geometric aspect</note>, within the orb of their lights. **Separation**, however, is their withdrawal. Therefore, separation occurs from fixed stars and slow planets, and application occurs toward them; both are better the more closely they are joined.

2 Applications and separations occur either between two planets, three, or more.

3 There are four species of application and separation between two planets. The first is simple: when both planets are **direct** <note>moving forward through the zodiac</note>, and the lighter <note>faster-moving</note> planet is at a lower degree while the slow one is at a higher degree. **Separation**, conversely, occurs when the lighter planet is at a higher degree, moving away from the slow one.

4 The second species is when both are **retrograde** <note>appearing to move backward in the zodiac from the perspective of Earth</note>, but the lighter planet is at a higher degree of the sign and overtakes the slow one by its own speed. If it is at a lower degree, it is separation.

5 The third is **mutual application**, when one is direct at a lower degree and the other is retrograde at a higher degree, and they move to meet each other. On the contrary, when the direct planet is at a higher degree and the retrograde is at a lower, both "flow away" from each other, which indicates a **frustration of the effect** <note>original: *frustrationem... effectus*; a technical term meaning the predicted astrological event or influence fails to materialize because the planets never complete their meeting.</note>.

6 The fourth is when the lighter planet is retrograde at a higher degree and the slow one is direct at a lower degree; for then, instead of separation, application occurs.

<summary>This page defines the "orbs" (ranges of influence) for stars and planets and explains "platic" aspects, detailing the four ways planets can approach or move away from one another based on their speed and direction.</summary>

<keywords>platic aspect, application, separation, planetary orbs, retrograde motion, direct motion, frustration of effect, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical classification of astrological relationships between planets. This section moves into complex interactions where a third planet mediates or interferes with the relationship between two others.</meta>

->OF ASTROLOGICAL MATTERS<-

<meta>catchword: 7 In the same way</meta>

7 In the same way, **applications** and **separations** <note>original: *defluxus*; literally a "flowing away," referring to a planet moving out of an aspect.</note> occur in **antiscia** <note>points on the zodiac that are equidistant from the solstice points (0° Cancer/0° Capricorn), sharing the same amount of daylight</note> and **equidistances**, and many other types are derived from these.

8 Regarding the aspects involving three **planets**, many types occur: namely, the **translation of light**, **restitution**, **collection**, **prohibition**, **perturbation**, and **abscission**.

9 **Translation of light** <note>original: *translatio luminis*; a scenario where a faster planet acts as a messenger, connecting two slower planets that are not in a direct relationship</note> happens in three ways. First, when a "light" planet <note>a faster-moving planet, like the Moon</note> passes between two planets slower than itself, either by physical body or by ray <note>a geometric aspect</note>, and transfers the light of the first to the second along with its own. Second, when a fast planet joins a slower one by ray, and that slower planet is configured to another slower one to which the fast planet is not; in this case, the slow planet "hands over" the light of the fast one to the third planet. Third, when they are all in the same zodiac sign, and the middle planet communicates with both outer planets, but the outer ones do not communicate with each other; then the middle planet transfers the power of the first to the second.

10 **Collection of light** <note>original: *collectio luminis*</note> also occurs in this way, specifically when one planet gazes upon two others who do not see each other; it is said to "collect" their light, either by moving toward them or by moving away from them.

11 **Restitution** <note>original: *redditio*; also called "return of light"</note> of light occurs when one or two planets gaze upon another planet that is weak—for example, if it is **combust** <note>so close to the Sun that its power is overwhelmed by the Sun's heat</note> or **retrograde**—and cannot retain their powers. Therefore, it is said to "restore" the light, since its light benefits the other planets more than it benefits itself.

12 **Prohibition** of light occurs in two ways. First, when a slow planet is found between two lighter ones in the same sign; for then it "prohibits" them from sharing light with each other. Such a prohibition is helpful when the meeting of the lighter planets would have been unfavorable, but harmful when it would have been good. Second, when a lighter planet is joined to a heavy one by physical body, and another planet gazing at it is at the same degree by ray as the lighter one; then the connection of the gazing planet's ray is prohibited by the lighter planet, because a physical body is considered more powerful than a ray. But if the gazing planet is several degrees away from the heavy one, it will prohibit the light of the lighter planet.

13 **Perturbation** <note>original: *perturbatio*; a disturbance or interference</note> is said to occur when two planets are moving toward a relationship, and before they can complete it, a third planet—being heavy and located at a further degree—is joined to the middle one, whether that third planet reached it through **retrocession** <note>moving backward through the zodiac</note> or through slow movement. In this case, the intended union of the first two is said to be "perturbed."

14 **Abscission** <note>original: *abscissio*; literally a "cutting off"</note> occurs when two slow planets are hurrying toward a conjunction, and a third fast planet, located at a lower degree, passes the first one before it can join the second. Thus, the lighter planet is said to "cut off" the light of the middle planet from the heavy one behind it.

<summary>This page defines the sophisticated mechanics of how light and influence are shared or blocked between three or more planets, detailing terms like "translation," "collection," and "prohibition." These concepts allow astrologers to determine if a predicted event will be fulfilled, delayed, or cancelled by the interference of a third celestial body.</summary>

<keywords>translation of light, collection of light, restitution, prohibition, perturbation, abscission, antiscia, planetary aspects, astrological mechanics</keywords>

# On certain other conditions of applications and separations.

## ARTICLE III.

1 Furthermore, these **separations** <note>original: *defluxus*; the movement of a planet away from an aspect</note> and **applications** <note>original: *applicationes*; the movement of a planet toward a precise aspect</note> undergo certain conditions which are called **frustration**, **refraining**, **void of course**, **ferality**, **pulsation**, **reception**, and **besiegement**.

2 **Frustration** <note>original: *frustratio*</note> is when a light <note>faster-moving</note> planet hastens toward a conjunction with a heavy <note>slower-moving</note> planet at the very end of a zodiac sign; but the heavy planet, entering into another sign, joins with the ray <note>aspect</note> of another planet that is looking toward it. Consequently, the light planet does not apply to the heavy one before it applies to the rays of the other; therefore, such a conjunction is said to be "frustrated."

3 **Refraining** <note>original: *refrænatio*</note> is when a light planet seeking a conjunction with another becomes **retrograde** <note>appearing to move backward in the sky</note> before the conjunction is joined.

4 A planet is said to be **void of course** <note>original: *vacuus cursu*</note> while it is separating from one planet and joins with no other, neither by body nor by ray, within the boundaries of the orb of its own light.

5 A planet is called **feral** <note>original: *feralis*; meaning "wild" or "beast-like"</note> when it is alone in one sign and is not supported by the radiation <note>aspect</note> of any other planet.

6 **Pulsation** <note>original: *pulsatio*; often called "pushing" or "giving" power</note> is twofold. One type is when a planet existing in the **dignity** <note>a sign or degree where a planet has specific influence, like its "home"</note> of another planet aspects that owner; for then it restores or sends its own dignity to it. The other type is when a light planet existing in its own dignity aspects a heavy planet that has no dignity in the light planet's location; in that case, the light planet hands over its own dignity to the heavy one.

7 **Reception** <note>original: *receptio*</note> is when each planet is in the dignity of the other, such as **Jupiter** <note>♃</note> in **Aquarius** <note>♒</note> and **Saturn** <note>♄</note> in **Pisces** <note>♓</note>. Or, it is when a planet existing in its own dignity aspects another that also has dignity in that same place; for it communicates its own dignity and the dignity of the other to that planet.

8 A planet is **besieged** <note>original: *obseſſus*</note> when it is surrounded by two others, either by body or by ray. If it is surrounded by two **malefics** <note>planets considered naturally harmful, like Mars or Saturn</note>, it is greatly afflicted; if by **benefics** <note>helpful planets like Jupiter or Venus</note>, it is aided. A malefic planet loses its power to do harm in this state, but at the cost of the benefics' strength—something I have experienced more than once.

# On the nature, lordship, and action of the fixed stars upon lower things, both by themselves and with the planets.

## CHAPTER XI. ARTICLE I.

1 Since the **fixed stars** are most distant from the earth, their powers are first communicated to the planets, and through them to our earthly affairs. Yet, according to whether they agree or disagree with those planets, they either increase or diminish the planets' powers.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature and influence of fixed stars, following the numbering established on the previous page regarding planetary conditions. ASTROLOGY, BOOK I.

2 Just as planets in the northern part are more powerful according to their latitude and **declination** <note>the distance of a star or planet north or south of the celestial equator</note> than they are in the southern part on this side of the equator, so it is with the **fixed stars**; but the reverse is true beyond the equator.

3 The fixed stars that are **vertical** <note>original: *verticales*; stars directly overhead at the zenith</note> are in the first rank of power for judging the customs of regions and for affecting lower things; second are the **horizontal** stars, because they are always **angular** <note>original: *angulares*; located at the four most powerful points of a horoscope: the rising, setting, highest, and lowest points</note>, which we spoke of a little while ago. Third are those within the **Zodiac**, but especially those on the **ecliptic** <note>the sun's apparent path across the sky; the center line of the Zodiac</note>. This is because the Zodiac is the higher place of the acting planets and those that carry their virtues, and from there the Sun pours out its powers, by which it changes all things. Therefore, that location is well-suited for action and for forming astrological configurations. In that place, stars can be joined with planets and increased in power. For this reason, the **Moon** is the most powerful of all over our worldly beings, because she is the nearest, and she collects and sends down the virtues of all the others; by her speed, she applies her influence to one planet before she has even separated from another, completing all **aspects** <note>original: *aspectus*; specific geometric angles between celestial bodies</note> with all others very swiftly.

4 The fixed stars rule over all things to which the planets most similar to them correspond.

5 The similarity of fixed stars to planets is distinguished first by **color**. For those that are clear and splendid are of the nature of **Jupiter**. Those that are very bright but have a certain faint redness are assigned to the **Sun**. Those that are most brilliant and the color of boxwood <note>a yellowish-white hue</note> belong to **Venus**. Those that are leaden are of **Saturn**, such as <term>Algol</term> <note>a star in the constellation Perseus, traditionally associated with misfortune</note>. Red stars belong to **Mars**, such as <term>Aldebaran</term> <note>the bright red "eye" of the constellation Taurus</note>. Ash-colored stars that are sparkling and varied in hue belong to **Mercury**. Those that are bright white, pale, and of a dull light are **lunar**. Cloudy and spotted stars, especially those that are somewhat reddish like <term>Arcturus</term> <note>the brightest star in the constellation Boötes</note>, are ascribed to the Moon and Mars. Indeed, the entire <term>Galaxy</term> <note>original: *Galaxia*; the Milky Way</note> appears to be lunar. However, those that are dark are considered lunar and Saturnine.

6 Stars of the **first magnitude** <note>the brightest stars visible to the naked eye</note> are the most effective; the others follow according to their size and position, as has been said.

7 Those stars that have the clearest light produce illustrious effects. Those that sparkle the most cause great disturbances. Those with a dense light are effective; those with a thin light are weaker. Those that are obscure and cloudy produce bad, hidden, and unhappy effects.

8 Furthermore, they act together with the planets when they are in the same circle of position, or in some angle, while those planets are rising, or reaching the highest point, the middle, or the bottom of the sky, or at any of the four points of rising or setting.

9 They rule over those regions governed by a similar planet, or by the **triplicity** <note>original: *triangulus*; a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element</note> in which they are configured, or where they are vertical or horizontal. For those stars that do not "gaze upon" <note>do not form a geometric aspect with</note> a place do not act upon it, as we shall say regarding eclipses.

# ASTROLOGICAL MATTERS
## BOOK THE SECOND.
### Concerning the great changes, beginnings, and causes of human affairs.

->*From which causes, principles, and signs from heaven the prognosis must be made; and which matters are left for the Astrologer to handle in the following books.*<-

### CHAPTER I. ARTICLE I.

<margin>1</margin><image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'P' decorated with scrolling leaves and flowers.</image-desc>After we have thoroughly discussed, as best we could, the celestial principles and causes of the changes in the lower world <note>The "lower world" refers to the Earth and its atmosphere, which medieval science believed was governed by the "higher" celestial spheres</note>, we shall now teach how to physically <note>original: *physicè*; meaning according to the laws of nature/physics as understood at the time</note> derive judgments of future effects from those same causes and principles.

2 Indeed, the causes themselves are the stars—and not just the **zodiac signs**—as **St. Thomas** <note>original: *S. Thomas*; referring to Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), who sought to reconcile astrology with Christian theology by arguing that stars influence the body and passions, but not the soul's free will</note> excellently proves. These stars cause bodily changes directly, but affect the human will only "by accident" <note>An Aristotelian term meaning the stars might influence a person's mood or physical state, which then influences their choices, rather than the stars forcing the will directly</note>. The **principles** <term>Principles: the specific geometric and temporal markers used to start a calculation</term>, however, are the **conjunctions** <note>when two planets meet at the same degree</note> of the stars, their **aspects** <note>the specific angles between planets, such as squares or trines</note>, the variation of their positions, their transition from sign to sign and into the **cardinal points** <note>the equinoxes and solstices that mark the changes of seasons</note>, and the intersections of circles. From these, therefore, we shall bring forth our judgments.

3 No single general effect from the heavens can happen in the entire lower world all at once and in the same way, unless the whole heaven acts identically simultaneously and everywhere in all its parts. Hence, not even the **Sun**, which is the most universal cause, shines everywhere on **Earth** <note>original: *telluris*</note>, nor does it create the same year everywhere at once; rather, it produces spring here, autumn there, heat in one place, and winter in another at the very same time. For this reason, it is necessary to contemplate which causes influence which regions, and at what beginnings; then, by which **luminaries** <note>The Sun and the Moon</note> and specifically in which matters.

<margin>4</margin> <meta>catchword: For</meta>

<summary>This page introduces Book II of the treatise, shifting from the physics of the stars to the methodology of astrological prediction. It defines "causes" as the stars themselves and "principles" as their movements and alignments, while noting that celestial influence varies by geographic location.</summary>
<keywords>astrological judgment, St. Thomas Aquinas, celestial causes, conjunctions, cardinal points, solar influence, regional astrology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introduction to the second book, transitioning from the theoretical causes of celestial influence to the practical application of astrology in human history, weather, and regional character.</meta>

4 Therefore, every <term>astrological judgment</term> <note>original: *iudicium astrologicum*; a formal conclusion or prediction based on celestial data</note> is either about the transformations of the air, the sea, and the earth—from which we calculate the scarcity or abundance of things both useful and harmful to us—or about the beginnings and changes of monarchies and republics, and the migrations of peoples, laws, and customs, and of cities and provinces; or about the birth, life, death, and events of every individual person; or finally, about the good or bad choices in matters to be done. For we do not choose to navigate in the winter, and human liberty uses the stars and does not serve them in this judgment, as the ignorant believe—so says **Albert the Great**, not the least among theologians <note>**Albertus Magnus** (c. 1200–1280) was a dominant figure in medieval science who argued that while stars influence the physical body and "lower" nature, the human soul remains free</note>. Therefore, it is necessary to write books on these four topics, setting aside the nonsense of the Arabian and Jewish astrologers, who derive judgments from non-causes and non-signs, and are entangled in various errors.

5 It is necessary, however, above all to speak of the changes of the air as the most certain matters, from which we shall proceed to the uncertain. But since the air changes differently in different regions, it seems necessary first to speak of the conditions and customs of regions according to the heavens.

### *A dissertation on the domains of the planets according to our opinion, and that of the Arabs by climates, and of Ptolemy by triangles over all regions of the world; and concerning the error of the Arabs, and moreover the insufficiency of Ptolemy.*

## CHAPTER II. ARTICLE II.

1 Although **St. Cyril** <note>Cyril of Alexandria (c. 376–444), a Church Father who wrote extensively against pagan philosophy</note> in his books against Julian, and **St. Clement of Rome** attribute the customs of nations to laws rather than the stars—indeed, they deny they should be attributed to the stars—nevertheless, **St. Thomas**, the explainer of the Fathers, praises **Ptolemy** in the book *On the Governance of Rulers* <note>original: *De Regimine Principum*; a political treatise attributed to Thomas Aquinas and his followers</note>, because he distinguished the customs of regions by the heavens. This is because heat, cold, the humors, and temperaments are produced and affected by the heavens, so that they dispose the <term>sensitive soul</term> <note>In medieval philosophy, the "sensitive soul" handles physical senses and emotions, which were believed to be influenced by the stars, whereas the "rational soul" remained free</note> toward certain customs. He also praises **Macrobius** for calling the Jews <term>Saturnines</term> <note>original: *Saturninos*; people characterized by the influence of the planet Saturn, often associated with melancholy or specific religious strictness</note>, and therefore shrinking from the customs of other nations. Those Church Fathers, however, were considering principal causes; St. Thomas considered them dispositively and instrumentally, as has been said. For this reason, we shall consider them in the same way.

3 Nations are distinguished by **Ptolemy** into **Northern** <note>original: *Aquilonares*</note>, **Southern** <note>original: *Australes*</note>, and **Middle** in our hemisphere. The same must be done in the others...

<summary>This page outlines the four main areas of astrological study (environment, politics, individual fate, and timing) and argues that celestial bodies influence human culture and physical temperament without overriding free will.</summary>
