## *Judgment of eclipses from their colors.*

### ARTICLE XI.

1 We further reason from the sign of an eclipse by considering its **colors**, and from those things which are usually gathered around them, such as **coronas** <term>coronas: original "arearum," circles of light surrounding a celestial body</term> appearing around the **Luminaries** <term>Luminaries: the Sun and the Moon</term> and stars, and **parhelia** <term>parhelia: "mock suns" or colored streaks appearing in atmospheric vapors</term> which are colored rods appearing in the vapors of the air and in objects reflecting the eclipsed light.

2 A lunar eclipse is indeed red, while a solar one is saffron-colored; but when it leans toward other colors, it takes on the nature of the planet of the same color. Ordinarily, however, the lunar color belongs to *Mars* ♂, the solar to *Venus* ♀, and the color of the rods and coronas to *Mercury* ☿.

3 Therefore, if they lean toward black or leaden-grey, they signify those things which *Saturn* ♄ brings; if toward white, *Jupiter* ♃; if toward a glowing red, *Mars* ♂; if toward yellow, *Venus* ♀; if toward a variegated color, *Mercury* ☿—only in terms of its motion and varied nature, not because the planet itself is colored that way. The other planets, however, truly possess the specific colors already mentioned.

4 If the stated property of the color is seen throughout the entire bodies of the **Luminaries**, or in the reflected locations, it affects the whole or the greater part of a region. But if it appears only from a certain part, the effect will be in those directions toward which the property inclines. For instance, if it is over Italy, it will affect that part of Italy which the color faces, whether South, North, the middle, etc.

5 A color signifying a dominant planet also arises from the approach and retreat of the **Luminaries** to the **node** <term>node: the point where the Moon's path crosses the ecliptic, where eclipses occur</term> where they are eclipsed, as **King Alfonso** <note>Alfonso X of Castile, patron of the Alfonsine Tables</note> considers. For example, if the **Sun** is eclipsed in the first degree from the node, the color will be a deep black; in the second, a dark black; in the third, dusky; in the fourth, dusky-saffron; in the fifth, clear dusky; in the sixth, reddish-dusky; in the seventh, red; in the eighth, rufous <note>a brownish-red</note>; in the ninth, shimmering-rufous; in the tenth, shimmering-red; in the eleventh, saffron; in the twelfth, white-saffron. Conversely, the **Moon** eclipsed at the 180th degree from its **apogee** <term>apogee: the point in an orbit farthest from Earth</term>...

# **On the indication and effect of comets and fiery impressions.**

## CHAPTER V. ARTICLE I.

1 The effect of comets and other fiery impressions <term>impressions: "impressionum," a term in early science for atmospheric or celestial phenomena believed to be "impressed" upon the air</term> is of the nature of **Mars** ♂ and **Mercury** ☿. Therefore, one must observe **comets**, **beams** <note>original: "trabes," long, beam-like meteors</note>, **barrels** <note>original: "dolia," rounded, barrel-shaped atmospheric fires</note>, **trumpets** <note>original: "tubæ," elongated celestial phenomena</note>, and **falling stars**, whether they shine during an eclipse or at another time; for they bring about wars, heatwaves, turbulences, and the consequences that follow from these.

2 Generally, they bring about dryness, a scarcity of water, the death of fish, winds, and battles in the place toward which they point.

3 Shooting stars and falling stars differ from comets: for the former have shorter and lesser effects; they rush in more quickly, and are always a sign of evil, except perhaps for that one man who stirs up a rebellion and triumphs. These are usually of a **Martial** <note>governed by Mars, associated with aggression</note> and wicked nature. Comets, however, have hair all around them, or a beard, or a tail. They last for six months at most, and have more lasting effects according to their duration, and according to subsequent **lunations** <note>the period between two new moons</note>, eclipses, or whether they are favored or hindered by other comets.

4 The place to be affected is that which lies beneath the **zodiac sign** in which the comet appears. The specific part of the region is known by the tilt of the tail. If it shines for a long time, the effect will be great. If it appears in the morning relative to the **Sun**, the effect will begin quickly and suddenly; if it appears in the evening, it will start slowly. The kind of thing to be affected is known from the shape of the comet.

5 Ten things must be noted in a comet: namely, color, size, brightness, shape, duration, its site <note>the specific astronomical position</note>, its location <note>the geographical area it oversees</note>, its motion, its relationship to the **stars** <image-desc>eight-pointed star symbol</image-desc>, and its position in the world.

## On the color of comets.

### ARTICLE II.

1 The color indicates which planet the comet matches in its quality and disposition. For instance, if it is dim and bald <note>original: "caluus," referring to a comet lacking a distinct tail or "mane"</note>, it produces the effects of **Saturn** ♄, which we described above; if white, the effects of **Jupiter** ♃; if ruddy, **Mars** ♂; if yellow, **Venus** ♀; if multi-colored, **Mercury** ☿.

2 A comet always adheres to the decrees of **Mars** ♂ and **Mercury** ☿. For even when it is of the nature of Jupiter, and thus beneficial for crops and health, it simultaneously indicates discord within the priesthood, brief battles, acute fevers, and the arrogance of princes. Such a comet appeared in the Galaxy <note>the Milky Way</note> in the year 1533 in the sign of **Aries** ♈︎ toward the Constellation of the Bears <note>Ursa Major or Minor</note>, and there followed the apostasy <note>referring to the break from the Roman Catholic Church</note> of Henry VIII, King of the English.

3 A comet of **Mars** ♂ produces excessive droughts; for example, the comet of Niphus <note>Agostino Nifo, a famous 16th-century Italian philosopher</note> deprived Insubria <note>a region in northern Italy, modern Lombardy</note> of rain from January until November. It also produces dreadful plagues and the most savage wars. Many examples of these exist in the history books. And Haly <note>Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer</note> tells of a comet in the sign of **Scorpio** ♏︎ (the sign of the Moors), which brought battles, the occupation of the kingdom, famine, and plague upon them.

4 A comet of **Venus** ♀ brings about "stunned" diseases <note>likely neurological conditions or apoplexy</note>, paralysis, violent fevers, heretics, and seditious people; it also brings princes who are powerful in speech, and sedition within the Law of Muhammad <note>original: "lege venerea Macometi," a common early modern polemical way of referring to Islam</note>. It acts as a Jovian influence <note>related to Jupiter</note> among Christians who live by their senses rather than being led by reason; it acts as a Saturnine influence among the Jewish people, and a Lunar influence in paganism.

5 A comet of **Mercury** ☿ brings lightning, thunder, earthquakes, great winds, savage storms, and "new arts" <note>novel inventions or ideologies</note> that are always destructive to the human race.

---

## On the splendor of comets.

### ARTICLE III.

1 Great splendor signifies effective actions which many people follow of their own accord; for this reason, leaders of heresy and invaders of foreign kingdoms often have many followers. Those comets that shine less brightly are less effective in their influence.

# On the location of comets.
## ARTICLE IV.

1 Regarding the location, note first: whether it is over land, the sea, or the waters; likewise in which province or city it appears. Second, note the stars that rule over that location, because they illuminate and influence the outcome <note>original: "negotium," meaning the matter or business at hand</note>. For example, if a maned star <note>a comet</note> is in **Leo** ♌︎, it is influenced by the **Sun** ☉. In the year 1607, in the horoscope of Emperor Rudolf <note>Rudolf II, Holy Roman Emperor</note>, there appeared in **Leo** ♌︎ a Saturnine and Mercurial star <note>a comet sharing the cold nature of Saturn and the volatile nature of Mercury</note> which deprived him of his rule, his freedom, and finally his life, as his brother Matthias waged war against him—who now rules in his place, having been raised to the first throne by the Sun. Third, note the latitude from the Zodiac; for if it is in the sign of **Aries** ♈︎, which rules over **Germany** and **England**, then you shall judge it to affect England if the latitude is northern <note>borealis</note>; or conversely Germany if it is southern <note>australis</note>. Fourth, note with which wandering star <note>planet</note> it is joined by body or by aspect <note>original: "radio," literally "by ray"</note>. Fifth, with which fixed star it is joined. Sixth, in which part of the sky it appears: for in the East it indicates youth; in the Midheaven <note>M.C., or "Medium Coeli"</note>, it indicates kings, temples, and men; in the West it indicates the elderly, ancient matters, and the death of things, as was mentioned regarding eclipses. Seventh, in which "angle" <note>one of the four pivotal points of an astrological chart: the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, or Imum Coeli</note> it falls; for indeed, according to Haly <note>the Arab astrologer Haly Abenragel</note>, when a comet fell in the angle of the conjunction <note>synodi</note> of the kingdom of the sons of Aben, Aben Aue-zir died in that same year. So it was in the horoscope of Rudolf. Eighth, regarding the shapes, the position in the eighth sphere <note>the sphere of the fixed stars</note> must be considered; such as in bestial signs <note>Zodiac signs representing animals, like Leo or Aries</note> it acts against beasts; in human signs <note>like Aquarius or Gemini</note> against humans; and in the constellation Argo over ships, as has been said; because similar things are signified by similar appearances.

2 The "location" of a comet is not the entire span of the sky through which its tail <note>original: "coma," literally "hair"</note> extends, but only that specific sign in which the body of the comet resides, from which the tail flows.

---

# On the form of comets.
## ARTICLE V.

1 The form provides an indication based on its likeness: for if it has the shape of a sword—such as the one that shone over Jerusalem before its destruction by Titus, as Flavius Josephus relates—it indicates war and the planet **Mars** ♂.

2 A pillar-shaped comet relates to **Jupiter** ♃, and it brings death to kings and priests.

## *On duration.*
### ARTICLE VI.

1 The duration of a comet indicates the magnitude of its effect and how long that state will last.
2 A brief duration, by contrast, indicates a short-lived effect. I also believe that for every month a comet lasts, its significance extends for a year, unless it is hindered or magnified by some other celestial configuration. 
3 For example, in the sixth year after the comet that shone from the east in the year 1260, the **Tartars** <note>A historical term for the Mongol Empire and associated Turkic peoples</note> invaded Asia.

---

## *On the timing of the effect.*
### ARTICLE VII.

1 The timing is likewise marked, just as in an eclipse, by when the comet appears: whether it is in the rising [the East], the <term>M. C.</term> <note>Medium Coeli, or Midheaven; the highest point in the sky at a given moment</note>, or in the setting [the West]. See what we have written on that subject elsewhere.

## *On the relationship to the Sun.*
### ARTICLE VIII.

1 If the comet is to the east of the **Sun** ☉, the effect will begin shortly; if it is to the west, it will begin late. The speed or slowness of the comet's movement signifies the same thing.

## *On Position.*
### ARTICLE IX.

1 The position declares the part of the earth toward which the tail of the comet points. The zodiac sign, however, indicates the land and the people who will be affected: specifically those who have their <term>apheta</term> <note>The "giver of life" or "releaser"; a specific point in a person's birth chart used to calculate life expectancy and major life events</note> or an aspecting planet in that sign.

On motion.</header>

### ARTICLE X.

1 Motion indicates from where the effect is to be expected: for example, if a comet moves slowly from the east toward the North <note>original: "Septentrionem"</note>, then from the east a plague, or a law, or a prince slowly traverses to the devastation of the northern regions. This is how **Tamerlane** <note>The Turco-Mongol conqueror Timur (d. 1405)</note> was signified, according to the testimony of **George of Trebizond** <note>A 15th-century Greek philosopher and scholar</note>.
2 Those which are carried against the order of the signs <note>This refers to "retrograde" motion, or moving in the opposite direction of the zodiac's usual progression</note> always portend a change of laws: because they follow the motion of the first sphere according to **Cardano** <note>Girolamo Cardano, a 16th-century Italian polymath</note>, or rather, because they move against the measure of human affairs, which are governed by failing and perishable things.
3 **Porphyry** <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> said: If a comet tends toward the South, it signifies rains; if toward the east, plague; if toward the North, droughts; if toward the west, an excellent seasonal temperature and many good things. And this is not without reason.

->*On the casting of a chart at the appearance of a comet, and the various effects derived from it.*<-

### ARTICLE XI.

1 A comet affects the place most in whose [zodiac] sign it first appears, then where it shows more splendor and strength; where it is weakened, there it operates weakly.
2 **Haly** <note>Likely Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer whose works were widely translated into Latin</note> observes the true beginning of the comet, if it can be obtained, or the place in which it resides during the first conjunction or opposition of the <term>Luminaries</term> <note>The Sun and the Moon</note> after its rising, if the beginning could not be known. Then he casts a square chart <note>The standard shape for astrological horoscopes in the Renaissance</note> for that beginning, or for the arrangement of the Luminaries, and notes all those things which we have said regarding the lordship and mixture of the stars during an eclipse. Look there for more.

## *On new stars.*

### ARTICLE XIII.

1 Some deny that "new stars" are created, because God ceased from the creation of new things; but these are not "new" in their essence, as they are made from pre-existing matter through the work of **Intelligences** <note>In medieval cosmology, "Intelligences" were angelic beings believed to guide the movement of celestial bodies</note>.

2 **Hipparchus**, according to the testimony of **Pliny**, observed a star in the heavens 120 years before the coming of Christ; this star prepared for and signaled the novelty of the age under the Romans and the coming of God. As **Saint Jerome** says: "All creatures sense their Creator." Hence, an unusual comet specified his birth, and an impossible eclipse <note>original: "Luminarium defectus impossibilis." This refers to the darkness at the Crucifixion; it was considered "impossible" by nature because it occurred during a full moon, when a natural solar eclipse cannot happen</note> of the sun and moon signified his death.

3 A new star appeared under **Tycho** in the year of Christ 1572. It appeared in the "Seat" <note>The constellation Cassiopeia is often depicted as a queen sitting on a throne or seat</note> of **Cassiopeia**, without "hair" <note>original: "sine crinibus." In Latin, *cometa* means "hairy star." Tycho’s star was a "nova," looking like a point of light rather than a comet with a tail</note>, and without parallax (therefore it was located in the starry firmament). It appeared in the month of November during a full moon, on the 5th day, at nearly the 8th hour after noon, at 24 degrees of **Scorpio** <note>original: "24. ♏"</note>, on the meridian of a region at 53 degrees longitude and 62 degrees latitude. At first, it was **Jovial** <note>original: "iouialis." Meaning it had the bright, clear appearance associated with the planet Jupiter</note>, exceeding the stars of the first magnitude...

# ON ASTROLOGICAL MATTERS
## BOOK THREE.
### On the changes of the seasons within the elements.

---

->*Concerning the changes of the elements caused by the heavens,*<-
->*and the effects of these changes.*<-

### CHAPTER I. ARTICLE I.

<margin>1</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'S' featuring a human face in the upper loop and elaborate foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>NEXT follow the astrological judgments <note>original: "iudicia sideralia"; these are the interpretations or "verdicts" drawn by an astrologer from the positions of the stars</note> of those things which happen in individual years, months, and days, within the air, waters, and lands, caused by the stars. From these, we may forecast <note>original: "prognosticamur"</note> concerning the abundance or scarcity of necessary goods, as well as the sickness, health, and plagues of both men and beasts. Furthermore, the primary effects from which the aforementioned consequences follow are: dryness, heat, cold, moisture, rains, clear skies, mists, the churning of the seas and the air, and calms. He who has foreknowledge of these primary effects will easily foresee the consequences.

->*On the year, its beginning, and its quarters.*<-

### ARTICLE II.

<margin>1</margin>
Since the progress and the ultimate ends of things lie hidden within their origins and causes, it is therefore necessary to first recognize the beginning of the year.
<margin>2</margin>
The heavens and the movements of the stars consist of a circle; for this reason, a single point cannot be easily designated as the beginning of the entire year.
<margin>3</margin>
There are four <term>cardinal points</term> <note>These are the two equinoxes and two solstices, which mark the turning points of the seasons</note> which rightly claim causality for themselves. Indeed, the turning point of **Aries** <note>the Ram</note> in the spring appears to be the beginning of the year for the Egyptians; this is also suggested by **Moses** <note>In the Book of Exodus, God instructs Moses that the month of the Passover—the spring month of Abib/Nisan—is to be the first month of the year</note>, by **Virgil** <note>The Roman poet (70–19 BC), who celebrated the arrival of spring in his agricultural poems, the *Georgics*</note>, and by others.

<summary>This page introduces the third book, which focuses on how celestial movements dictate Earth's weather, seasons, and agricultural outcomes. It identifies the spring equinox (the "turning point of Aries") as the most significant starting point for the astrological year.</summary>

<page-num>97</page-num>
<header>BOOK THREE.</header>

...and many others, because spring is warm and moist, and suitable for youth and new beginnings, causing the birth and growth of plants. At that time, the day begins to exceed the night. But for the Greeks, the sign of Cancer [the Crab] is the hinge <term>cardo</term> <note>original: "cardo"; literally 'hinge', referring here to the turning point or peak of a season</note> of summer and the beginning of the year, because the day is then at its longest and the Sun is nearest to us. For the Hebrews, however, Libra [the Scales], the hinge of autumn, begins the year; they believe that the world was created with ripe fruits, and because we then store the old crops and sow the new. Finally, for the Romans, the hinge of Capricorn [the Sea-Goat] is celebrated as the beginning of the year, because the day and the light then begin to increase and draw closer to us.

4 Since the cardinal points <note>the four turning points: the equinoxes and solstices</note> often remain hidden, and preparations precede all beginnings, one must immediately consider the preceding oppositions or conjunctions <note>Full Moons or New Moons</note> of the Luminaries <note>the Sun and Moon</note>. For from these, one may forecast the entire quarter, just as from the hinges; each hinge holds its own judgment over its particular quarter.

5 according to the Romans, as Pliny testifies, they divide the four quarters of the year based on the setting and rising of the fixed stars. Indeed, when the Lyre <note>original: "Fidicula"</note> sets in the month of February, the Favonian <note>West</note> winds begin to blow for many days, and spring opens; it is confirmed by the emergence of the Belt of Orion. In Naples, the earth begins to sprout on the 57th day after the winter solstice <note>original: "bruma"</note>, earlier in some places and later in others. On the 48th day after the vernal equinox, the rising of the Pleiades <note>original: "Vergiliarum"</note> marks the beginning of summer, and the South winds blow. Nearly 25 days after the summer solstice, the rising of the Dog Star <note>original: "Canicula"</note> increases the heat, stirs the seas, drives dogs into a frenzy, and the Etesian <note>periodical Mediterranean</note> winds blow. But later, during the setting of the Lyre, autumn begins nearly 43 days after the solstice, and the East wind blows. About 46 days after the autumnal equinox, at the setting of the Pleiades, winter begins, which is forecasted more from the setting of Orion, and the North winds blow.

6 I truly believe that the fixed stars have the greatest power during their seasons; however, I have found from experience that the quarters determined by the hinges are more certain. The cycle of the fixed stars remains the same for a long time, but that of the hinges changes almost constantly; yet the rising of the fixed stars is not entirely independent of their indication.

7 Since no chronology gives a certain beginning for the world or the year, as we have proven elsewhere, we shall make our forecasts from the four aforementioned beginnings.

For those that agree produce the necessary signified effect; those that disagree produce only a shadowy or faint effect, such as a misty humidity instead of actual rain, etc.
5 When stars agree in nature with the quarter of the year—such as **Venus** with spring, **Mars** with summer, **Saturn** with winter, **Jupiter** with summer and spring, and **Mercury** with autumn—they increase the decrees of that quarter. Those that disagree do not bring about what they promise; for **Saturn** in the sign of Cancer <note>The sign associated with the height of summer</note> will not cause wintery weather, but will instead temper the heat of the air. You should speak similarly regarding regions: for it causes winter in Italy, but merely tempers the air in Numidia <note>A region in North Africa, modern-day Algeria and Tunisia</note>.

### *A more specific judgment from the quarters of the year.*

## A R T I C L E I V.

1 When the Sun enters any of the cardinal points <note>The start of Spring, Summer, Autumn, or Winter</note>, look to where the Moon is. For if it is near the Sun and below the earth, the constitution [of the air] will be drier; if remote and above the earth, it will be wetter. If mixed with **Jupiter**, the air will be serene, temperate, and clear; with **Venus**, moist and rainy; with **Saturn**, extremely cold; with **Mars**, very hot and foggy.
2 The same reasoning applies to the fixed stars configured with the Moon at that time.
3 Consider also the lords <note>The planets that "rule" the zodiacal sign in which the Moon is located</note> of the Moon’s place, and their constellation based on nature, mixture, and signs.
4 But if you do not have the exact cardinal points, you shall consider these same things in the preceding lunation; and I have certain experience of these things.
5 Retrograde planets <note>Planets that appear to be moving backward in the sky from the perspective of Earth</note> show their powers most greatly, for they are then closest to the earth.

## Concerning the judgment of the quarters of the year and months, and the nature of the signs and fixed stars.

### CHAPTER II. ARTICLE I.

1 Make for yourself a table of the risings and settings of the fixed stars in your region: and observe over many years what wind, or cold, or heat, or storm the rising, setting, and relation to the Sun of each star produces. In this way, you will be able to provide prognostications for many years, until the stars pass into another sign <note>Due to the precession of the equinoxes, the position of fixed stars relative to the zodiac signs changes very slowly over centuries.</note>. Some require an observation of 30 years to fully investigate the configuration of **Saturn** and the planets with the fixed stars and their effects.

2 The properties of the signs are described by **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose "Tetrabiblos" was the foundational text for Western astrology.</note> as follows:

♈︎ **Aries**, because it is the equinoctial sign, is generally thunderous and prone to hail: specifically, this is intensified or diminished according to the nature of the wandering stars <term>planetae</term> within it. The first parts cause rain and winds; the middle parts are temperate; the final parts are sweltering and pestilential. The northern region is sweltering and corrupting; the southern is icy and somewhat cold.

♉︎ **Taurus** is generally somewhat warm: specifically, the first parts, where the **Pleiades** <note>original: "Vergiliæ"</note> are located, are turbulent, windy, and cloudy; the middle parts are moistening and cold; the final parts, where the **Hyades** <note>original: "suculæ"; literally "little sows," a common Latin name for this cluster</note> are located, are fiery, and prone to lightning and thunder. The northern region is temperate; the southern is uncertain.

♊︎ **Gemini** is universally temperate. In the first parts, it brings a corrupting humidity; in the middle, it is temperate; in the final parts, it is uncertain and mixed. The northern region is windy and causes the earth to shake; the southern is arid and sweltering.

♋︎ **Cancer** universally brings clear skies and heat: specifically, in the beginning near the **Manger** <note>original: "Præsepe"; a star cluster also known as the Beehive Cluster</note> it is suffocating, shakes the earth, and pours out thick mist. The middle is temperate; the end is windy. In both the northern and southern regions, it is fiery, corrupting, and sweltering.

♌︎ **Leo** universally swelters and suffocates: specifically, the beginning is suffocating and sweltering. The middle is temperate, and the end is dry. From the North, it is unstable and fiery; from the South, it is humid.

♍ **Virgo** is generally moist and thunderous: specifically, it is somewhat warm and unhealthy in the beginning; temperate in the middle; and windy at the end. The northern part is windy, while the southern part is temperate.
♎ **Libra** is generally varied and changeable: specifically, it is temperate in the beginning and middle, and watery at the end. ## *An examination of Ptolemy's decrees on the nature of the signs.*
### ARTICLE II.

<margin>1</margin> These are the properties we have from **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, whose 2nd-century work "Tetrabiblos" defined these associations.</note> regarding the signs, in which he seems to have considered two things: namely, the effects of the **Sun** in each individual sign, and this in regard to general qualities. For indeed, it thunders in **Scorpio**; it stirs up winds in **Sagittarius**; it rains in **Capricorn**, etc., because the forces of the Sun relative to our climates are such that where it is near, it sends forth heat; where it is remote, it sends thick vapors easily converted into moisture; at medium distances, it sends moderate vapors from which winds are produced, as we discussed in our *Physiology* <term>Phyſiologia</term> <note>In this period, "physiology" referred to natural philosophy—the study of how the physical world and nature function.</note>. Secondly, he considered the particular natures of the stars within each sign. For this reason, he says **Cancer** produces a "suffocation" <note>A sense of heavy, sultry air.</note> in the beginning because the **Manger** <term>Præſepe</term> <note>The star cluster M44, also known as the Beehive Cluster.</note> was located there; and he attributes the turbulence of clouds and winds to the first parts of **Taurus** because the **Pleiades** <term>Vergiliæ</term> <note>The famous "Seven Sisters" star cluster.</note> were located there. Thus, he arrives at special decrees by considering specific stars and their effects.

<margin>2</margin> But indeed, it seems that Ptolemy has erred in two ways. First, because <meta>catchword: quoniam (because)</meta>

<summary>This page concludes a list of the weather-altering characteristics of the zodiac signs and begins a critical analysis of Ptolemy's meteorological astrology, noting that his theories were based on solar effects and the positions of specific star clusters like the Pleiades.</summary>

### BOOK THREE. 101
<sig>N 3</sig>

...since those signs which he described do not produce the same effects everywhere: for they behave one way across the equator toward the South, another way under the equator, and another way at the poles. Therefore, the doctrine is insufficient. Secondly, he errs because the fixed stars pass from one sign to another; those stars that were in Aries <note>original symbol: ♈. Aries is the first sign of the zodiac.</note> during the time of Ptolemy are now in Taurus <note>original symbol: ♉</note>, and those that were in Taurus are now in Gemini <note>original symbol: ♊</note>. For this reason, he does not provide a permanent Physics based on the properties of the stars, but perhaps only in a general sense, which his commentators have not fully understood. <note>This refers to the "precession of the equinoxes," where the positions of the stars slowly shift relative to the calendar year over centuries.</note>

<margin>3</margin> Cardano <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian mathematician and astrologer who attempted to defend classical astrology.</note> responds that this doctrine is perpetual because those properties are inscribed in the **ninth sphere** (which we claim is nothing at all, but merely empty space without stars). He thinks that even if this sphere lacks stars of its own, and even though the stars migrate from sign to sign, the "impressions" made by the eighth sphere <note>In ancient cosmology, the eighth sphere held the fixed stars.</note> during Ptolemy's time remain impressed upon the ninth; and thus, the philosophy is made certain.

<margin>4</margin> But this wise man is hallucinating far too much. For that space is incapable of being affected by us <note>original: "expers est passionis nobis." In Aristotelian terms, this means it cannot undergo physical change or "passion."</note>. Indeed, the sky in that space is similar to the sky described by Ptolemy following Aristotle, who introduced a "fifth nature" <note>The "aether" or "quintessence," believed to be unchangeable and incorruptible.</note> that is unalterable. But even if the stars did imprint heat and light into the heavens at the time they were passing through, when they move on and others succeed them, the previous heat and light would move on too. Or, if it remained, it would be pulled into a different temperament and different powers by the other incoming stars. Therefore, the signs would not act as they did before. Certainly, even the earth, when affected by heat, does not produce the same effects when a different heat arrives. How much less would the unchangeable sky or space do so?

<margin>5</margin> Therefore, we have satisfied the first point, since we have transferred the general powers to the opposite signs in the Antarctic hemisphere; and since we have distinguished the houses of the Planets under the equator, we philosophize similarly about the particular powers under the poles in various ways. Now, **Martial** <note>Stars or planets with the hot, aggressive nature of Mars.</note> stars create a terrible heat at the equator; in the sub-polar regions, they create less heat; and in the middle regions, a moderate amount. You may say the same for **Saturnine** <note>Cold, restrictive nature of Saturn.</note> and **Jovial** <note>Temperate, benevolent nature of Jupiter.</note> stars, according to their proportion. Likewise, we contend that the general and specific powers are modified according to the nature of the Planet ruling in each climate. For the **Pleiades** <note>original: "Vergiliae," a cluster of stars in Taurus traditionally associated with storms.</note> disturb the lower regions differently in a middle Jovial climate—that is, moderately and temperately—whereas under a **Venereal** <note>Influenced by Venus.</note> climate they blow too much; they cause disturbances under a **Martial** climate, adding storms and lightning; and under a **Saturnine** climate, they will bring hail and thunder. This data, however, ought to be set down in a table based on observations in each region, as has been said. For that reason, they will also affect other signs differently.

<margin>6</margin> Regarding the second point, we respond that the nature of all signs concerning...

...specific effects do not persist, but only the general ones. For example, the Sun <note>original symbol: ☉</note> now brings about spring and the characteristics of spring while in Pisces <note>original symbol: ♓</note>, just as it once did in Aries <note>original symbol: ♈</note>; and it brings summer while in Gemini <note>original symbol: ♊</note>, just as it once did in Cancer <note>original symbol: ♋</note>. The same applies to the rest. The general properties of the four quarters of the year are caused by the Sun, but they are modified by the planets and the fixed stars. Therefore, I maintain that the nature of the signs has changed regarding their specific effects. For the star Aldebaran <note>A prominent red giant star, the "Eye of the Bull."</note> does not cloud or disturb the sky in the same way now that it is at 5 degrees of Gemini <note>original symbol: ♊</note> as it once did when it was at 7 degrees of Taurus <note>original symbol: ♉</note>. This is because Taurus, being closer to winter, was generally colder than Gemini, which possesses more of the heat of summer. Therefore, the heat from Aldebaran now thins out the air and the clouds more effectively than before. When we make a prognosis, we must take this into account: we should increase or diminish the perceived power of the fixed stars depending on whether they have moved into a sign of a hotter or colder season, or we must temper our judgment accordingly. Likewise, we must observe how much the star agrees or disagrees with the following sign.

### *Forecasts based on the quarters of the year: and first, concerning spring.*

## CHAPTER III. ARTICLE I.

1 Signs of great humidity in spring—judged by the Sun's <note>original symbol: ✳</note> entry into Aries <note>original symbol: ♈</note>, the preceding new moon, and the rising of the fixed stars—partially determine the rotting of fruit and a surplus of useless weeds. Furthermore, if a cold winter preceded and a rainy spring follows, fevers and eye inflammations <note>original: *lippitudines*, a common historical term for various eye infections or discharges.</note> will abound in the summer as the humors <note>The "four humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) were believed to govern health; it was thought they could "melt" or "boil" depending on the weather.</note> collected in the body heat up and are released; this is even more likely if it also rains during the summer.

2 Signs of great heat signify early flowering and leafing, and fruits that appear beautiful but lack flavor and scent; they also indicate the onset of acute diseases.

3 Signs of cold and dryness signify that frost will fall during the new moon when the fixed stars rise, or during the "cardinal" points <note>The equinoxes and solstices.</note>. Very little fruit will be produced and no wine at all. Indeed, if a southern <note>original: *austrina*. In the Northern Hemisphere, a "southern" winter was considered unseasonably warm and moist.</note> winter preceded, the thick humors built up during that winter are congealed in the spring and then liquefied by the summer. From this follows hoarseness, eye inflammations for those of a bilious temperament, dysentery for women, and a state of lethargy <note>original: *stupor*</note> for the elderly.

4 Signs of dryness produce few but high-quality fruits, but no grain.

5 Signs of coldness produce late-ripening fruits, as has been stated.

## On the Forecast of Summer.

### ARTICLE II.

1 A rainy summer rots summer fruits, causes a shortage of grain <note>original: frumenti</note>, pestilential diseases, suffocating catarrhs <note>A term for the buildup of mucus in the nose or throat, which was often viewed as a dangerous "downflow" of humors in early medicine.</note>, eye pains, and bowel fluxes <note>original: fluxus alui, likely referring to dysentery or diarrhea.</note>.

2 A drier summer brings a scarcity of grain, but healthy summer fruits; it causes the death of fish and very acute diseases, especially for those of a bilious temperament <note>In the system of the four humors, "bilious" (or choleric) individuals were thought to be naturally hot and dry; excess heat in summer would push them into illness.</note>, as well as insanity and dry inflammation of the eyes <note>original: aridam lippitudinem</note>.

3 A hotter summer brings many acute diseases, an abundance of summer fruits, burning fevers, and delirium.

4 A cold summer brings a year of safety and health, but late-ripening fruits.

## Forecast of Autumn.

### ARTICLE III.

1 A wetter autumn rots the grapes and makes wines that will spoil in the spring; a scarcity of grain follows in the coming year. Likewise, it brings rheumatisms <note>In this context, "rheumata" refers to the pathological flow of watery humors through the body.</note> and quartan fevers <note>A type of malaria characterized by paroxysms that occur every fourth day.</note>. And if a northern <note>original: borealis</note> summer preceded it, they will together produce a disease-ridden winter with headaches, coughs, hoarseness, and wasting diseases <note>original: tabes</note>; these are caused by many collected humors which are further increased by the winter.

2 If it is drier, there will be a shortage of millet; and if a dry summer also preceded it, there will be good health for the phlegmatic <note>original: pituitoſis; those with a cold, moist temperament were thought to benefit from dry weather.</note> and for women; but it will be hostile to the bilious, bringing mania, delirium, and so on.

3 If it is hotter, it will be sickly and bad. Almost all wines will be sweet; olives, chestnuts, acorns, myrtles, and many herbs will ripen quickly.

4 If it is colder, there will be a loss of autumnal fruits in terms of quantity, beauty, and flavor; grass will be scarce, common garden vegetables will be tough, fodder will be parched, and there will be indigestion <note>original: cruditas</note> and frost-bite <note>original: aſſideratio; can also refer to being "star-blasted" or a sudden stroke caused by cold.</note>.

5 After a northern winter, a southern spring, and a dry summer, there usually follows an autumn ruinous to all, especially children; it brings indigestion in the belly, bleary-eyedness in the head, and phlegm in the lungs.

## *Forecast of Winter.*

### ARTICLE IV.

1 A colder and drier winter is praised. An extremely cold winter kills trees that are warm by nature, as well as wild beasts, livestock, figs, peaches, and citrus trees: if it rages more fiercely, it even kills olives, apricots <note>original: chrysómela, literally "gold-apples."</note>, and cherries.

2 A warm and humid winter is unhealthy and hostile to the grain crops; it is full of joint pains, as the humors <note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were the bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—whose balance determined health. Warm, wet weather was thought to stir them up excessively.</note> are overflowing and stirred up. It will abound in useless weeds. There will be many vegetables and fish. Plants will bloom early, especially almonds. But if cold follows this warmth, the flowers will wither, and a sterile year will follow.

## *Appendix of various forecasts in the quarters of the year.*

### ARTICLE V.

1 All immoderate weather is bad: likewise the perversion of the seasons <note>referring to when a season behaves like its opposite, such as a "wintry" spring.</note>: likewise excessive consistency: likewise much inconsistency.

2 A multitude of winds is harmful to fruits, but a lack of them is bad for grain crops. A calm across the whole year usually brings pestilence, since persistent heat accumulates smoky vapors <note>original: fuliginefos vapores; these were thought to be "miasma" or polluted air that carried disease.</note>.

3 A conjunction of the Luminaries <note>original: Synodus Luminarium; an alignment of the Sun and the Moon, such as a New Moon.</note> is hotter in summer, because they then hang over us at the same time: but in winter, the opposition <note>a Full Moon, when the Sun and Moon are on opposite sides of the Earth.</note> is hotter: for then the Moon reaches its highest point <note>original: culminat</note> for us.

4 I say the same of hot planets, and the opposite of cold ones.

5 The Galaxy <note>the Milky Way</note> overflows with milky moisture for the crops; it passes through Capricorn <note>original: ♑</note> and Cancer <note>original: ♋</note>. There, the northern Eagle <note>the constellation Aquila</note> and the southern Dog Star <note>Canicula or Sirius</note> are in the junctions. At the rising of these stars, if there is a full moon in summer alone during clear nights, or a new moon <note>original: interlunium</note> in winter, then blight <note>original: carbunculus</note>, smut <note>original: vredo</note>, and rust <note>original: rubigo</note> occur. This happens because the Moon is freezing and fills that "milky moisture" with bitterness, killing the crops following their birth, whether they are winter or autumnal crops.

6 The same occurs if this happens at the rising of the Pleiades <note>original: Vergiliarum</note>; it destroys olives and vines, according to the testimony of Democritus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who also wrote on natural phenomena and agriculture.</note>, especially when Arcturus is setting at the same time.

God has balanced the world so that good things do not always overflow for everyone at once. We have seen in past years that while Saturn [♄] traveled from Aries [♈] to Libra [♎], there were sterile years; while it moved from Libra to Aries, the years were abundant.

10 When all the planets that are closer to the earth go into retrograde <note>Retrograde motion is an optical illusion where a planet appears to move backward in the sky; astrologically, it was thought to concentrate or alter the planet's influence.</note> in winter and hang over us longer, the winter becomes very warm; the summer will be burning hot, but only in proportion to how they retrograde, for they are always in opposition to the Sun. Therefore, in winter they are at the zenith <note>The point directly overhead.</note>, but in summer they are further away. However, they always add heat, especially when many of them move in retrograde at once.

For this alignment signifies the character of the entire month.

3 One must also consider the "angles" <note>In an astrological chart, the angles (the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli) are considered the most powerful points of influence.</note> following the position of the new or full moon, and the stars dominating the cardinal points, or the angles, and the new or full moon itself.

4 Likewise, consider the "applications" and "separations" <note>original: applicationes, & defluxiones; these terms describe planets moving toward or away from an aspect (a specific angular relationship) with one another.</note> of the planets and their specific properties.

5 And also the properties of the locations.

6 And which winds each star, and each part of the zodiac sign in which they reside, tends to stir up.

### *On the quarters of the month.*

### ARTICLE II.

1 The month, just like the year, has four quarters; these are determined not by the signs of the zodiac, but by the Moon's aspects <note>geometric relationships</note> to the Sun. For the Moon is to the month what the Sun is to the year.

2 It has periods of intensification and relaxation from the beginning of each quarter until the aspect changes. However, the start of every quarter serves as an indicator for the whole period, just as the Sun’s entry into the cardinal points <note>the Equinoxes and Solstices</note> acts for the quarters of the year. Other aspects increase or decrease these effects, much like lunations do within the quarters of the year.

3 Therefore, one must consider not only the status of the individual quarters, but also the sextiles <note>60° apart</note> and trines <note>120° apart</note>. In fast-moving affairs, even the twelfth aspect <note>the semi-sextile, 30°</note> and the octagonal aspect <note>the semi-square, 45°</note> should not be dismissed, as we wrote in the first book.

4 Likewise, consider the aspects of the Planets: for from their nature, the specific property of the effect is grasped, corresponding to the "familiarity" or affinity of the aspecting stars and the signs toward the air and the winds. It is very often true that the Moon, when beholding a certain star in a conjunction <note>original: synodo</note> or opposition <note>original: diametro</note>, produces the same effect when it reaches a different aspect with that same star as it did at the beginning—unless it is led astray by a new and far stronger atmospheric configuration.

5 Furthermore, the three days before or after a syzygy <note>the New or Full Moon</note> must be considered; for these are the indicators of all weather and storms. Indeed, those who...

## On the prognostics of days.

### CHAPTER V. ARTICLE I.

1 Daily intensifications and relaxations [of weather] are derived from the morning and evening rising and setting of the fixed stars, by which they usually convert the particular state of the air to their own nature. For example, when the *Vergiliis* <note>the Pleiades</note> are setting, the *Africus* <note>the Southwest wind</note> blows the following day. The *Etesiæ* <note>periodic Mediterranean summer winds</note> begin eight days before the *Canicula* <note>the Dog Star, Sirius</note> and last for forty days; and after these, the *Austri* <note>South winds</note> blow until the rising of Arcturus; after this, the *Eurus* <note>the East or Southeast wind</note> blows. Furthermore, *Favonius* <note>the West wind</note> opens the spring at the setting of *Fidicula* <note>the constellation Lyra</note>, and continues for eight days, as mentioned above.

2 The morning rising is the strongest, then the evening rising, then the morning setting, and finally the evening setting.

3 They produce different effects in different regions and at different times because the horizons are different; nor is the effect always the same in the same place due to a different aspect of the Planets. Likewise, some stars have power for one day, others for several, such as the *Canicula* for 30 days and Arcturus for 10.

4 The alignments <term>syzygies</term> of the Planets change the days.

5 When the Moon reaches the ascendant <term>horoscopus</term> <note>the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</note> of the Full Moon or New Moon <note>original: interlunij</note>, the air is usually changed.

6 Likewise, when the ascendant of the Full Moon or New Moon reaches a Planet that rules them through "direction" <note>an astrological timing technique where one degree or a set distance represents a period of time</note>, allotting 13 degrees and 11 minutes for each day.

7 The entry of Planets into the signs of their fall <note>the sign opposite that of their "exaltation," where a planet's influence is traditionally weakened</note> changes the weather.

# Prognostication specifically from the alignments <term>syzygiis</term> of the planets: and first from Saturn <note>represented by the symbol ♄</note>.

## ARTICLE II.

1 A conjunction of Saturn with Jupiter <note>represented by the symbol ♃</note>, according to the quality of the signs and the stars, affects the air for several days with clear skies, or rain, or winds: especially by the agreement of the Luminaries. However, in opposition <note>an aspect of 180 degrees</note>, the effect is less. In squares <note>90 degrees</note>, less. In trines <note>120 degrees</note>, less. In sextiles <note>60 degrees</note>, the least.

2 Saturn and Mars <note>represented by the symbol ♂</note> affect the air according to the nature of the signs for three days before and three days after their meeting: but they specifically cause hail. You shall rank <note>original: *graduabis*; to assign a degree of intensity</note> the aspects as described above.

3 Saturn joined with the Sun <note>represented here by the symbol ✶</note>, or in opposition, or in square, very often causes hail: but it always cools the air for a few days, more or less according to the quality of the zodiac signs.

4 Saturn joined with Venus <note>represented by the symbol ♀</note> specifically brings rains and cold: but nevertheless, this depends on the quality of the signs and the quarter of the season. Always understand it thus, and rank the intensity of the aspects.

5 Saturn works with Mercury <note>represented by the symbol ☿</note> according to the quality of the signs, since Mercury is ambivalent <note>original: *anceps*; meaning its influence changes depending on which planet it is near</note>: nevertheless, expect somewhat chilly winds depending on the season and the lunar cycle.

6 Saturn with the Moon <note>represented by the symbol ☽</note> always cools the air, and depending on the season, you shall predict frost and ice, or much moisture, and so on.

## From Jupiter.

## ARTICLE III.

1 Jupiter and Mars joined together specifically cause rains, lightning, and thunderbolts: but this is according to the quality of the signs, their proximity, their condition, and their configuration.

2 Jupiter with the Sun <note>✶</note> brings fair winds and lasting clear skies, unless other subsequent constellations interfere. But you shall rank the aspects by their strength.

## Prognostication concerning the hours of the days.
### CHAPTER VI. ARTICLE I.

1 Just as an age is divided into four trigones <note>groups of three zodiac signs</note>, and a year into four quarters, and a month into four cardinal parts: so the day is divided into four quarters corresponding to the year and month, occurring at the four cardinal points: namely morning, noon, evening, and midnight, in the four accidental angles.
2 Under the equator, one and the same wind blows from the east <note>the rising</note> to the west <note>the setting</note> in a circle by night and day, because the Sun, by its heat, thus leads the air and the waters of the sea around. Small variations occur at the extremities.
3 In the four quarters, the Sun, by a six-hour <note>original: "fexhoraria," likely hexhoraria</note> division of the 24 hours, makes the seas swell: for where heat is present, the water boils up and increases, and is diffused through the sides; and at the opposite point, those waters meeting <note>original: "occurfantes," likely occursantes</note> are raised up, so that at the same time, under the presence and absence of the Sun, elevations occur—just as in a boiling pot the water closest to the fire is raised, and simultaneously that which is furthest away at the handles, while it is depressed at the sides. And when the Sun changes its quarter, elevations and depressions occur subsequently until the circle is completed.
4 The Moon is not the cause of these motions, as Ptolemy thinks <note>referring to the 2nd-century astronomer Claudius Ptolemy</note>, since she is not capable of so much—especially during conjunctions <note>synods</note> when deprived of light, and at opposite points—but the Sun is. However, the Moon rules the motion of the growing Ocean <note>likely referring to the tidal variations beyond the basic solar cycle</note>.

### THIRD BOOK.
<meta>catchword: Growing</meta>

...of the growing [moon] for fifteen days, like the Moon, and for as many days of the decreasing. See our *Physiology* <note>original: "Physiologia," likely referring to the author's own treatise on natural philosophy</note>.

5 Just as the Sun acts in the sea under the equator, so it does in the air. And just as there is a six-hourly increase and decrease <note>referring to the tidal cycles</note> in the sea, so there is in the air; and other variations arise from the mixture of the planets and the fixed stars. For it is evident that in the morning a breeze blows from the eastern corner, as the Sun thins the vapors in the air and drives them into a heat. Similarly, in the evening, it blows from the west toward us and toward the Antipodes <note>people living on the opposite side of the Earth</note>. But at noon the air is still, because the central principle of heat is within it, not the flight of hot air; and in the sea the tide is stirred, because the direct Sun generates more vapors.

6 Outside the tropics, however, winds are produced in the same way according to the approach and retreat of the Sun.

7 Regarding the angles <note>the four main points of an astrological chart</note>, Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer and astrologer</note> says this occurs according to the Moon’s latitude toward the North <note>original: "Boream"</note> and the South. But if the Moon is beneath the earth <note>below the horizon</note>, what power does it have? Perhaps while it is above the earth, it inclines the solar vapor toward its own latitude, or impels it from its own, adding to the thinning and the heat.

8 The six-hourly arrangement seems to persist, so that just as the day began at the rising of the Sun, it lasts until midnight, and from midnight until morning.

9 The configuration of the planets and fixed stars in these angles <note>original: "cardinibus"</note> varies the day according to their own nature. For Saturn <note>♄</note> is of coldness; Jupiter <note>♃</note> and Mercury <note>☿</note> are of winds; Venus <note>original symbol: ✶, likely representing the Morning Star</note> is of heat; Mars <note>♂</note> is of rains with thunder, lightning, flashes, and hail; and the Moon <note>☽</note> brings all these things.

10 In the meetings of planets, the one who has more dignity <note>a measure of a planet's strength based on its zodiacal position</note> in the place of conjunction and agrees more with the stars positioned nearby is superior. Second, the one who has more influence in the following angle. Third, the one faster in motion. Fourth, the one closer to the angle. Fifth, the one who has northern latitude for us, or southern for those in the south. Sixth, the one who is more powerful in the location of the Light <note>original: "Luminaris," referring to the Sun or Moon</note> placed above the earth.

11 One must consider the general causes together—both the prior and subsequent—then the particular ones. For an effect is certain and great when the general causes agree with the specific ones signifying the same thing. They are uncertain and small when they do not agree; judge according to the prevailing factor.

12 Therefore, first consider under which triplicity <note>a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element</note> and anomaly the vapor <note>original: "fumus," literally "smoke," used here for atmospheric exhalations</note> exists; second, the preceding eclipses and comets; third, the quarter of the year in which the vapor occurs; fourth, the property of the month; fifth, the quarter of the month; sixth, the property of the day; and seventh, the six-hourly arrangement of the angles.

## CHAPTER VII. ARTICLE I.

1 After we have spoken about the effect and significance of the stars, it remains for us to consider the causes and signs following from them, and from the lower concurrent causes.
2 Forecasting from the "face of the sky" was approved not only by natural wisdom, but even by the Incarnate Wisdom of God in the Gospel <note>A reference to Matthew 16:2–3, where Jesus speaks of interpreting the sky: "When it is evening, you say, 'It will be fair weather, for the sky is red'"</note>. Therefore, let us not be burdened to speak of these things one by one.

->*Forecasting from lower signs derived from the Sun.*<-

### ARTICLE II.

1 If the Sun rises or sets free from haze, variation, or clouds, it promises clear weather for the day or night.
2 If it appears varied, flaming, shooting out red rays—whether direct or refracted—or if it forms **parhelia** <term>parhelia: "sun dogs," or bright spots in the sky caused by the refraction of light through ice crystals</term> in a cloud and produces reddish clouds, it then signifies fierce winds for those angles <note>the four cardinal points of the horizon</note> toward which those sightings were directed.
3 Likewise, whether the Sun is bright or dark <note>original: "niger," perhaps referring to an eclipse or heavy obscuration</note> at rising or setting, if it is wrapped in clouds, or surrounded by a **halo** <term>area: a ring of light or "threshing floor" around a celestial body</term>, or if those solar clouds appear on both sides with rays that are pale or black, it threatens storms and rains.
4 A circle around the Sun threatens wind from the direction where the circle begins to break.

## From the phenomena of the Moon.

### ARTICLE III.

1 **S**ome note the fourth day, others the third day after the **conjunction of the Luminaries** <term>synod of the Luminaries: the "meeting" or conjunction of the Sun and Moon, marking the New Moon</term>, believing that the winds and storms that begin then will endure through the entire month, as Virgil sings <note>A reference to Virgil’s *Georgics*, a famous Roman poem on agriculture and weather signs: "But if on her fourth rising... she sail through the sky with clear, undimmed horns, then that whole day... shall be free from rain and wind."</note>. But in truth, such a weather pattern is hardly extended to the fourth day of the month unless it is very strong, and not hindered by subsequent influences, and is given power by a **cardinal lunation** <note>referring to a New or Full Moon occurring near the equinoxes or solstices</note>. Everyone understands this to be the time when the Moon first appears above the horizon. Because of the "tortuosity" or "rectitude" of the zodiac signs <note>signs that rise more slowly or quickly relative to the horizon</note>, and the speed or slowness of the Moon itself, it may happen that she appears on the very day of the conjunction. Therefore, her omens are understood from the day of her appearance, even if it is the first day; but the actual effect is determined by the first planet she encounters, as was said before.

2 The Moon, three days before or after the New Moon, the Full Moon, and the **square** <term>square: an astrological aspect where two bodies are 90 degrees apart</term>, provides the serenity of a pure and thin light.

3 If she appears black, pale, and "thick" <note>likely referring to a hazy or obscured atmosphere</note>, she threatens rains and storms.

4 If she glows with a thin red light, and the circle of her orb appears clear—even in the part that is not illuminated <note>This refers to the phenomenon of "Earthshine," where the dark portion of the Moon is visible due to light reflected from the Earth</note>—and she seems to tremble, she stirs up the winds of her **declination** and **latitude** <note>referring to the Moon's specific coordinate positions in the sky</note>.

5 Let this same judgment apply to the dark moons, full moons, and squares.

6 Regarding the rising and setting of the Moon on the horizon, you shall observe and judge the same things that you do for the rising and setting of the Sun.

7 Furthermore, if the fifth-day Moon has blunt **horns** <note>the pointed tips of the crescent Moon</note>, she brings rain; if she has many sharp points, she brings northern winds; if the northern horn is so sharpened, she brings southern winds, especially if that same horn is twisted toward the South. The horn signifies the same thing we said regarding the whole orb, etc.

8 If a single **halo** <note>original: "area"</note> circles the Moon, gradually vanishing and thin, it promises fair weather. If there are two or three, it promises storms. If these are also reddish and "broken," they indicate turbulent winds; if they are misty and thick at once, they indicate snow; if they are lurid, black, and "torn," they signify both wind and snow, and are more violent the larger they appear.

9 You shall observe not only the Moon’s squares, but also her **trines** and **sextiles** <term>trines and sextiles: favorable astrological aspects where bodies are 120 and 60 degrees apart, respectively</term>, and her configurations with the planets. At those times, look at her horns, her halos, and her colors ranging between white and black. In this way, you will arrive at a judgment regarding rains, fair weather, and intermediate seasons.

## *From the phenomena of fixed and wandering stars.*
# ARTICLE IV.

1 The **halo** <term>area: the circular glow or "atmosphere" immediately surrounding a celestial body</term> around both the fixed stars and the wandering stars <term>wandering stars: the planets</term> portends effects according to the property of its color, following the nature of those stars. For example, if the halo is red, it portends the effects of Mars; if it is wan and blackish, the effects of Saturn; if clear, the effects of Jupiter, and so on. However, a Jupiter-like halo around a Saturnian star indicates a mixture of influences and requires a combined judgment. The same applies to the others.

2 We should observe the "turbulence" of the fixed stars, noting what color and size they appear to be. If they appear more splendid and larger than usual, wherever they shine, they stir up winds from that direction.

3 Regarding the **nebulous stars** <note>clusters of stars that appear as faint clouds to the naked eye</note> which are found in the Milky Way, in Orion, and especially in the **Manger** <note>original: *Præſepi*, also known as the Beehive Cluster (M44) in the constellation Cancer</note>: if they grow faint in a clear sky so that they escape one’s sight, or if they become so thick that they cannot be seen at all, they portend rain-clouds. If they appear pure and vibrating, they promise a turbulence of winds.

4 If the **Northern Donkey** <note>original: *Aſinus boreus*, a star in the constellation Cancer associated with weather lore since antiquity</note> is not visible, the North Wind will blow; if the **Southern Donkey** <note>original: *auſtralis*</note> is hidden, the South Wind.

5 The same may be said of the other small, nearby stars. For if the star to the south, or the north, or the east, or the west, or the one in the middle is hidden, a wind or a rain-cloud will arise from that direction. This is because a thin, windy vapor takes away the sight of them and is stretched out in that direction, or a thick vapor is rising there.

6 It is no wonder if nebulous stars draw forth clouds, even though they are actually clusters of hidden stars, as is made clear through the **Telescope** <term>Telescope: the author refers to the relatively recent invention (c. 1608) which proved that "nebulae" were actually composed of many individual stars</term>. For their faint light is well-suited to such vapors, just as the light of other stars is suited to other types. The prognosis based on color and disposition is proven here, since these nebulous stars signify such things more readily than others.

## *Concerning the portents of the heavens.*

### ARTICLE VI.

1 Portents, such as **comets** <term>crinita sidera: literally "hairy stars," the standard term for comets before they were understood as icy bodies</term>, always foretell winds and "squalor" <term>squalor: a technical term here for the parching of the earth</term>. These are more violent the larger they are and the more parts of the sky they appear in. "Squalor" is the harmful dryness of grasses and the wilting of lower-growing plants.

2 The breaking apart and "shooting" of **falling stars** <note>meteors</note>, if they burst forth from one corner of the world, send wind from that direction too. If they come from opposite sides, they stir up "battles of the winds" <note>conflicting wind currents or storms</note>. If they fall from all four quarters, they bring winter storms, lightning, and thunder.

3 If it lightens during clear weather, expect rain, cold, and wind—especially if the lightning comes from every part of the sky.

4 Morning thunder announces wind; midday thunder usually announces rain.

5 Summer thunder indicates wind more, while flashes of lightning indicate rain more.

6 Note that the meanings of portents in particular seasons are similar to the meanings of those same things explained above regarding their material and arrangement.

2 Darker and denser clouds are full of water. White, "hot" clouds occupying the entire sky on all sides bring snow if cold follows. Red clouds indicate winds, but thin ones indicate clear weather.

# THE FOURTH BOOK OF ASTROLOGICAL MATTERS.

## On Nativities. <note>A "nativity" refers to the moment of a person's birth and the specific planetary alignment occurring at that time.</note>

---

->Why the judgment of life and death is taken by Astrologers from the moment of birth.<-

### CHAPTER I. ARTICLE I.

<margin>1</margin>
After having spoken of those things which happen to nations and of the changes of the seasons, these judgments regarding those things which happen to the individual human being remain to be discussed.

<margin>2</margin>
Since progress and ends are hidden within their own causes and beginnings—and because the causes that were present at a human's first beginning, which is conception, are hidden from us—we shall judge a person's life, fortune, and death from those things present at their birth.

<margin>3</margin>
The birth is not the cause of the person, nor does it contain a power exactly like that of conception for producing effects, as <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note> said; nor is it the beginning of the human being in the same way that conception is the beginning of the embryo. For the "animation" <note>The moment the soul was thought to enter the body.</note>—if it occurs once the physical organization is complete—would be the beginning of the human being rather than the birth. Instead, birth is the beginning of life existing by itself and not joined with another. Nor does this beginning "cause" anything; rather, the causes found in the heavens at that moment indicate those causes that came before them, and they take up the governance of the life that follows.

<margin>4</margin>
For it is clear that <term>Jupiter</term> <note>In traditional astrology, Jupiter is the "Great Benefic," associated with growth, health, and a fair complexion.</note> in the <term>horoscope</term> <note>original: "horoscopo"; here referring specifically to the Ascendant, or the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note> does not make a newborn child "white" <note>Referring to a fair or healthy complexion or temperament.</note> unless a white temperament was already present in the womb. Therefore, the constellation of the one conceived and the one born are very similar. However, when the constellation is dissimilar, the newborn will not survive; for he is taken up to be ruled by hostile causes.

<meta>catchword: 5 He said</meta>

<summary>This page introduces the study of individual horoscopes (nativities), explaining that while conception is the true biological beginning, the moment of birth serves as the primary data point for astrologers to understand a person's life and destiny.</summary>

<header>OF ASTROLOGICAL MATTERS</header>

<margin>5</margin> Hermes spoke not unskillfully, therefore, when he said that the Moon at the time of birth is in the sign that was rising <note>The "ascending sign" or the sign on the eastern horizon.</note> at the time of conception. Haly <note>original: "Haly". Referring to Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arabic astrologer widely cited in Latin translations.</note> found this to be the case frequently, though not always.

<margin>6</margin> And for this reason, those born in the eighth and sixth months do not survive, because the Sun is in a sign that does not "behold" <note>In astrology, signs "behold" each other if they form a standard geometric relationship (aspect). If they do not, they are "disjunct" and provide no support.</note> the sign of conception, unless there is an <term>antiscium</term> <note>A point of shadow-symmetry across the solstice axis (the Cancer/Capricorn line).</note> or an <term>equidistance</term>. However, in the fifth, fourth, and third months, the fetus is not survive because it is not yet released nor strengthened enough to endure the suffering caused by the air; thus, seven-month babies have imperfect nails and unpolished skin. In our works on physics, we have discussed this differently.

# On the Ascendant. <note>original: "horoscopo". In this period, "horoscopus" specifically refers to the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon, known today as the Ascendant.</note>
## ARTICLE II.

<margin>1</margin> Just as it is extremely difficult (to the point that it was considered impossible by <term>Pico</term> <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, a famous Renaissance philosopher and critic of astrology.</note> and Saint Ambrose), it is also absolutely necessary to know the exact degree and minute of the ascendant; otherwise, we cannot correctly judge fortune, journeys, temperament, or diseases.

<margin>2</margin> Therefore—since we are often misled by clocks when astrolabes are missing, or by the voice of the person announcing the child's exit from the womb—it is necessary to identify the ruling planet at the location of the immediately preceding <term>conjunction</term> <note>The New Moon.</note> of the luminaries (the Sun and Moon), or at the location of the luminary existing above the earth if an <term>opposition</term> <note>The Full Moon.</note> preceded the birth. Or, if both are above the earth, the one in the east. Consider in which degree of any sign it is found; then consider the degree of the <term>Midheaven</term> <note>original: "medij cœli". The highest point of the zodiac at the moment of birth.</note> and the degree of the ascendant given to you under doubt (not measured by an astrolabe). Whichever of these locations has a degree number closer in numerical proximity (not by zodiacal position) to the number of that ruling planet in its sign, you shall establish that angle—whether the Midheaven or the Ascendant—under that number of the culminating or rising sign. This planet is called the <term>Animodar</term> by the Arabs.

<margin>3</margin> Where two planets are equal in number and lordship, take the angle according to the number of the sign in which the more powerful planet resides.

<margin>4</margin> The ascendant of the figure is also rectified through past accidents in the lives of those who are judged after birth, by taking note of illnesses or travels, which are indicated by the <term>direction</term> <note>A predictive technique where one degree of the zodiac is equated to one year of life.</note> of the ascendant at such a time. Add the directions of the significators of the Midheaven, and you will be more certain.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the precise timing of birth (rectification) and transitions into Article III, which addresses the practical construction of the astrological chart and the significance of the Twelve Houses.</meta>

<header>BOOK FOUR</header>

<margin>5</margin> Since every action has a beginning depending on a true cause, a subsequent principal part (when it cannot be pulled back), and an end in which the act is perfected—just as deliberating about killing, striking a mortal blow, and dying—so it is in birth, which is an act of nature. The beginning is when the head turns downward; the principal part is when the head emerges and breathes; and the end is when the entire infant has exited. Therefore, the <term>horoscopus</term> <note>original: "horoscopus". In this context, it refers to the Ascendant, or the specific degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note> ought to be taken from the principal part of the act, namely from the time when the infant begins to breathe. This is divided into three parts: the beginning of drawing in air, the middle when the air can be consumed vitally, and the end when respiration through the umbilical arteries ceases. For this reason, <term>Cardanus</term> <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath and astrologer who proposed using multiple charts for a single birth.</note> erects three figures <note>Astrological charts.</note>: namely of the beginning, the middle, and the end—the first for the starts of the native's events, the second for the middle stages, and the third for the end. Consequently, when these charts are in discord, the final outcomes do not match the beginnings. We have, therefore, a natural, a principal, and a final Ascendant. Thus, the birth of **Pope Paul V**, who poked his head out of the womb at the start of the day and, after his mother’s dire struggles, emerged entirely at the end of the day with the Sun hastening toward the west, should by no means be judged unless the Sun is placed in the east, or by using both methods.

<margin>6</margin> A birth time captured by an <term>astrolabe</term> does not always agree with the <term>Animodar</term> <note>A traditional method used to "rectify" or correct a birth time by linking the degrees of the previous New or Full Moon to the positions of the planets at birth.</note>, either because of fate, or the management of the midwife, or the father, or because the Planet of the Animodar is weak.

<margin>7</margin> Those who take the Ascendant through sorceries, superstitious tables, and the "Wheels of Moses" <note>original: "rotas Moysi". These were likely medieval or Renaissance numerical wheels or "lots" falsely attributed to Moses, used for divination rather than astronomical calculation.</note> falsely attributed to him, are deceivers and are themselves deceived.

-> ## On the construction of the figure, its division, and the inquiries in individual houses, and the signifying Planets. <-

### ARTICLE III.

<margin>1</margin> After you have found the Ascendant or the <term>medium coeli</term> <note>The Midheaven, or the highest point of the zodiac at the time of birth.</note>, from which the other angles and <term>domicilia</term> <note>The "Houses" of the astrological chart.</note> are known (as was said in the first book), you shall not proceed by "lots" or chance. Instead, choose in the heavens the appropriate signifying Planets for the questions at hand, as well as the places and the lords of those places. Thus, from their state in relation to the position of the world, the Sun, the birth-chart, their configuration, motions, the quality of their light, and their aspect, you shall judge the success or failure of the event, as well as its time, magnitude, and quality.
