# BOOK FIVE.

...to a general comet, or great conjunctions, or another event decreeing the ruin of a city, and to a celestial arrangement causing the ruin of a ship. Those who become one in some way—whether by city, friendship, kinship, shared lodging, navigation, or military service—are subject to the same evils and goods. For this reason, many are spared by changing their location: and many escape in that same place whose <term>aphetae</term> <note>the "life-giver" or specific points in a birth chart used to determine lifespan</note> are strongest. If [Pico della] Mirandola <note>original: "Picus"; referring to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous philosopher who wrote a massive critique of astrology</note> had considered this, he would not have condemned Astrology in such a manner.

<margin>4</margin> If the general constitution <note>the overarching astrological state of the world or region</note>, whether good or bad, is weak, those who have good or bad <term>genitures</term> <note>individual birth charts or horoscopes</note> are affected, and they change their aphetic places with the constellation, or are in a sufficient aspect <note>the geometric relationship between planets</note>.

<margin>5</margin> If the general constitution is stronger, those who change [places] and do not have a repugnant <note>conflicting</note> geniture are affected.

<margin>6</margin> If it is even stronger, those who have excellent genitures for good or ill [are affected], and they only change in their processes <note>astrological progressions used to time events</note>.

<margin>7</margin> If it is very strong, those who only change in their processes [are affected].

<margin>8</margin> If it is extremely strong, those who have opportunistic genitures [are affected], even if they do not change in their processes.

<margin>9</margin> If it is the most powerful of all, everyone who agrees in place and group [is affected], such as the Turks under **Osman I** <note>original: "Ottomano Primo"; the founder of the Ottoman Empire</note>, and the Romans under **Julius Caesar**.

<margin>10</margin> Therefore, the Astrologer must be highly skilled in history, as well as **cosmography** and **chronology** <note>the study of the world's regions and the measurement of time</note>, so that he knows the laws and customs of nations, their temperaments and climates, and under which constellations those laws and customs were introduced. He must be able to measure durations, and know under which **anomaly**, **eccentricity**, **obliquity**, **apsis**, **triplicity**, **great conjunction**, and **comet** the beginnings of customs, laws, cities, and governments took place. For in this way, he will easily conjecture regarding a wife, character, occupation, temperament, and type of death, by comparing particular genitures to universal constitutions, just as one compares the cold of **Saturn** (♄) with the [winter] quarter of the year.

<margin>11</margin> It seems that God alone understands all causes, great and small, past and present, as well as the contributing causes, their mixtures, moderations, the duration of their effects, their temperaments, and their applications toward a specific outcome placed within the harmonic series of fate. We, however, know very few; yet we must not stop for that reason, but rather venture forth with God as our leader, who loves neither our ignorance nor our arrogance. *In great things, to have willed [is enough]* <note>original: "In magnis voluisse [sat est]"; a common Latin sentiment suggesting that the attempt at a noble goal is worthy even if human knowledge is limited</note>.

### ARTICLE II.

1. First, consider the region in which the person was born and the <term>trigon</term> <note>one of the four groups of three zodiac signs (Fire, Earth, Air, Water) that rule specific parts of the world</note> to which it is subject. Next, consider the laws and customs, then the city, then the family of the person born. Then consider their age: for we shall pronounce one thing regarding the wife of a Turk and another for a Christian; one thing for an Italian and another for a Dane; and one thing for a boy, another for a man, and another for an old man. The same applies to their way of life and complexion <note>original: "colore"; literally color, but referring to the "humoral" appearance or temperament</note>, where you will also take the family into account.
2. Just as there are four quarters in a year, so there are distinctions of ages in a human being, acting as general causes. From there, we arrive at particular details: just as we look to months and days in the year, here we look to specific times through <term>directions</term>, <term>progressions</term>, and <term>transits</term> <note>three primary methods in astrology for predicting the timing of future events based on the movement of planets after birth</note>.

---

->*On the System of Ages*<-

### ARTICLE III.

1. The Moon governs the first four years from birth, because she matches the infantile humidity of the body, its weakness, sudden growth, inconstant health, and a mind where everything is unformed and unrefined—much like the Moon's own variability and her newness [at the start of a cycle], and because she is closer to our Earth.
2. Mercury governs the next ten years. He begins to settle the mind; he grants speech and the elements and seeds of intelligence and learning; he displays and prepares the specific qualities of character and interests, and initiates the child into their first exercises.
3. Venus governs the following eight years, up to the age of 22. She stirs and fills the seminal pathways, stimulates the urge for sexual union, and incites one to occupy themselves with insanity and wretched desire, wandering in error and blindness even with eyes wide open.
4. Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the foundational authority for Western astrology</note> believes that the Sun governs the following youthful age for 19 years, up to the age of 41; for after the wantonness of Venus, [man becomes] master of himself...

...[the Sun] grants the use of reason to the mind, instills a desire for household property and honor, and sets a limit to life; once childish vanity, inconstancy, and sins are removed, it brings about a love of modesty, integrity, and law. To me, however, it seems that Mars rather rules the subsequent period of governance up to the 36th year: for true integrity and majesty are not acquired before this time, nor is the love of law; instead, Martial <note>referring to qualities of the planet Mars: aggression, energy, and drive</note> strengths and desires prevail, and then until the age of 56, the Sun shows its aforementioned indications.

5. For Mars (says Ptolemy <note>original: "Ptolemæus"; Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, which defined the traditional seven ages of man</note>) rules for fifteen years; he brings sadness and malice to life, fills the soul and body with cares and pains, instilling a sense and thoughts of a fading age, and urging one toward some memorable deed to be laboriously accomplished before death. So he says. But in truth, that ambition belongs more to the Sun. It is the nature of Mars to grant unregulated desires, such as strong physical powers and savage angers, all of which tend to cease at age 41 rather than begin. Likewise, no age is more dangerous than that from 22 up to 37.

6. Jupiter rules for twelve years until age 68, commanding one to gradually turn away from a laborious and turbulent way of living, and to take up a more decent, dutiful, quiet, and holy path. He teaches us to admit the truth about ourselves, and, having set aside ambition, to understand that human honors and pleasures are nothing, nor is knowledge certain. Those of us who previously seemed wise to ourselves in some matter, he makes doubtful and "Socratic" <note>original: "socraticos"; referring to the philosopher Socrates, who famously claimed to know only that he knew nothing</note> in that same matter. Likewise, he teaches us to do nothing precipitously, to advise and console others, and to be eager for honor, praise, and generosity, combined with frugality, modesty, and natural honesty.

7. Saturn rules extreme old age after the 68th year, for 30 years until the age of 98, when the body's strengths appear hindered and cooling, and nature—languishing in more vigorous pleasures—is deprived of its vigor <note>original: "neruis"; literally nerves or sinews, representing physical strength</note>. Life is then shaken, miserable, and weak, exposed to injuries, and peevish toward all movement due to the sluggishness of one's powers. Then, a lack of confidence in one's own strength expels trust in external goods, from which greed follows. We wish for the promises of religion to be true, desiring another life and striving for its acquisition; we accuse those devoted to the present life, and we become talkative, so that we may at least seem to be alive in that way, or so that we may leave behind a memory of ourselves in lasting words.

# APPENDIX.

## *Examination of the previous statements concerning the ages.*

### ARTICLE IV.

1 Ptolemy <note>original: "Ptolemæus"; the 2nd-century astronomer whose "Tetrabiblos" established the traditional seven ages of man</note> assigns all the remainder of life to Saturn, but since in our own times men have been seen to "grow young again" and live up to 300 years—such as a certain man from Taranto, a nun from Sagunto, another from Astorga, and a Frenchman, all of whom Delrio <note>Martin Delrio (1551–1608), a Jesuit scholar famous for his "Disquisitions on Magic"</note> mentions in his book on magical investigations—in such a way that they recovered youthful color, strength, and voice: it must be said that life sometimes returns to the Moon after the period of Saturn. This happens when all the planets have agreed at the time of the "senile directions" <note>a technical astrological method for predicting life events in old age</note> to restore the lunar age, with the <term>hylegial places</term> <note>original: "loca aphetica"; specific points in a birth chart used to determine the length of life</note> being occupied by the life-giving planets and with certain others looking on favorably. Nor can it happen, even after 36,000 years, as Albumasar <note>the Latinized name of Abu Ma'shar, a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer</note> ignorantly thinks, that all the rotations of the heavens return simultaneously to their original points, as we have taught in the *Metaphysics*.

2 It should be known that Ptolemy preserved the order of the planets according to his own dogmas, which does not sufficiently align with the truth, nor with the observations of the Pythagoreans or of Copernicus. For Mercury and Venus do not have an epicycle <note>a small circular orbit whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one</note> beneath the Sun, but they actually surround the Sun: so that they are found sometimes above it and sometimes below it. It is certain, however, that Venus is closer to the Earth at its lowest point than Mercury is. Therefore, the age following the lunar stage should rather be dedicated to Venus. And indeed, if you consider the moisture of the temperament, it suits Venus and not Mercury; if you consider fertility, it suits Mercury and not Venus, for the power of procreation begins in the 14th year. But even then Mercury has its part: for young youths are almost like hermaphrodites <note>suggesting a blend of male and female qualities before full maturity</note>, which they receive from Mercury. Therefore, it is true that the position of the planets must be considered, and that Mercury and Venus are joined in the governance of the ages. But because Mercury approaches us more frequently, and the first steps of language begin from the fourth year, he himself shall be the ruler until 14. Venus, however, is the second lord: from age 14 to 22, Venus holds the mastery, but Mercury accompanies her; for this reason, we also then acquire more of the sciences and the art of debate. Furthermore, I have given Mars fif-

...the ten following years for the stated reasons, even if it is more distant <unclear>from</unclear> us. For it too surrounds the Sun, and sometimes it is closer to us than the Sun is, such as when it is <term>acronychal</term> <note>original: "acronyctius"; referring to a planet that rises in the east just as the sun sets in the west, putting it at its closest point to Earth</note> in its opposition: as **Tycho**, the most diligent of astronomers, well observed. <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), whose planetary model was a hybrid between the geocentric and heliocentric systems</note>
Yet all these ages are produced by the Sun, just as the four quarters of the year are produced through the actions of innate heat, as we have taught in the *Physics*. They are attributed, however, to the planets whose constitution of heat they most closely match: thus spring is also given to Venus, summer to Mars, winter to Saturn, and autumn to Mercury; as are their diseases and influences in the heavens, on the earth, and in the sea.

3 Note that **Ptolemy** assigned the durations of the ages to the planets according to the return of the planets to the same position of their <term>epicycle</term> <note>a small circle around which a planet was thought to move, while the center of that circle moved around a larger circle</note> relative to the Sun, with the exception of Mercury and the Sun. To the former, he gave half of its time on account of its weakness; but to the Sun he gave the lunar cycle, when it returns in its epicycle and with the Zodiac to the same point. This is because the Moon herself carries the Sun's powers to us more directly, acting as the Sun's sister. We, however, think these matters are so only in part, since we lack perfect knowledge. Nevertheless, we are certain that the ages vary, but we do not know the exact limits of that variation—just as we know the turning points of the seasons but only grasp them approximately. Jupiter (♃) however, retained the years of the Zodiac.

4 One should know that age is not to be divided the same way in all regions. For those who live in the tropics, especially in the kingdom of **Guinea**, extend their life to forty years: in their fortieth year they are decrepit old men. Similarly, for those who live near the poles, the morning heat <note>the vital, life-giving heat associated with youth</note> is dulled and extinguished by the cold; whereas for those in the tropics, it is exhausted outward by excessive heat. Therefore, in the tropics, the Moon will have two years, Mercury five, Venus six, the Sun ten, Mars seven, Jupiter eight, and Saturn will possess the remainder. In our own regions as well, some are precocious in intellect, others in sexual lust, according to whether they are granted a more powerful Mercury or Venus; or perhaps because the planet is at its <term>lowest apse</term> <note>original: "ima abside"; the point in a planet's orbit where it is closest to the Earth</note>. Furthermore, some become "Martial" <note>aggressive, vigorous, or warlike</note> after 22 years, while some do so after 41, as Ptolemy thought, depending on the proximity and vigor of Mars. I propose that this is something to be considered in birth charts, though I have not yet examined it fully.

## On directions declaring the times of events.
### CHAPTER II. ARTICLE I.

1 **A**fter you have considered what is suitable for each age, under which region, and under what laws and upbringing, just as we consider the four seasonal dispositions of that year, we shall then proceed to particular years—just as we proceed there from years to months, and from these to days.

2 Years are indicated by <term>directions</term> <note>original: "directionibus"; a predictive technique where the chart is "rotated" at a rate of roughly one degree per year of life</note>, <term>progressions</term>, and the <term>ingresses</term> <note>original: "ingressibus"; the entry of a planet into a specific sign or sensitive point in the birth chart</note> of planets into the places of the direction and the progression of the <term>aphetas</term> <note>original: "aphetarum"; from the Greek 'apheta' (releaser), these are the points in a horoscope that "release" or trigger life events and determine the length of life</note>: just as months are indicated by monthly progressions and directions.

3 There are five principal aphetic subjects of directions and progressions: the Sun, the Moon, the Part of Fortune, the <term>Horoscope</term> <note>original: "horoscopus"; in this era, the term specifically refers to the Ascendant, or the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth</note>, and the <term>Midheaven</term> <note>original: "medium coeli"; the highest point of the southern sky at the time of birth, representing career and public life</note>.

4 We consult the Sun for dignity, glory, honors, magistracies, and the father; the Moon for the soul, the senses, the wife, the mother (sometimes), and for health and honor; the Part of Fortune for riches of every kind, inheritances, and acquisitions; the Midheaven for children, actions, friendships, and promotion to religious office or a doctorate, etc.; and the Horoscope for the body, health, disease, and things done with the body, such as travels.

5 Since there are several aphetas located in different positions, it happens that at the same time a person may be fortunate in spirit but not in body, or in children but not in wealth. Therefore, no one is blessed in every respect, nor does human weakness allow for the highest degree of good or bad fortune all at once.

6 These are the permanent significations of the aphetas. But sometimes they can be "directed" for diseases and other effects for which they are the indicators; for instance, the Moon may be directed toward a "cloudy" spot for blindness, toward Mars for miscarriage, or toward Mars in Libra for leprosy, etc. Mercury can also be directed for the mind and learning; Jupiter for liberty, etc. However, these have meager strength compared to the five aphetas and they vary the outcome very little. Therefore, they are usually not considered. When, however, they are "Lords of Time" and hold primary authority in the <term>nativity</term> <note>original: "genitura"; the birth chart or the moment of birth</note>—such as the **Alcocodem** to the Arabs—then they can be directed, because they possess a strong indication. <note>original: "Alcocodem"; an Arabic astrological term for the "Giver of Years," the planet that determines the expected lifespan of the native</note>

7 We do not direct the causes of events, which are the indicators, nor the "qualifiers" (who are the Lords of the places in which the aphetas are found), nor the stars configured with them which increase or decrease...

### ARTICLE II.

1 You shall consider three things in any direction. First, the **subject**, which we also call the **significator**. Second, the **promissor**. Third, the **dispositor**, or "qualifier." The **significator** is one of the aforementioned <term>aphetas</term> <note>original: "aphetis"; the life-giving points used to determine the length of life and major events</note>. The **promissor** is a planet, or fixed star, or a <term>ray</term> <note>original: "radius"; an astrological aspect or beam of light from a planet</note>, or a location encountered in the direction, by which some event is "promised" upon the meeting of the apheta with it: such as death or high rank. The **dispositor** is the one who most closely precedes the place of the direction by body or ray, who governs until the body or ray of another star is encountered. There is also a second dispositor, the <term>lord of the term</term> <note>original: "dominus termini"; the planet that rules the specific degree-segment or "bound" of a zodiac sign</note>.

2 When hunting for the span of life, we consider the **interemptors** <note>original: "interemptores"; "killing" planets or points that indicate the end of life</note> encountered. But in leading the other aphetas, we consider all stars met by body or ray, whether hostile or friendly: such as by opposition, conjunction, square, octagon, <term>antiscion</term> <note>original: "antiscio"; a point of mirror-image symmetry across the solstice points</note>, equidistance, trine, and sextile.

3 Therefore, the planet most closely preceding the apheta by body or ray disposes and rules the first period of the direction. When such a planet is not present, the planet placed in the same degree (<term>partile</term>) <note>original: "partiliter"; occurring at the exact same degree and minute</note> with the apheta by body or ray disposes it. Along with that planet, the lord of the term also governs; the lord of the term governs alone when no planet precedes or accompanies the apheta. It rules for as many years as there are <term>right ascensions</term> <note>original: "ascensiones rectæ"; a measurement of time/distance along the celestial equator</note> between it and the succeeding star, or the new terms, when the apheta is in the <term>Midheaven</term> <note>original: "medio cœli"</note>. However, when it is in the horoscope, it rules for as many years as there are <term>oblique ascensions</term> <note>original: "obliquæ ascensiones"; a measurement of time/distance that accounts for the viewer's specific latitude</note> for that region.

## *On the method of directing the aphetas.*

### ARTICLE III.

1 There are various methods of "directing" among Astrologers, and so far experience has not sufficiently clarified the truth. For the **Arabs**, establishing the <term>houses</term> <note>original: "domos"; the twelve divisions of the sky representing different life areas</note> from equal sections of the <term>Zodiac</term> <note>original: "Zodiaci"</note>, also count the degrees in the Zodiac: and however many degrees are between the <term>significator</term> and the <term>promissor</term>, they assign that many years until the manifestation of the effect. Others, however, divide the celestial equator, and perform the direction based on its degrees. Others use the vertical circle. Others use a parallel circle, following **Porphyry** <note>a 3rd-century philosopher and astrologer</note>, using the degree of the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>the sun's path</note> rising between the horizon and the meridian circle. Others, following **Alcabitius** <note>an 10th-century Arabic astrologer, also known as Al-Qabisi</note>, divide the hourly times—both day and night—into three parts, and from these they construct the ascending houses above and below the horizon: from which they describe the opposite houses. Because of this, they perform various types of directions, each according to his own theories. **St. Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> concedes in his commentary on *On Generation and Corruption* <note>original: "2. de gen. & cor."</note> that lifespans are to be measured in the <term>oblique circle</term> <note>the path of the zodiac as it appears slanted relative to the observer's horizon</note>.

2 This, however, is certain: the times between the promissor and the significator must be considered. Therefore, measure how much time is required for the promissor to rise to the significator, and assign fifteen years of time to one hour of <term>ascension</term> <note>the movement of a point as it "rises" or moves through the sky</note>, and one month to four minutes of an hour of ascension, and you shall give seven and a half days to one minute. And then, divide a minute into sixty parts, which you will distribute across those seven and a half days, and you will arrive at the specific days and hours of the event.

3 When the <term>apheta</term> is in the **Midheaven** <note>original: "M. C." or "Medium Coeli"; the highest point in the chart</note> or in the **Bottom of the Sky** <note>original: "I. C." or "Imum Coeli"; the lowest point in the chart</note>, everyone agrees that the direction must be made through <term>right ascensions</term> <note>measurements of the sky's movement relative to the equator rather than the horizon</note> placed between the promissor and the significator. For those indicate the hourly parts, where every single degree is surely the fifteenth part of an hour, which therefore signifies one year: because the Sun completes one day by traveling through one degree. And since two hours are required for one sign (containing 30 degrees) to rise through the peak of heaven, and since right ascensions vary because of the variation in the Sun's <term>obliquity</term> <note>the tilt of the Earth's axis</note>, we shall hereafter use the tables described by **Tycho** <note>Tycho Brahe, the famous Danish astronomer whose precise observations revolutionized the field</note>.

4 But when the <term>apheta</term> <note>original: "apheta"; the "life-giver," a point in the chart used to determine the length of life</note> is in the <term>horoscope</term> <note>original: "horoscopo"; the Ascendant or first house</note>, or in the seventh house, while the degrees of the <term>Zodiac</term> <note>the belt of constellations through which the planets move</note> rise between it and the <term>promissor</term> <note>original: "promissorem"; the planet "promising" a certain influence or event</note>, the same number of degrees does not rise simultaneously on the celestial <term>equator</term>. This is due to their "straightness" and "crookedness" <note>referring to right ascension (straight) and oblique ascension (crooked)</note>. Therefore, the direction must be calculated through hourly times. These correspond more closely to the degrees of the equator and its oblique ascensions along the zodiac. In different regions, however, these ascensions vary; for this reason, you shall work using the oblique ascensions of your specific region, and for every degree found, you shall assign one year. You may work by these same means when directing an apheta in the West [the descendant], since the descensions there are the same as the opposite ascensions; signs that rise "straightly" descend "crookedly," just as the <term>M.C.</term> <note>Medium Coeli, or Midheaven</note> and <term>I.C.</term> <note>Imum Coeli, or Bottom of the Sky</note> are the same in their right ascensions.

5 If, however, the apheta should be located between the angles <note>in the "succedent" or "cadent" houses</note>, you shall work through the ascensions of the circles of position. There are eight of these placed between the angles, each having thirty degrees; or you may work through the descensions of the circle in the opposite places.

6 If the apheta is in the seventh house and the <term>M.C.</term> is the promissor, but the promissor is actually between the <term>M.C.</term> and the horoscope, bring the apheta to the <term>M.C.</term> through the ascensions of its own circle; then bring the promissor to the <term>M.C.</term> through right ascensions, and combine both times. You shall do the same for the spaces surrounding the <term>I.C.</term> The spaces surrounding the horoscope and the seventh house do not require the mixing of times, but are calculated through the unvaried ascensions of the circle of position.

7 These operations are performed using the tables of <term>Regiomontanus</term> <note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg, a 15th-century German mathematician who revolutionized astronomical calculations</note>, by the <term>astrolabes</term> <note>complex handheld instruments used to map the stars and tell time</note> of the specific region, or on a solid sphere by counting the ascensions. But <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian authority on astronomy</note> easily resolved all these matters through right ascensions and hourly times.
> "Seek," he says, "the hourly times of the <term>apheta</term>, and by those divide its distance from the <term>M.C.</term> in right ascensions; the result is the number of the distance of the hours of the <term>apheta</term> from the <term>M.C.</term> itself. Having found the difference of the hours of the <term>apheta</term> from the <term>M.C.</term>, seek the hourly times of the promissor—diurnal [by day] if it is above the earth, nocturnal [by night] if it is below the earth. Multiply these times by the hours of distance of the <term>apheta</term> from the <term>M.C.</term> If the <term>apheta</term> was between the horoscope and the <term>M.C.</term>, subtract the result from the difference of the right ascension of the promissor and the <term>M.C.</term> Or, if the <term>apheta</term> is between the <term>M.C.</term> and the western angle [the descendant], and the promissor is between the <term>M.C.</term> and the horoscope, add them. Or, if both are between the <term>M.C.</term> and the west, subtract the difference of the right ascensions from the product. The result is the number of degrees and minutes of the direction."

8 Indeed, according to this teaching of <term>Ptolemy</term>, it seems the chart ought to be erected according to the dogma of <term>Alcabitius</term> <note>a 10th-century Arab astrologer whose system of house division was standard in Europe before Regiomontanus</note>. <meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding "directions"—the mathematical methods used to predict when specific events will occur in a person's life. It contrasts the methods of the ancient Greeks (Ptolemy), the medieval Arabs (Abenafre), and the modern Renaissance authors like Regiomontanus and Cardano.</meta>

<page-num>202</page-num>
<header># ASTROLOGICAL MATTERS</header>

Since <term>Abenafre</term> <note>original: "Abenafre"; likely referring to the influential 11th-century Arab astrologer Albohazen Haly, or Ibn Abi al-Rijal</note>, in the division of the houses, follows <term>Regiomontanus</term> <note>a prominent 15th-century German mathematician and astrologer who revolutionized house systems</note>, you should also follow his directions. These differ from the <term>Ptolemaic</term> <note>referring to Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century authority on astronomy and astrology</note> directions by one or two years and are calculated through the poles of the circles.

9 In this business, there is great uncertainty. For <term>Firmicus</term> <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman author</note> and the <term>Arabs</term> claim that they have always predicted correctly by directing within the <term>Zodiac</term>. <term>Cardanus</term> <note>Gerolamo Cardano, a 16th-century Italian polymath</note>, following Ptolemy, adheres to his directions because they were proven to him through many experiments. All the moderns agree with Regiomontanus and claim that they can predict the timing <term>to the nail</term> <note>original: "ad vnguem"; an idiom meaning "with perfect precision," as a sculptor checks a joint with a fingernail</note>.

10 I truly believe that this controversy cannot be resolved. This is because directions never proceed exactly according to the given rules, but are instead advanced or delayed. Sometimes this is due to the nature of the <term>terms</term> <note>original: "terminorum"; specific subdivisions of each zodiac sign ruled by different planets</note>; for before the <term>significator</term> <note>the planet or point representing the person</note> reaches a malefic planet, if it falls into the two or three preceding terms of that planet, the person incurs its harm early. Sometimes it is accelerated because of the rays of the <term>apheta</term> <note>the "life-giver" point in the chart</note> reaching the location of the direction before the actual body of the planet does, or due to the strong rays of the <term>promissor</term> <note>the planet "promising" a future event</note> preceding its body. Sometimes also a fixed star of the same or opposite nature in the location of the direction multiplies its force, or else removes, advances, or delays the event. Sometimes also a good or bad <term>progression</term> <note>original: "progressio"; a secondary method of advancing the chart to time events</note> does the same, advancing or delaying the year. Sometimes it is the <term>ingress</term> <note>the entry of a planet into a specific sign or house</note> of good or bad planets into the locations of the direction, progression, or aphetic points. Occasionally, the general state of the heavens <note>original: "constitutio generalis"; the current alignment of all planets</note> advances an event if it agrees, or delays it if it disagrees. For this reason, if the person's age is unsuitable, a direction for marriage is useless. At other times, a comet or an eclipse configured with the aphetic points is mixed into the directions and progressions. There is no such thing as a "certain" direction; even if someone has predicted the timing correctly beforehand, once the effect actually happens, he cannot be certain that it came from that specific direction, since other causes concur. We might just as easily say that the event ought to have been advanced or postponed. Likewise, Ptolemy always teaches that a planet in the <term>angles</term> <note>the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses, the most powerful positions</note>—especially at the very beginning of the angles—and swift in its course, produces its effect in youth and quickly. But in <term>cadent</term> <note>weak houses that "fall away" from the angles</note> houses and at the ends of the angles, or when slow, it produces its effect in old age or late. Therefore, a direction will not be certain simply from its meeting with the promissors, unless that meeting happens early or late according to how the significator was situated from the start. When these two factors disagree, return to the progressions and <term>transits</term> <note>the current movement of planets over the birth chart</note> that agree with the radical <note>original: "rationi radicali"; the root or birth chart logic</note> calculation. You shall consider all the aforementioned differences, and you shall also predict from the progressions; when the significator is in the center and moving swiftly, it advances the time of the direction. Therefore, use the progression. The same applies to the centers.

11 Regarding other matters pertaining to the verification of directions, see Book 4, Chapter 4.

## *On Annual Progressions.*

### CHAPTER II. ARTICLE I.

1 Not only do the degrees of the equator between the <term>aphetas</term> <note>points in a birth chart that represent life and vitality, often called the "hyleg"</note> and the <term>promissors</term> <note>planets or points that "promise" a specific event to the apheta as they move toward it</note> signify years—since they are derived from the daily motion of the Sun, which represents its own annual cycle—but the subsequent signs also have their own governance over the years. Each sign represents one solar year within a lunar year <note>this refers to the symbolic "profection" where one sign of the zodiac equals one year of life</note>.

2 Therefore, count thirty degrees from the <term>aphetic</term> places at the start of a person’s life. You shall make the lord of the degrees in between (if it is one sign) or the lords (if there are multiple signs) the governors of that year. Continue this through the sequence of signs up to twelve, and from there you will return to the first sign. These lords of the progressions shall govern alongside the lords of the directions.

3 Thus, in making a judgment, the hierarchy is as follows: first place belongs to the <term>lord of the age</term> <note>the planet ruling the current stage of life, such as the Moon for infancy</note>; second, the more powerful <term>lord of the direction</term>, combined with its partner; third, the lords of the progressions; fourth, the <term>radical lord</term> <note>the planet that ruled that point in the original birth chart (the "radix")</note> from which the progressions began; fifth, the natal position of that lord; sixth, the place of the progression; and seventh, any planet currently entering these places. Such a planet can be so powerful that it draws the entire meaning of the prediction to itself, as we shall explain.

4 In examining a direction and progression: First, see whether the progression moves toward <term>benefics</term> <note>favorable planets like Jupiter or Venus</note> or <term>malefics</term> <note>challenging planets like Mars or Saturn</note>, which either harm or help. Second, consider the condition of the planet at the hour it takes up governance of the progression—specifically if it is <term>oriental</term> <note>rising before the Sun</note>, increasing in light, in its own <term>dignity</term> <note>a sign where the planet is naturally strong, like its "home" or "exaltation"</note>, or the opposite. Third, check if such a governor is favorable to the event in the <term>radical figure</term> <note>the birth chart</note>. For if it was in <term>opposition</term> <note>an aspect of 180 degrees, indicating conflict</note> to the apheta or its ruler, it is ill-suited to govern that specific effect during the progression. Fourth, consider whether that lord of progression or direction was fortunate or unfortunate in the <term>root</term> <note>the birth chart</note>. Fifth, observe when it meets benefics during its time of governance, or forms an aspect with the apheta, or is otherwise strong; in those cases, the cause will be helped. But if it meets discordant malefics, or views the apheta poorly, or is <term>inconjunction</term> <note>lacking a major geometric relationship</note>, or <term>under the rays</term> <note>so close to the Sun that it is invisible and weakened</note>, or <term>retrograde</term> <note>appearing to move backward</note>, then it will cause harm.

5 When the annual progression spans parts of two signs, the lords of the first sign will govern first for a corresponding number of months and days...

### *On Monthly Progress.*

#### ARTICLE II.

1 Monthly progress is twofold. The first is taken from the <term>aphetic</term> <note>the "life-giving" points in a birth chart, such as the Sun, Moon, or Ascendant</note> places at the beginning of one's life, assigning twenty-eight days to each subsequent month according to Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century scholar whose "Tetrabiblos" is a foundational text of Western astrology</note>, just as one zodiac sign is assigned to each year.

2 The second type of monthly progress is found by dividing the sign of the <term>annual progression</term> <note>a technique where the chart is "rotated" by one sign for every year of life</note> into twelve parts. Consequently, it will happen that two degrees and thirty minutes are assigned to a single month. In that case, observe the lords of those signs and degrees, just as we described for the annual progression. From this, the instability and variety of human affairs is continually revealed through so many concurrent causes.

3 The Arabs <note>referring to the influential medieval Islamic astrologers whose works were translated into Latin</note> assign thirty days to the monthly process; otherwise, a year would be composed of thirteen months. Cardanus <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath and physician-astrologer</note> agrees with them and thinks Ptolemy’s text should be corrected, so that in place of 28, the number 30 should be set; and where it says "two days and a third," "two days and a sixth" <note>original: "duos dies cum triente... aut sextante"</note> should be placed instead. Yet Ptolemy’s text does not actually admit such a correction. Therefore, I believe that just as the Sun possesses the aforementioned monthly "arbiters" derived from the sign of the annual process, so too, by lunar logic, there must be other arbiters based on the subsequent <term>lunations</term> <note>the period of time between two new moons</note>. For just as we judge diseases by the motion of the Moon—not by starting from the <term>syzygies</term> <note>conjunctions or oppositions of the Sun and Moon, i.e., new or full moons</note> or full moons, but from the place where the Moon was at the moment of <term>decumbiture</term> <note>the moment a patient first takes to their bed with an illness</note>—so we judge the stages of life starting from the lunar position. And since the Moon returns to that same spot in twenty-eight days, we shall take the monthly arbiters according to the lunar days. There is no harm in making thirteen months while dividing the twelve signs. However, since the Moon adds extra hours to those twenty-eight days, and there are twelve lunations in a year plus eleven days, the aforementioned ratio does not strictly follow. For this reason, it is necessary to always calculate lunations separately, and to take the lords of the places where the Moon is perpetually situated, and to perform other <term>reversions</term> <note>astrological "returns" where a planet returns to its birth position</note> which, though more intricate, are not irrational. For the Moon measures time secondarily to the Sun, and our life is measured by both lunar and solar time. If this is so, look incessantly to the lords of the Moon’s position, and always take them as the arbiters of events in relation to the <term>aphetas</term>, together

## *On Daily Progress.*

### ARTICLE III.

1 There also seems to be a twofold process for daily progressions. The first occurs if you make the twelve signs progress from the day of birth through twelve years, and simultaneously through twelve months, and finally through thirty days, assigning one sign to every two and a half days, according to the Moon’s <term>mansion</term> <note>one of the 28 divisions of the sky through which the Moon passes daily</note>.

2 The second type of progress occurs if a partition is made of that lunar process of twenty-eight days such that we grant two and one-third days to the governors of a single sign, as Ptolemy <note>the 2nd-century astronomer whose "Tetrabiblos" defined Western astrology</note> used to say. But if the text is faulty, we will say what was said above: we shall divide the monthly sign into thirty days, and simultaneously divide the thirty annual degrees into two and a half for each month; and for the thirty days, we shall divide two and a half degrees, subdivided into 150 seconds. Then we shall consider the state of the lords and the <term>ingresses</term> <note>the moment a planet enters a new sign or house</note> of the planets, as mentioned above.

3 We perform such exquisite calculations in vain, since other causes vary the timing of events, as has been said. Paris Caesararius <note>likely an astrologer of the period; the text notes his interactions with the high-ranking Farnese family</note> once predicted the year, months, and days of the papacy for Cardinal Farnese <note>Alessandro Farnese, who became Pope Paul III in 1534</note>; he correctly divined the year, but nothing further.

## *On Ingresses.*

### CHAPTER III. ARTICLE I.

1 Planets entering the <term>aphetic</term> <note>the "releasing" or life-giving points in a chart, such as the Sun, Moon, or Ascendant, used to calculate length of life</note> places—or rather, the places reached by the direction and progress of these aphetic points—contain the decrees of time. Saturn governs general periods because of its slowness; Jupiter governs annual ones, since it remains in one sign for about that long; the Sun, Mars, Venus, and Mercury govern monthly periods, since they stay in a sign for roughly that duration (though Mars exceeds this); and the Moon governs daily periods, since it remains in one sign for only two and a half days.

2 The decree of the entering planet lasts as long as the planet itself

[The planet] remains in the same sign. Saturn, therefore, will cause affliction for thirty months; for eclipses <note>original: deliquia</note> cannot exert influence beyond that time. Jupiter provides help for one year, and so on for each planet according to the rate of their stay in a sign; and for this reason, they are most powerful when they are retrograde <note>when a planet appears to move backward in the sky, often interpreted as intensifying its influence</note>.

3 The general <term>arbiters of time</term> <note>the specific planets or points designated as rulers over certain periods of a person's life</note> are more powerful for finalizing a decree after the arbiters of age have been considered. The arbiters of specific matters either assist or resist through their harmony or discord. These are the masters of <term>direction</term> <note>a method of predicting life events by moving planets at a rate of roughly one degree per year</note> and <term>progression</term>. Truly, the transits of those entering a sign either increase or decrease the effect.

4 Indeed, I have found through experience that transits are so powerful that I have predicted many things more certainly from them alone than from direction and progression. Even <term>Cardanus</term> <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an influential Italian physician and astrologer</note> admits this. For "a fly that is present hurts more than a lion that is absent" <note>original: Plus enim nocet praesens musca, quàm absens leo; a proverb suggesting that immediate, physical influences outweigh distant, symbolic ones</note>. Hence <term>Hermes</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Western astrology</note> and <term>Galen</term> <note>the famous physician of the 2nd century</note> predicted life and death in illnesses based on these transits alone. That comets, eclipses, and great conjunctions occurring in <term>aphetic</term> <note>points in the birth chart related to life force and longevity</note> places—as well as in direction and progression—can change or cut short the whole course of life is beyond doubt, since these are transits of the general state of the heavens. 

But it is clear that Saturn <note>original: ♄</note> prolongs evil when it retrogrades in the same sign. In my case, in the direction of the Sun and Venus <note>original: ♀</note>, the mistress of my birth, Saturn was in Libra <note>original: ♎</note> in the year of Christ 1599. It was also in opposition to the direction of my Moon and in its <term>antiscia</term> <note>a "shadow" or reflection point across the solstice axis, used to find hidden planetary influences</note>. It held me in prison for fifteen years, and there is no end yet. I omit what it did to others who were executed or tortured alongside me. Therefore, transits do not only increase an effect, but they achieve something more. No eclipse preceded my misfortune that was contrary to me, but there was a comet near the earth that was not sufficiently observed, as I have mentioned elsewhere.

# BOOK FIVE.

## On the success and failure of the outcome.

### ARTICLE II.

1 Whether an event will be successful <note>original: fœlix</note> or unsuccessful <note>original: infœlix</note> must be considered from those planets which are the masters of the event. This is determined by their own natural and mixed inclination to do well or poorly. Likewise, it is determined by the friendship and enmity they held from the beginning with the significators <note>the planets representing specific life areas</note>, and among themselves with those they are configured with.

## *When the outcome will shine forth more certainly and clearly.*

### ARTICLE III.

1 An effect will shine forth more clearly when the signs of the monthly and annual <term>progression</term> <note>a method of symbolic time-keeping where each day or year after birth corresponds to a specific period of life</note> are configured with the <term>aphetic places</term> <note>original: locis apheticis; the sensitive points in a chart that "release" or trigger life events and vitality</note> for better or worse, and according to the ingress of the <term>Luminaries</term> <note>the Sun and the Moon</note> and the planets into the signs of annual, monthly, and daily progression.

2 Likewise, if the ingress of the planets agrees with the aphetic places from the beginning of the <term>nativity</term> <note>original: genituræ; the original birth chart</note>, and according to the direction and progression, and they are well-configured, it aids the outcome of the matter proposed. If they disagree in nature and in their "ray" <note>the aspect or angle of light cast by a planet</note>, those entering stars passing through in a hostile manner cause harm—though not as much if they are not quite so poorly configured.

3 If, for example, at the beginning of the year the principal places of progression—and especially the Moon—fall into the locations of the <term>malefics</term> <note>traditionally "unlucky" planets, such as Saturn or Mars</note> in the <term>root</term> <note>original: radicis; the birth chart</note>, or if a bad "return" occurs through the circle, then death will happen in that year, or a misfortune related to the type of principal place signified.

4 Therefore, first see whether an effect is promised in the root chart by the general significator; then we will hunt for the time through the ages and directions. If the progression also reaches a matching sign in that time, a powerful effect will follow in that year without hindrance, especially if the ingress of the planets helps in the places of progression and directions—or even if the Sun or Moon alone looks upon them. But if the malefics then hinder (even if the sign is good), or if the benefics <note>lucky planets, like Jupiter or Venus</note> hinder (if the sign is bad), one must seek a more favorable sign following in that cause. But if the contrary planets signified in that found sign

## APPENDIX.

1 **A**ll configurations signifying something good or bad in the <term>radix</term> <note>the "root" or original natal birth chart</note>, such as <term>epilepsy</term>, dignity <note>social rank or status</note>, etc., which have been discussed in this entire book, are also valid in <term>progressions</term>, <term>directions</term>, and <term>ingresses</term> <note>three different methods of symbolic and actual time-keeping used to predict when a birth promise will manifest</note>, if they are similar; however, they do not operate as effectively unless they first existed in the root chart. For in that case, the effect will be powerful.

2 Consider in every inquiry: **First**, the place of the inquiry, which can also be a <term>significator</term> <note>the planet or point that "points to" the subject being asked about</note>, such as the <term>M. C.</term> <note>Medium Coeli or Midheaven; the highest point in the chart, signifying career and honor</note> and the <term>horoscopus</term> <note>the Ascendant or rising sign</note>, and for servants, the 12th [house], etc. Sometimes it is the place of the significator, such as the place of the Sun signifying honor, or the horoscope [signifying] temperament; for these describe the essence of the matter sought, while their signs describe the substance or matter and genus. **Second**, their lords <note>the planets that rule the signs where these points are located</note>, who describe the quality of the matter. **Third**, the stars configured [to them], which increase or decrease, certify or take away. **Fourth**, the four more principal planets in order, such as the Moon [☽], Jupiter [♃], and so on. **Fifth**, the <term>Almuten</term> <note>the planet that holds the most combined essential dignity (strength) in a specific degree of the zodiac</note>, who rules over the principal places. **Sixth**, the more powerful one, that is, the one closer to the center of a principal angle <note>the "angles" are the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses; planets here are considered most active and influential</note>. **Seventh**, the one who rules, or is more powerful, whether it be a <term>benefic</term> <note>a "good-doer" like Venus or Jupiter</note> or a <term>malefic</term> <note>a "bad-doer" like Mars or Saturn</note>. **Eighth**, their disposition relative to the world, to the Sun, to the <term>apsides</term> <note>the points in a planet's orbit where it is nearest or farthest from the center</note>, to latitude, to <term>dignity</term>, to <term>fall</term> <note>a sign where a planet is weakened</note>, to <term>peregrination</term> <note>a state where a planet has no specific dignity or strength, like a wandering stranger</note>, etc. **Ninth**, the mixture with other planets and fixed stars. **Tenth**, which planet is elevated above the others. If it is a benefic and fortunately situated, judge all things for the best in the inquiry; if it is not fortunate enough, judge them to be less good. If it is a malefic, powerful and discordant, judge the worst; if it is weak, it harms less. If it rules the place over which it is elevated, the good things will be frequent but minor; if it is opposed, they will be frequent and greater. If it is <term>peregrine</term>, the effects will be great but not frequent. If the place over which a malefic is elevated is also the sign of its <term>fall</term>, it signifies rare misfortunes, yet the greatest ones; nevertheless, it will retain reputation and profit.

3 For the effect, note: planets are either in their own dignities, or in mutual ones, or in common ones, and they are divided into those that disagree and those that agree. In their own places they are strong, and they overcome a planet that is in a foreign place. In their own places, they gaze upon one another with a hostile aspect: in mutual falls they bring an unconquered evil, if one alone resists in fall, and...

However, it will obey the other like a servant in a master's house, unless it is oppressed by it, as if by a thief—just as Mercury [☿] when <term>combust</term> <note>so close to the Sun that its influence is "burnt up" or obscured</note> acting as a host to the Sun [☉] in Scorpio [♏].

If one planet is in the place of the other's fall, it will be hindered by it, but only slightly.

Planets in <term>common signs</term> <note>Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces</note> signify agreement, such as Saturn [♄] and Mars [♂] in Aquarius [♒], and simultaneously signify the favor of the people.

In a mutual fall, they are enemies, and neither will fulfill any promise made to the other.

If they are in different <term>triplicities</term> <note>the four groups of signs belonging to the same element: Fire, Earth, Air, Water</note>, the means used to achieve an end will be inconsistent, and men's judgments of them will vary.

If one planet is in its own triplicity, the promise of the other will not falter.

<term>Peregrine</term> <note>original: "peregrini"; planets wandering in signs where they have no essential dignity or "home" comforts</note> planets indicate difficulty in obtaining and completing a matter.

Note these things in the <term>radix</term> <note>the root or birth chart</note> and in the timed processes.

## *On Revolutions.*

### ARTICLE V.

<margin>1</margin> The Arabs observe the return of the Sun to the exact same point it occupied when a person was born; thus they erect a chart and make judgments from it, just as they do from the birth chart, to predict the events of the entire year. This practice is used by all astrologers who calculate both annual and world revolutions.

<margin>2</margin> Cardano <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an influential and controversial Italian physician and astrologer</note> judges this "revolution" chart to be useless. First, because progression according to the natural succession of the signs is more reliable, as it is similar to <term>directions</term> <note>a method of timing where one degree of movement equals one year of life</note>. Second, because the revolution is unequal. For instance, in the coming year, Libra [♎] does not necessarily follow in the <term>horoscope</term> <note>here meaning the Ascendant or rising sign</note> where I currently have Virgo [♍]; instead, it might be Sagittarius [♐] or another sign. Likewise, in a progression, all planets are taken in turn, but in a revolution the same ones often recur if the same sign is rising, or if the <term>aphetae</term> <note>the "givers of life" or primary significators in a chart</note> have moved into the same signs.

<margin>3</margin> But these reasons actually recommend progressions; they do not exclude the revolution. For the succession of signs is not the primary requirement here, but rather the radical status of the Sun. Since the Sun is the prince of the planets, its position varies the configurations of the other planets and the heavens. Otherwise, you would have to accuse the heavens of error because they do not return to the exact same point and position on the same day, hour, and minute...

### BOOK FIVE.

...stopping the Sun every year. The second reasoning is of no value, for events are mixed, and the successions of things are anticipated or postponed; for this reason, the signs are as well. Nor do we require anything except what the Sun does in the layout of the world with all the planets at the time of its <term>revolution</term> <note>the "Solar Return," or the moment the Sun returns to the exact degree it occupied at birth</note> back to its root. Regarding the third point, nothing stands in the way of the fact that the same planets sometimes succeed each other, for the events are likewise similar. A revolution does not have as much power as a <term>procession</term> <note>the movement of planetary points over time through "profections" or "progressions"</note>, yet it is not without influence. It also indicates the entry of planets into various places and their configuration to the world, and to the locations of directions and processions; wherefore it, as it were, renews life, and not without reason was the birthday celebrated in ancient times.

4 Therefore, once the <term>figure</term> <note>the astrological chart for the year</note> is drawn, we shall examine all the <term>aphetas</term> <note>original: "aphetas," the planets or points designated as "life-givers" or "releasers" that govern the vitality of the subject</note>, just as in the <term>genesis</term> <note>the original birth chart or nativity</note>, along with the lords of the places, the signs, the configured stars, and what they portend, according to the reasonings previously established for birth charts.

5 We shall derive the monthly processions of the signs from this chart, imitating the <term>radical</term> <note>the "root" or original birth chart</note> chart, and we shall compare everything just as we did in that one, which there is no need to repeat now.

6 When, however, it happens that the locations of the root chart are the same in the revolution—especially the <term>horoscope</term> <note>the Ascendant, or the sign rising on the eastern horizon</note>—expect a renewal of life, as it were, provided that the <term>benefics</term> <note>favorable planets, specifically Jupiter and Venus</note> are present and the direction and progress do not conflict.

7 But if they are at opposite locations, or in <term>cadent</term> <note>houses that "fall away" from the main angles of the chart, usually considered weak or hidden</note> or <term>inconjunct</term> <note>signs that do not "see" each other by standard aspect, creating a lack of harmony</note> places, you shall be fearful, just as the logic of progressions has also declared.

8 Consider the same regarding the return of the life-givers to a good or bad position.

# ON ASTROLOGICAL MATTERS
## SIXTH BOOK.
### On sidereal elections. <note>The practice of "electing" or choosing the most auspicious time to begin an endeavor based on the positions of the stars.</note>

### *That by natural reason and divine authority, the science of elections is true and necessary for natural philosophers, and not to be condemned.*

### CHAPTER I. ARTICLE I.

<margin>1</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'N' containing elaborate foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>
All the arts declare that the science of choosing the right time <note>original: "electione temporis"</note> is necessary for performing human operations correctly and successfully—especially those arts which do not work alone, but in partnership with nature. For unless a Physician takes the Moon into account and the <term>critical days</term> <note>specific days during an illness when a change or "crisis" is expected, historically tied to lunar cycles</note>, he kills while he heals, or fails to correctly complete what he has prepared. Sailors too, if they commit themselves to the sea in winter during a harmful <term>lunation</term> <note>a period of the Moon's cycle; here referring to an ill-aspected New or Full Moon</note>, are not immune from drowning. If a farmer sows grain in the month of August in our region, he will not reap a harvest. Therefore, he chooses the autumn quarter; if he adds a fertile lunation to this, he will do even better. Nor will he prune his vines in December, but in February; nor will he plant them in September, but in March. Travelers, if they do not consider beforehand the winds and rains and their causes, are afflicted by many evils. Solomon said rightly: *To everything there is a season.* <note>original: "Omnia tempus habent," quoting Ecclesiastes 3:1</note>

God also chose the times for those things He intended to do with us—namely, when He foreknows that we are prepared. For *when the fullness of time had come, He sent His Son.* <note>original: "quando venit plenitudo temporis misit filium suum," quoting Galatians 4:4</note> And in the sacred [writings]...

the Scriptures, <note>original: "litteris"</note> He always says that He chooses a time for judging, for showing mercy, for moving nations, and for multiplying them. But this is the difference between God’s choices and our own: He Himself creates the times He chooses, and He established the stars as the causes of those times. He is subject to no times, nor to fates, nor stars, being Himself the creator of times, fates, and stars, as Saint Augustine teaches regarding that passage:
> [ My hour has not yet come. ] <note>John 2:4. Augustine argues that Christ was not subject to the stars, but chose the timing of his own miracles.</note>
We, however, do not create the times we choose, but in our bodies, we are subject to them and serve them. For I cannot make it not rain, nor make the heat of summer cease. Yet with our minds we *use* those times, rather than serving them—unless the mind voluntarily subjects itself to the physical urges of the body, and thus, as a consequence, to the stars and the causes of fate. But whoever clings to God, the author of the stars, escapes fate, being elevated above <term>secondary causes</term> <note>In medieval philosophy, God is the "Primary Cause," while natural forces like the stars are "Secondary Causes" that influence the physical world but not the soul.</note>; as Saint Thomas excellently teaches in the first part of his treatise on fate, and as experience and reason demonstrate. For he who enjoys the friendship of the King does not fear the executioner, <note>original: "lictorem"</note> nor the King’s slaves and ministers. Thus, **the wise man will rule the stars.** <note>A famous medieval proverb: "Sapiens dominabitur astris."</note>

<margin>3</margin> The Lord says:
> You know how to judge the face of the sky, but how do you not judge this time of the Messiah? <note>Matthew 16:3. Jesus rebukes those who can predict the weather but cannot see the signs of his arrival.</note>
And rightly so. For just as we ought to foresee events from the physical stars, so too should we judge the times of God’s judgments from the "prophetic stars" of the Holy Scriptures. Wherefore He rebukes them in Jeremiah, saying that
> the turtle-dove, and the swallow, and the stork, and the kite, have known their time; but my people have not known the judgment of the Lord. How then do you say, "We are wise, and the law of the Lord is with us"? <note>Jeremiah 8:7–8.</note>
Therefore, Astrology should be embraced by us as a ladder to prophecy, if only because of the example of animals for which the Lord reproached us. Pliny also considers the same thing when he relates that ants cease their work during the <term>interlunium</term> <note>the "New Moon" period when the moon is invisible in the sky</note>, and many animals sense the course of the stars beforehand; however, they are affected by the physical sensation <note>original: "passione"</note> of those stars, not fortified by reasoning as a wise man is regarding primary and secondary causes. We do not, therefore, subject our free will to the stars; rather, we use our knowledge of the stars in our "elections" to save ourselves from the evils brought on by them and to find a way to obtain good things. This is as Albertus Magnus teaches in his *Mirror* <note>The *Speculum Astronomiae*, a 13th-century text defending astrology.</note> and as Saint Thomas also teaches: even demons, through their great knowledge, freely choose certain constellations for the works they begin. Let these points suffice against the <term>Astrologomachi</term>. <note>Literally "those who fight against astrology."</note> It is superstition, however, when we subject our work to demons rather than stars (as a cook subjects a pot to the fire), and when sorcerers and Necromancers treat stars as causes or signs when they possess no such power. ## On Sidereal Election in Sacred Matters.

### CHAPTER II. ARTICLE I.

<margin>1</margin>It is necessary to speak individually about all "elections" <note>In astrology, an "election" is the practice of choosing the most auspicious moment to begin a specific activity.</note> that require consideration of the stars; first, however, regarding those that pertain to the soul, then those concerning the body, and finally those regarding external goods and business matters.

## *Whether prayer requires consideration of the stars.*

### ARTICLE II.

<margin>1</margin>The Arabs place the <term>Head of the Dragon</term> <note>Also known as the North Node of the Moon, this point in a horoscope was traditionally associated with increase, favor, and spiritual growth.</note> in the <term>Midheaven</term> <note>Latin: *Medium Coeli* or M.C.; the highest point in the sky at the moment of the chart, representing one's aim or relationship with the divine.</note> and Jupiter in a favorable position; thus they believe they are heard by God in their prayers. They could also add the "flow" of the Moon as it moves from Jupiter to a <term>sextile</term> aspect <note>A harmonious 60-degree angle between planets.</note>.

2 It can be proven that prayer requires consideration of the stars: for Solomon, in the Book of Wisdom, teaches that one should worship at the rising of the Sun, and rise before the light for prayer. Nor is reason lacking for this: for from the East the Sun always rises together with the stars Mercury and Venus, which affect the soul. For this reason, the dawn is dedicated to the study of philosophy—being "most pleasing to the Muses," as the proverb goes—and as Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), an influential priest and philosopher who sought to reconcile Platonic philosophy and astrology with Christianity.</note> writes to students. 

Likewise, all ancient Christian temples have their door in the West and the altar in the East. The Hebrew Rabbis desire the same. Likewise, the sect of the Turks <note>A common early modern term for Muslims.</note> requires prayer three times a day, as the Psalmist says: "In the evening, in the morning, and at noon I will announce your praise." The sect of the Sufis <note>original: "Sofiorum"</note> in Persia prays seven times, just as David says: "Seven times a day I have spoken praise to you." 

This the Christians observe in the seven <term>canonical hours</term> <note>The set schedule of daily prayers performed by clergy and monks, including Matins, Lauds, and Vespers.</note>. Astrologers, however, claim these hours are dedicated to the seven planets, just as the seven days of the week bear their names, as do the seven ages of the world, the seven seals, the seven bowls, the seven trumpets, and the seven ages of the Church described in the Apocalypse by Saint John. Likewise, David chose the dawn for the praises of God. And we sing:
> [ Now that the star of light has risen, let us pray to God. ] <note>original: "Iam lucis orto sidere, Deum precemur." A traditional hymn for the hour of Prime.</note>
and elsewhere:
> [ At midnight I rose to confess to God. ] <note>original: "Mediam noctem ad confitendum Deo." A reference to Psalm 119:62.</note>
as the monks do in their morning offices.

-># BOOK SIX.<-

...they do this, when the great star <note>original: "sidus magnum" - referring to the Sun</note> agitates the air and lower things less, and all is silent. Likewise, Saint Ambrose says that the body ought to imitate the soul in praying so that the prayer may be effective—by kneeling, just as the soul humbles itself, and by stretching the hands toward the stars, just as the soul extends its devotion. The heavens, however, act directly upon the body and indirectly upon the soul, as Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> testifies.

<margin>3</margin> I respond that prayer, in respect to God, requires neither place, nor time, nor stars, nor the health or position of the body. On the contrary, God hears the troubled even more, even if they are in the belly of a whale <note>A reference to Jonah</note> or in the underworld. For He is everywhere, and He does not need "secondary causes" <note>The physical laws or celestial bodies through which God's will is normally mediated to the world.</note> to hear us. In respect to ourselves, however, if you look at the soul, prayer does not need the stars. For the soul is not a body, but consists of power, wisdom, and love—the metaphysical <term>primalities</term> <note>Campanella’s philosophical concept of "Primalities" (Prototypi) identifies Power, Wisdom, and Love as the fundamental attributes of all being.</note> by which bodies are ruled. Therefore, wherever and however it may be, the free soul is heard and is not hindered by bodies. 

If, however, you consider the body, into which the soul is infused (but not confused <note>meaning the soul is present in the body but maintains its distinct essence</note>), it does require consideration of the stars, place, and time. For when a person is under violent physical influence, they are distracted from prayer. Likewise, when full of food, or entangled in other business, or when raving or insane, or pressed by some other passion, the body hinders the soul. Therefore, prayer is approved in the night, where there is no distraction, and during fasting and vigils, when the soul is not troubled by vapors nor weighed down by the flesh, as Saint Jerome teaches by citing <term>Galen</term> <note>A famous Greek physician whose medical theories dominated Western medicine for centuries; Jerome uses him to show that physical health affects spiritual clarity.</note>. 

To the first point, therefore, it is answered that we worship beautifully at the rising of the Sun, not because God is only present there, but because light comes from there, gladdening the soul and inviting it to contemplate the beauty of God, while it soothes and refines the bodily senses; in this, Venus **♀** and Mercury **☿** also participate <note>In astrology, Venus and Mercury are often close to the Sun (oriental), adding their qualities of harmony and intellect to the morning hours.</note>. Nevertheless, it remains true that a good man can pray in any location and be heard. I say the same regarding the placement of temples and the singing of the Church at the rising of the "star of light." 

To the third point: whether you pray three times or seven, the number itself does not commend us to God, but rather our devotion. He who always prays through his words and deeds is better. We use, however, the <term>seven canonical hours</term> <note>The traditional schedule of daily Christian prayer (Matins, Lauds, etc.).</note> dedicated to the actions of Christ and the gifts of the Holy Spirit; not, however, dedicated to the planets—except as signs, not as causes—of prayer, of gifts, and of our offering to God. For it is fitting that the works of God be consistent with Him, and that bodily things agree with spiritual ones, yet the physical world does not dictate the law to the spiritual. And thus it must be said of days, ages, and trumpets: that all things are in harmony.

# On the choice of timing in philosophizing.
## ARTICLE III.

<margin>1</margin> In the pursuit of philosophy, morning study is praised if Venus ♀ and Mercury ☿ are <term>oriental</term> <note>rising in the east before the Sun, which was thought to increase their active, outward influence.</note> to the Sun. I, however, study at all times, although I prefer the morning hours (provided I have slept well), when I have a purer sense, clouded by no vapors <note>referring to the "fumes" of digestion which were thought to rise to the brain and cloud the mind.</note>, and a mind sharper and more capable for contemplation. Whatever you begin, however, make sure that the <term>aphetic</term> <note>From the Greek "aphetes," the "giver of life." In an astrological chart, these are specific points that govern the vital force and success of an undertaking.</note> places of your <term>nativity</term> <note>original: "genesis" - the birth chart or the moment of a project's "birth."</note> are well-disposed toward the business you have started.

<margin>2</margin> Whatever you take up in your mind, see which of the planets it corresponds to. For **Saturn** ♄ governs firmness, perseverance, the deepest doctrines, and theological and metaphysical secrets. **Jupiter** ♃ governs civil and canon laws, justice, practical affairs, politics, morality, liberality, and magnificence. **Mars** ♂ governs fortitude, victory, wrath, depraved loves, bitterness, false speech, slander, and such things. **The Sun** <note>represented by * in the source text</note> possesses the peak of all virtues contained in magnanimity: honor, ambition, majesty, sovereignty, medicine, and the like. **Venus** ♀ governs oracles, beauty, mercy, delights, jests, and so on. **Mercury** ☿ governs commerce, the publication of books, physical sciences, Rhetoric, and all rational doctrines, as well as Geometry, Astrology, patronage, industry, and cleverness. **The Moon** ☽ possesses sociability, embassy, inconstancy, variability, and the other qualities we have mentioned regarding different character traits. 

Therefore, when you begin something suitable to a certain star in matters concerning the soul, place that star in the <term>ascendant</term> <note>the sign rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of beginning.</note> or the <term>midheaven</term> <note>original: "medio coeli" - the highest point of the zodiac at that moment.</note>, strong, oriental, and in its own <term>dignity</term> <note>a state where a planet is in its own sign or exaltation, making it more "dignified" or powerful.</note>. Ensure also that it is not discordant in its aspect or conjunction with the <term>apheta</term> which signifies such an outcome in the root of your nativity. But it is better to commend yourself through prayer to the Author of the stars.

## On the choice of timing in the governance of the body.
### CHAPTER III. ARTICLE I.

1 Similarly, from the conditions of the body, you can recognize which planet is dominating you at that time: for the "heavy" planets make one slow. But **Saturn** ♄ does so with dejection, pain, and lofty, brooding thought; **Jupiter** ♃ makes one slow with majesty, without pain, but rather joyful and just; **Mars** ♂ makes one heavy with ambition, leaping into quarrels, swellings, and insolent words. The other planets make one mobile: either with majesty, like the **Sun** ☉; or with charms and allurements, like **Venus** ♀; or with agility and dexterity, like **Mercury** ☿; or with great variability and softness, like the **Moon** ☽.

2 Choose your lunch and dinner only when you are hungry, for this is better than any observation of the stars. But if you are able, place the <term>horoscope</term> <note>The Ascendant, or the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note> in a good position relative to the world, and with a good <term>aspect</term> <note>The angular relationship between two celestial bodies.</note> of the Moon applying to it: just as in <term>evacuation</term> <note>referring to purging the bowels or other medicinal cleansing.</note>, we want the Moon to be waning; we desire the same in walking, provided the Moon applies to <term>benefics</term> <note>The "helpful" planets, Jupiter and Venus.</note> or encounters no <term>malefics</term> <note>The "harmful" planets, Saturn and Mars.</note>.

3 Go to sleep with the Sun and rise with the same, if you live under the equator; but while there is still light above the earth after the Sun has set, you may go about your business; and while the dawn is rising, anticipate the day.

4 In regions where the day is not equal to the night, if the climate is very humid, go to sleep early and rise late; use many lights in place of the Sun while you are awake. If the weather is dry and temperate, you shall work in the morning and evening; you shall rest at noon and at midnight.

5 Humid bodies, and those who suffer from joint pains <note>likely referring to gout or arthritis.</note>, should lunch well with the Sun but dine sparingly with the Moon; since at night the Moon herself increases the humors and flows of fluid, and sends them into the joints. Dry bodies that are unable to sleep should dine well and lunch moderately.

## On choices regarding physical medicine.
### ARTICLE II.

1 While the Moon is in <term>ruminant signs</term> <note>original: "signis ruminantibus" - the "cud-chewing" zodiac signs: Aries, Taurus, and Capricorn. In medical astrology, these were thought to cause medicine to be vomited back up.</note>, take medicine that evacuates through the upper parts; in humid signs, take that which evacuates through the lower parts.

2 While **Saturn** ♄ or the **Sun** ☉ is in <term>conjunction</term> or <term>opposition</term>, abstain from purging medicine and <term>phlebotomy</term> <note>The practice of bloodletting to balance the humors.</note>, except where the severity of the disease is urgent. However, beware of that exact moment in acute cases; in all others, avoid the day before and the day after.
